sentences.text: Yes — in the Belgian Interuniversity Research on Nutrition and Health cohort followed for 10 years, a low serum chloride level was associated with higher cardiovascular mortality: the adjusted risk ratio for CVD death for subjects with a serum chloride level of 100 mmol/l or less compared with those above that limit was 1.65 (95% CI 1.06-2.57) in men and 2.16 (95% CI 1.11-4.22) in women.

In that cohort, Cox regression analysis identified serum chloride level as one of the strongest predictors of total, cardiovascular disease (CVD) and non-CVD mortality, independently of age, body mass index, sex, smoking, systolic blood pressure, total and high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, uric acid, serum creatinine, serum total proteins and intake of diuretics.

The relation was independent of levels of other serum electrolytes and was similar for men and women, and analysis of adjusted risk ratios across four groups defined by baseline serum chloride revealed a decreasing log-linear dose-response relation to total and cardiovascular mortality.

These results are based on 4793 men and 4313 women, a random sample aged 25-74 years and free of symptomatic coronary heart disease at baseline, with serum chloride measured among other electrolytes and 10 years of follow-up for subsequent cause-specific mortality.
As an observational cohort association, this finding does not establish that altering serum chloride levels would change cardiovascular mortality risk.

The cited evidence is mixed on whether oral endotracheal intubation efficacy is impaired in the helicopter environment: in-flight intubation took significantly longer than intubation in the control setting, but the difference in appropriate endotracheal placement between the two settings was not statistically significant.

In flight nurses' manikin intubations, the mean time required for in-flight intubation was 25.9 +/- 10.9 seconds, significantly longer than the 13.2 +/- 2.8 seconds required in the control setting (ANOVA, F = 38.7, p<.001).

All intubations performed in the control setting were placed correctly in the trachea, whereas there were two (6.7%) esophageal intubations in the in-flight setting; the difference in appropriate endotracheal intubation between the two settings was not significant (chi 2 = 0.3; p>0.05).

The comparison was made with manikin intubations, not patients: flight nurses each performed three manikin intubations in both study environments, on an emergency department stretcher and in-flight in an MBB BO-105 helicopter.

Longer term outcome after stroke was examined in a cross sectional follow up study in south east London of people who had their first in a lifetime stroke in 1989-90 aged under 75 years, using a structured interview questionnaire together with measures of impairment, disability, handicap and general health; the mean interval between the stroke and follow up was 4.9 years.

The scales used in that follow up assessment were the hospital anxiety and depression scale, mini mental state examination, Barthel index, modified Rankin scale, London handicap scale, Frenchay activities index, SF36, Nottingham health profile, life satisfaction index, and the caregiver strain index.

Barthel index scores at this long term follow up correlated with general health and wellbeing measures, with rank coefficients of r = -0.189 (sleep dimension of the Nottingham health profile, not significant) to r = -0.840 (physical mobility dimension of the Nottingham health profile), r = -0.563 with the hospital anxiety and depression scale depression component, and r = 0.361 with the life satisfaction index.

The study compared and correlated individual Barthel index scores with scores on other outcome measures; the correlations were not uniform across dimensions, ranging from weak or non-significant for emotional and sleep domains to strong for physical domains, which is the reported basis for questioning whether the Barthel index alone is an adequate measure of long term outcome.
Rank correlation coefficients between the Barthel index and the dimensions of the SF36 ranged from r = 0.217 (role emotional dimension) to r = 0.810 (physical functioning dimension).

With the Nottingham health profile the range was r = -0.189 (sleep dimension, not significant) to r = -0.840 (physical mobility dimension); the coefficient was r = -0.563 with the hospital anxiety and depression scale depression component, r = 0.361 with the life satisfaction index, r = 0.726 with the London handicap scale, and r = 0.826 with the Frenchay activities index.

Perforation of the appendix is reported as a risk factor for subsequent tubal infertility, with a risk estimate of 4.8 (95% CI 1.5 to 14.9) in a systematic review of epidemiologic studies on appendectomy and infertility or ectopic pregnancy.

The review's validity assessment concluded that recall bias and poor adjustment for confounding variables in some of the reports weakened the validity of the studies on which this tubal infertility estimate rests.
For ectopic pregnancy, the review yielded a risk estimate of 1.6 (95% CI 1.1 to 2.5) after an appendectomy, which addresses appendectomy in general rather than perforated appendicitis specifically.

The review also noted that recall bias and poor adjustment for confounding variables in some reports weakened the validity of the studies of appendectomy and adverse fertility outcomes, so the ectopic pregnancy estimate is limited by these methodological weaknesses.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: risk of ectopic pregnancy specifically after perforated appendicitis (rather than appendectomy in general).

The cited single-centre study of adults undergoing pulmonary valve replacement (PVR) late after tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) repair reports no postoperative improvement in right ventricular (RV) volumes or function, a finding the authors use to address the question of whether surgical timing is too late; interpreted from these results, the data are consistent with operation being performed too late in this population rather than demonstrating benefit from late PVR.

The study comprised 25 consecutive adult patients who underwent PVR for significant pulmonary regurgitation late after TOF repair, with radionuclide angiography performed in all patients at a mean of 8.2 months (+/- 8 months) before PVR and repeated at a mean of 28.0 months (+/- 22.8 months) after the operation.

Mean RV end-diastolic volume, RV end-systolic volume and RV ejection fraction remained unchanged after PVR (227.1 ml versus 214.9 ml, p = 0.74; 157.4 ml versus 155.4 ml, p = 0.94; 35.6% versus 34.7%, p = 0.78, respectively).

Of the 10 patients with RV ejection fraction > or = 0.40 before PVR, 5 (50%) maintained an RV ejection fraction > or = 0.40 following PVR, whereas only 2 out of 15 patients (13%) with pre-operative values < 0.40 reached an RV ejection fraction > or = 0.40 postoperatively (p < 0.001).

Yes — the manic/mixed episode distinction appears to run true over time: over an 11-year period, episodes were consistent (all manic or all mixed) in significantly more patients with bipolar disorder than would be expected by chance.

That comparison used the observed distribution of manic and mixed episodes (N=1,224) among patients with three or more entries in the management information system of a community mental health center (N=241), set against an expected distribution determined by averaging 1,000 randomly generated simulations.

The retrieved evidence does not establish a direct incidence or risk of venous air embolism by patient position during liver surgery: the one relevant study measured central and hepatic venous pressures in 10 patients during liver surgery rather than tracking air embolism events.
It is generally believed that positioning the patient in a head-down tilt (Trendelenburg position) decreases the likelihood of a venous air embolism during liver resection.
In that study, hemodynamic indices were recorded with the operating table in the horizontal, 20 degrees head-up and 20 degrees head-down positions.

There was no demonstrable pressure gradient between the hepatic and central venous levels in any of the positions, although absolute pressures varied in a predictable way, being highest in the head-down position and lowest during head-up tilt.
On no occasion was a negative intraluminal pressure recorded in any of the tested positions.

Because this study recorded venous pressure in 10 patients rather than observing venous air embolism events, its design cannot demonstrate that changing patient position alters the risk of venous air embolism during liver surgery.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: Direct incidence or risk of venous air embolism by patient position during liver surgery.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: reduction in concussion incidence.

The cited evidence does not establish definitive confirmation or exclusion of Crohn's disease in an individual patient; the source is a retrospective study assessing whether 99mTc-white blood cell scintigraphy and upper gastrointestinal small bowel follow-through could exclude inflammation in children suspected of having inflammatory bowel disease.

Of a population of 313 children who had a 99mTc-WBC scan, 130 were studied exclusively to rule out IBD; among those 130, the final diagnosis was Crohn's disease in 27, ulcerative colitis in nine, miscellaneous colitis in 13, probably normal in 42, and normal in 39, and 51 additional controls were studied with 99mTc-WBC scintigraphy.

The 99mTc-WBC scans were positive in all but three newly diagnosed Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, or miscellaneous colitis children, and the false-negative 99mTc-WBC studies were seen in children with mild inflammation on biopsies and normal UGI-SBFT studies.

In the 46 children with a true-positive 99mTc-WBC scan, 81% (17/21) of UGI-SBFT studies were normal, and in five children with equivocal UGI-SBFT studies the 99mTc-WBC scan correctly predicted whether inflammation was present in the terminal ileum.

Because the reported data are group-level results of a retrospective series of children suspected of IBD rather than an individual diagnostic determination, they cannot by themselves establish that any single patient does or does not have Crohn's disease.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: Definitive confirmation or exclusion of Crohn's disease in an individual patient.

Yes — among dying nursing home residents with documented daily pain, Medicare hospice enrollment was associated with more frequent regular analgesic treatment than nonhospice enrollment: 51% of hospice versus 33% of nonhospice residents received regular treatment for daily pain, and after controlling for clinical confounders hospice residents were about twice as likely to receive it (adjusted odds ratio = 2.08, 95% CI = 1.68–2.56).

This finding comes from a retrospective, comparative cohort study of a daily-pain subset of 709 hospice and 1,326 nonhospice residents drawn from a matched cohort of 2,644 hospice and 7,929 nonhospice nursing home residents in over 800 nursing homes in Kansas, Maine, Mississippi, New York, and South Dakota, whose last Minimum Data Set assessment was completed between 1992 and 1996 and who died before April 1997; analgesic use was taken from detailed drug data on the last MDS before death.

Untreated and potentially inappropriate analgesic use was less common in the hospice group: 15% of hospice residents versus 23% of nonhospice residents in daily pain received no analgesics (OR = 0.57, 95% CI = 0.45–0.74), and a lower proportion of hospice residents (21%) than nonhospice residents (29%) received analgesics not recommended by the American Medical Directors Association (OR = 0.65, 95% CI = 0.52–0.80).

The pattern of drugs differed by group: acetaminophen (not in combination with other drugs) was used most frequently for nonhospice residents (25% of 1,673 prescriptions), whereas morphine derivatives were used most frequently for hospice residents (30% of 1,058 prescriptions).

Because this was a retrospective, comparative cohort design using MDS drug data, it can show an association between hospice enrollment and guideline-concordant analgesic prescribing but cannot establish that hospice enrollment itself causes better pain management; moreover, the reported outcome is a process measure — any recommended analgesic given at least twice a day for each of the 7 days before the last MDS — rather than a measure of pain intensity or relief.

Yes: in a retrospective review of patients undergoing cholecystectomy for acute cholecystitis between 1 January 1996 and 31 December 1998, a special interest in laparoscopy was associated with better laparoscopic treatment, as 31 laparoscopic specialist (LS) patients (65%) versus 44 general surgeon (GS) patients (36%) had successful laparoscopic treatment (p = 0.001).

Of the 170 patients, 48 were cared for by three laparoscopic specialists (LS group), whereas 122 were treated by nine general surgeons who perform only laparoscopic cholecystectomy (GS group); the GS patients were older (median age 63 vs 53 years; p = 0.01).
Operating time was the same in the two groups (median 70 min), and the proportion of patients with postoperative complications was similar (37% in the GS group vs 31% in the LS group; p = 0.6).
The median postoperative hospital stay was shorter in the LS group (3 vs 5 days; p<0.01).

On logistic regression analysis used to control for baseline differences, significant predictors of a successful laparoscopic operation included LS group (p<0.01) and age (p = 0); predictors of prolonged length of hospital stay were age (p<0.01) and comorbidity score (p<0.01), with LS group status not a significant factor (p = 0.21).

Because the comparison comes from a retrospective record review rather than a prospective trial, the reported association between care by laparoscopic specialists and treatment outcomes cannot by itself establish that specialist care causes the difference.

The cited evidence does not establish whether circumcision should be performed in childhood at all, because the only relevant retrieved study compared the timing of circumcision (neonatal versus 5 months of age) rather than circumcision versus no circumcision, and it reported no overall benefits-versus-harms balance.

In a prospective cohort study of 350 infants at King Faisal Specialist Hospital and Research Center, Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, complications including meatal deformities, meatal stenosis, adhesions and infection were more frequent and more significant in the 250 neonates circumcised at 1 to 4 days (early group) than in the 100 infants circumcised at 5 months (late group).
The retrieved evidence does not establish: circumcision should be performed at all during childhood, including overall benefits versus harms or comparison with no circumcision.

Neutrophils isolated from 17 adult blunt major trauma patients (Injury Severity Score > or = 18) at admission (0 hrs) and 8 and 24 hrs later exhibited an enhanced migratory response to high concentrations of interleukin-8 throughout the first 24 hrs of admission, in contrast to the normal physiologic attenuation of migration seen in neutrophils isolated from normal laboratory volunteers (n = 9).

Significantly greater numbers of trauma patients' neutrophils migrated to interleukin-8 concentrations of 30 and 100 ng/mL at each time point when compared with normal volunteers (Mann-Whitney U test, p <.05).

Neutrophil infiltration of the lung is characteristic of early posttraumatic acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), and interleukin-8 is elevated in the lung within 2 hrs of major trauma in patients who later develop ARDS, which the source describes as a central role in the recruitment of neutrophils to the lung and their subsequent activation.
Neutrophil counts in the whole blood specimens obtained from trauma patients who later developed ARDS were elevated significantly at admission and declined rapidly throughout the next 24 hrs.

The hypothesis that enhanced interleukin-8-mediated neutrophil migratory activity in the early postinjury phase, before the development of ARDS, may be a crucial factor in the etiology of ARDS was examined in a prospective observational study, a design that can describe the association between posttrauma neutrophil migration and later ARDS but cannot establish that increased neutrophil migratory activity causes ARDS.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: increased neutrophil migratory activity is a causal/etiologic factor in ARDS.

Yes — the cited evidence reports spinal subdural hematoma (SSDH) occurring after subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) caused by a ruptured internal carotid aneurysm, and states that such a case had never been reported before.

In that case, a 52-year-old woman underwent craniotomy for the ruptured internal carotid aneurysm, and computed tomography showed SAH located predominantly in the posterior fossa together with subdural hematoma beneath the cerebellar tentorium.
On the sixth postoperative day the patient complained of severe lower back and buttock pain, and magnetic resonance imaging showed a subdural hematoma in the lumbosacral region.

Because this evidence comes from a single reported case, it documents that SSDH can follow SAH from a ruptured intracranial aneurysm but cannot by itself establish the frequency or generalizability of SSDH as a sequela of ruptured intracranial aneurysm.

Tumor depth should not be treated as an independent prognostic factor in soft tissue sarcoma: in a population-based series of 490 adults, multivariate analysis showed no major prognostic effect of tumor depth once grade and size were taken into account.

The authors considered it unlikely that tumor depth per se influences a tumor's metastatic capability, and hypothesized that any unfavourable prognostic importance of depth could be explained by the close association between size and depth, deep-seated tumors being on average larger than superficial ones.

Tumor depth did influence prognosis within the subset of high-grade and large tumors, where deep-seated tumors had a poorer survival rate than superficial tumors, which could be explained by the larger mean size of the deep-seated tumors.
The mean size of small tumors was the same whether superficial or deep, but the mean size of large and deep-seated tumors was one third larger than that of large but superficial tumors.

These analyses drew on 490 adult patients with soft tissue sarcoma of the extremity or trunk wall with complete follow-up of 4.5 years minimum, in a series in which the associations between tumor size and depth and the prognostic importance of grade, size and depth were assessed; most staging systems for soft tissue sarcoma are based on histologic malignancy grade, tumor size and tumor depth, with size generally dichotomized at 5 cm.

The cited evidence is mixed on whether double reading of barium enemas is necessary: adding a second reader increased the number of positive examinations from 249 to 315 (p<0.0001) and potentially altered clinical treatment in 98 patients (9.9%), yet it did not improve sensitivity and lowered specificity and inter-reading agreement.

Sensitivity of the first and combined readings for detection of all lesions was identical at 76.3% (95% CI, 65.4-87.1%), specificity fell from 91.0% (95% CI, 87.9-94.3%) for the first reading to 86.4% (95% CI, 82.2-90.0%) for the combined reading, and overall agreement fell from a kappa value of 61.8 (95% CI, 51.2-72.4%) to 52.9 (95% CI, 42.2-63.6%).
The second reading required an average of 3.3 min, and sensitivity for the detection of adenocarcinomas was 100%.

Independent double readings were performed prospectively on 1,003 consecutive barium enemas (822 double-contrast and 181 single-contrast examinations), of which 994 were included in the study, and results were correlated retrospectively with endoscopic or surgical results in 360 patients to determine agreement between first and combined readings and endoscopic results.

Because the clinical correlation with endoscopic or surgical findings was retrospective, the reported increase in positive examinations and the potential alteration of treatment do not by themselves establish that double reading improves patient outcomes.

Sub-classification of low-grade cerebellar astrocytoma was not clinically meaningful in the reviewed Danish cohort of children aged 0-14 years treated between 1960 and 1984 and followed to January 2001 or death: no difference in survival time was demonstrated when pilocytic astrocytoma was compared with fibrillary astrocytoma.

In that study, the histological specimens from each patient were re-reviewed for revised grading and classification according to three different classification schemes: the WHO, the Kernohan and the Daumas-Duport grading systems.
The Kernohan and the WHO classification systems had no predictive value, and the Daumas-Duport system was reported to be unsuitable as a prognostic tool for low-grade posterior fossa astrocytomas.

The prognostic factors that were significant for survival in this cohort were surgically gross-total removal of the tumour and tumour location in the cerebellum proper rather than in the fourth ventricle, rather than any histological sub-class.

Yes — in a survey of 30 surgeons in northern Jordan, fear of anaphylaxis and/or dissemination was the main reason given by 21 of the 27 surgeons (78%) who did not consider percutaneous or laparoscopic treatment for liver hydatid cyst for not using minimal-access techniques.
In that survey, only 3 surgeons (10%) considered laparoscopy the first line of treatment, leaving 27 surgeons who did not consider percutaneous or laparoscopic treatment.

The survey of 30 surgeons in northern Jordan used a questionnaire on each surgeon's preferred surgical technique, and additional information was collected from those who had not adopted minimal-access techniques to determine their reasons for not doing so.
This study was a population-based 13-year follow-up survey of community-dwelling adults living in East Baltimore in 1981.
Subjects were the continuing participants of the Baltimore Epidemiologic Catchment Area Program.
Participants interviewed between 1993 and 1996 with complete data on depressive symptoms and covariates were included (n = 1727).

Using structural equations with a measurement model for dichotomous data (the MIMIC—multiple indicators, multiple causes—model) to compare symptoms between women and men in relation to the nine symptom groups comprising the diagnostic criteria for major depression, adjusting for age, self-reported ethnicity, educational attainment, marital status, and employment, there were no significant gender differences in the self-report of depression symptoms even taking into account the higher level of depressive symptoms of women and the influence of other covariates.

Women were no more likely to endorse sadness than were men, as evidenced by a direct effect coefficient that was not significantly different from the null [adjusted estimated direct effect of gender on report of sadness = 0.105, 95% confidence interval (-0.113, 0.323)].

Yes — the type of remission after a major depressive episode was an important risk factor for relapse in this 4-year naturalistic follow-up: relapses occurred in 91.4% of the partial remission group versus 51.3% of the complete remission group, and partial remission versus complete remission was one of four factors with predictive relapse value, alongside the intensity of clinical symptoms, age, and the number of previous depressive episodes.
Among the four predictive factors identified, the existence of partial remission was reported as the most powerful predictor of relapse.

Rates of relapse and predictive relapse factors were studied over more than 4 years in a sample of Spanish outpatients meeting DSM-III-R criteria for a unipolar major depressive episode; a final sample of 139 outpatients was followed monthly in a naturalistic study.
Over that follow-up, a higher rate of relapses was observed in the partial remission group (91.4%) compared with the complete remission group (51.3%).
The authors note that the decreasing sample size during the follow-up and the difficulty in warranting treatment compliance limit the study.

Yes — expert breast pathology assessment is treated as necessary in DCIS management: current guidelines recommend that a pathologist with expertise in breast disease review all ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) specimens because of significant variability in pathologic reporting of DCIS, and in a single regional cancer centre review secondary pathology assessment changed the assessment of local recurrence risk in 100 cases (29%) and contributed to a change in treatment recommendation in 93 cases (43%) between 1996 and 2000.
In that review, 481 individuals with DCIS were referred to the regional cancer centre and pathology review was performed on 350 patients (73%).

Inter-observer agreement between the initial and secondary reports was high for the main pathologic features of DCIS, so the reported impact on risk assessment and treatment recommendation occurred despite good agreement on the principal features rather than because of poor agreement on them.

This evidence comes from a retrospective review of patients referred to one regional cancer centre between 1982 and 2000, so it documents the observed frequency with which expert review altered risk assessment and treatment recommendations rather than establishing by controlled comparison that expert review improves clinical outcomes.

Irregular bleeding affects many users of combined menopausal hormone therapy (HT) and commonly leads to invasive and expensive investigations to exclude underlying malignancy, although in most cases no abnormality is found; the study enrolled 117 postmenopausal women taking combined HT.

In this prospective observational study, outpatient endometrial biopsies were taken during and outside bleeding episodes and the relationship between endometrial uNK cells (CD56+) and bleeding patterns was measured; endometrial CD56+ uNK cells were significantly increased in biopsies obtained during bleeding episodes (P<0.001) compared with HT users with no bleeding, and the highest level of IL-15 expression was also seen in biopsies taken during bleeding.

The study sought to develop a more reliable structured implicit chart review instrument for assessing the quality of care for chronic disease and to examine whether ratings are more reliable for conditions in which the evidence base for practice is more developed.

The study developed a structured implicit review instrument to assess the quality of care over one year of treatment; 12 reviewers conducted a total of 496 reviews of 70 patient records selected from 26 VA clinical sites in two regions of the country.

Each patient had between one and four conditions specified as having a highly developed evidence base (diabetes and hypertension) or a less developed evidence base (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or a collection of acute conditions).

Multilevel analysis that accounts for the nested and cross-classified structure of the data was used to estimate the signal and noise components of the measurement of quality and the reliability of implicit review.

For COPD and a collection of acute conditions the reliability of a single physician review was quite low (intra-class correlation = 0.16-0.26) but comparable to most previously published estimates for the use of this method in inpatient settings.
For diabetes and hypertension the reliability is significantly higher at 0.46.

Peer review reliability differed by condition: for COPD and a collection of acute conditions the reliability of a single physician review was quite low (intra-class correlation 0.16-0.26), though comparable to most previously published estimates for this method in inpatient settings, whereas for diabetes and hypertension reliability was significantly higher at 0.46.

The higher reliability for diabetes and hypertension arose because reviewers collectively could distinguish more differences in quality of care between patients (p<0.007), and not because of less random noise or individual reviewer bias in the measurement; for these conditions the level of true quality, defined as the rating that would result from the full population of physician reviewers reviewing a record, varied from poor to good across patients.

Yes — correlated BCRABL quantitative real-time PCR results were achievable from laboratory-specific (homebrew) TaqMan-based assays: among 22 BCRABL-positive paired results drawn from 70 clinical specimens analysed in parallel at Vanderbilt University Medical Center and Virginia Commonwealth University, the Spearman rank correlation coefficient was r(s) = 0.9435 (p<0.00001), indicating a strong correlation of results.

The two laboratories' assays were not standardized to each other: although both used the same positive control cell line (K562) and quality control gene (BCR), they differed in RNA isolation technique, cDNA synthesis, BCR control cell line, and PCR primer and probe sequences.
BCRABL-positive results spanned a dynamic range from 10(0) to 10(5) per 100,000 cells, and 43 samples were negative at both facilities.
One discordant result was obtained for consecutive samples from one patient with a low BCRABL copy number, attributable to a minimal RNA yield at one laboratory.
The report notes that without some form of standardized methodology between laboratories, the correlation of results is difficult.

As a limitation entailed by the design, this was a comparison of paired results from two laboratories in a single specimen series, so it demonstrates assay-to-assay correlation rather than clinical interchangeability or treatment-related outcomes.

Fetal gender was not associated with emergency department (ED) visits for asthma during pregnancy: in a multivariable logistic regression of linked provincial administrative databases of in-patient deliveries and ED visits, having an ED visit for asthma was not associated with fetal gender (OR 1.01, 95% CI 0.85-1.19).

The analysis was based on women who delivered a live singleton baby between April 2003 and March 2004; among 109,173 live singleton deliveries, 530 women had visited the ED due to asthma during pregnancy.
Having an ED visit for asthma was positively associated with teenage pregnancy, low income, and presence of pregnancy-induced hypertension, whereas fetal gender was not among the associated factors.

Because the finding comes from an analysis of linked administrative health databases in which fetal gender was one predictor in a logistic model of ED visit risk, the result describes an association and does not establish that fetal gender causes or prevents ED visits for asthma in pregnancy.

In a prospective study of consecutive patients admitted within 24 h of stroke onset to two hospitals, bedside assessment did not reliably exclude aspiration following acute stroke: 94 patients underwent videofluoroscopy; 20 (21%) were seen to be aspirating, although this was not detected at the bedside in 10.

Where possible, all patients had their ability to swallow assessed on the day of admission by both a doctor and a speech and language therapist using a standardized proforma, and a videofluoroscopy examination was conducted within 3 days of admission.
In 18 (22%) of the patients the speech and language therapist considered the swallow to be unsafe, while in the medical assessment 39 patients (41%) had an unsafe swallow.

Bedside assessment by a speech and language therapist gave a sensitivity of 47%, a specificity of 86%, positive predictive value (PPV) of 50% and a negative predictive value (NPV) of 85% for the presence of aspiration, whereas a weak voluntary cough and any alteration in conscious level gave a sensitivity of 75%, specificity of 72%, PPV of 41% and NPV of 91% for aspiration.

Yes — in a French study of 48 scenarios, lay people and psychologists found it much more acceptable than physicians to breach confidentiality to protect the wife of a patient with a sexually transmitted disease: breaching confidentiality was accepted by 144 lay people, 10 psychologists and 7 physicians, with mean ratings of 11.76 for lay people, 9.28 for psychologists and 2.90 for physicians on a 0-22 scale.

In the same French study the scenarios were all combinations of five factors (severity of disease, time taken to discuss it, the patient's intent to inform the spouse, intent to adopt protective behaviours, and decision to consult an STD expert; 2 x 2 x 3 x 2 x 2), and the patient's stated intentions to protect his wife and to inform her of the disease had the greatest impact on acceptability.

A cluster analysis of the 144 lay participants identified subgroups finding breaching confidentiality 'always acceptable' (n = 14), 'depending on the many circumstances' (n = 87), requiring 'consultation with an expert' (n = 30), and 'never acceptable' (n = 13).

Because the reported figures are acceptability ratings for hypothetical scenarios rather than observations of actual practice, the study design cannot establish whether physicians would in fact breach confidentiality in such situations.

Supervised colorectal trainees did not differ significantly from consultants in the quality of mesorectal excision: there was no statistically significant difference between the two groups in the quality of mesorectum excised after potentially curative resection (P = 0.717).

In a series of 130 consecutive patients undergoing potentially curative resection for primary adenocarcinoma of the rectum between 2001 and 2003, 89 operations were performed by consultants and 41 by senior colorectal trainees under consultant supervision, and the excised mesorectum was graded by pathologists according to the staged classification proposed by Quirke.
A good mesorectum was reported in 44 patients (49%) operated on by consultants compared with 17 (41.5%) operated on by trainees.

In a cohort of 190 patients (157 men and 33 women; mean [SD] age 61.75 [10.85] years, range 33-85 years) diagnosed with non-small cell carcinoma in stages IV or IIIB with pleural or N2-N3 involvement and an ECOG performance status of 2 or below, 144 received cytostatic treatment and 46 received palliative treatment.

Median survival in this cohort was 31 weeks and was related to absence of weight loss (hazard ratio [HR], 1.73; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.26-2.39; P=.001), cytostatic treatment (HR, 1.85; 95% CI, 1.25-2.76; P=.002), and an ECOG score of 0 to 1 (HR, 2.84; 95% CI, 1.62-5.00; P=.0001).

Among patients with ECOG scores of 0 to 1, weight loss and treatment were significant prognostic factors, whereas in the ECOG 2 group survival was 15 weeks for patients undergoing cytostatic treatment and 11 weeks for patients receiving symptomatic treatment.

The authors note that few studies have assessed whether the advantage chemotherapy has been shown to have in treating advanced non-small cell lung carcinoma in clinical trials is transferrable to normal health care activity, and state that this could explain the skepticism of a large number of pneumologists towards this treatment.

In this single cohort, cytostatic treatment was an independent predictor of longer survival (HR, 1.85; 95% CI, 1.25-2.76; P=.002), and even in the ECOG 2 group survival was 15 weeks with cytostatic treatment versus 11 weeks with symptomatic treatment; as an observational prognostic-factor analysis, this association does not by itself establish that the clinical-trial survival advantage transfers to routine care, which is the transferability question the authors identified as largely unstudied.

In a retrospective cohort analysis of 247 patients with obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) in a tertiary care setting, aerobic fitness was measured as maximum oxygen consumption (VO2max) during cycle ergometry and compared with normative data from 1.4 million US Air Force tests; overall, the OSA patients had increased VO2max relative to the normalized US Air Force data (p<.001).
Within that same OSA cohort, patients with an apnea-hypopnea index greater than 20 had decreased VO2max compared with the normalized values (p<.001).
No differences in VO2max were observed after either medical or surgical therapy for OSA.

Because the comparison was a retrospective cohort analysis of VO2max against normative US Air Force reference data rather than a prospectively followed matched control group, the reported associations between OSA severity and aerobic fitness cannot establish that OSA causes changes in VO2max or that treating OSA alters it.

Yes — renal warm ischemia exceeding 30 minutes during laparoscopic partial nephrectomy (LPN) was reported as feasible: from July 2004 to June 2005, 18 patients underwent LPN with a warm ischemia time greater than 30 minutes, in a study designed to evaluate renal damage and impairment of renal function 1 year after such surgery.

Yes — in a prospective randomized clinical study of patients undergoing spinal surgery, a postoperative infection developed in 4 of 371 patients whose incision site was shaved immediately before surgery versus 1 of 418 patients in whom presurgical shaving was not performed (P<0.01), indicating a higher infection rate in the shaved group.

The study randomly allocated 789 patients scheduled for spinal surgery to a shaved group (371 patients) or an unshaved group (418 patients), and both groups' infection rates were recorded and compared.

Yes — in 300 patients with Type 1 diabetes (158 male; HbA(1c) median 8.2%, range 5.2-12.8%; median age 36 years, range 16-88; diabetes duration 14.5 years, range 2-49), none taking renin-angiotensin system blocking drugs, serum ACE showed a statistically significant but clinically weak relationship with severe hypoglycaemia (SH) incidence.

Participants recorded how often they had experienced SH, and glycated haemoglobin (HbA(1c)) and serum ACE were measured; the difference in SH incidence between ACE activity quartiles and the serum ACE-SH relationship were examined with non-parametric statistical tests and a negative binomial model.

The overall incidence of SH was 0.93 episodes per patient year, and the mean incidence in the top versus bottom quartiles of ACE activity was 0.5 versus 1.7 episodes per patient year, a difference that was not statistically significant (P = 0.075).

Spearman's test showed a very weak but statistically significant association between serum ACE level and SH incidence (r = 0.115, P = 0.047), and the binomial model likewise showed a statistically significant (P = 0.002) though clinically weak relationship between serum ACE and SH.
In total, 38 adults (age range 20-72 years; mean age of 36 years) with ID participated in the study; IQs ranged from 45 to 69 with a mean IQ of 58.
The intervention programme involved 15 weekly lessons of 1 h each, taught during 3 months.

In this study, teaching text comprehension strategies improved reading comprehension: direct programme effects - as determined by posttest-pretest contrasts for strategy tests - were substantial, except for the questioning strategy.
The transfer effect to general text comprehension was even more substantial than the direct effects, and the results on this test were well maintained at a follow-up test.
Results indicated no significant difference between group and individual instruction conditions.

Yes — body diffusion-weighted (DW) MR imaging added incremental value to conventional nonenhanced MR imaging for detecting uterine endometrial cancer: in 23 patients examined with a 1.5-T MR scanner, detection sensitivity for the carcinomas was 83% on T2-weighted images alone and rose to an overall 96% when DW images and fused DW/T2-weighted images were used in addition.

Endometrial cancers were detected only on T2-weighted images in 19 of the 23 patients, corresponding to an 83% detection sensitivity for the carcinomas; in the remaining 4 patients, two of whom had coexisting leiomyoma, no cancer was detected on T2-weighted images.

When DW images and fused DW images/T2-weighted images were used in addition to the T2-weighted images, cancers were identified in 3 of the remaining 4 patients in addition to the 19 patients, giving an overall detection sensitivity of 96%.

In a prospective, randomized, double-blind clinical trial of 41 children aged 4-16 years undergoing tonsillectomy, the aim was to determine whether postoperative administration of topical ropivacaine hydrochloride decreases morbidity following adenotonsillectomy.

Patients received 1.0% ropivacaine hydrochloride soaked swabs packed in their tonsillar fossae, while the control group received saline-soaked swabs; McGrath's face scale was used to compare the two groups in respect of pain control.
Only first hour there was no significant pain-relieving effect seen in the ropivacaine group (p>0.05); the other hours and days there were statistically significance between the two groups (p<0.001).
As 10 the authors made 11 comparison between groups, for Bonferroni correction, p<0.005 was accepted as statistically significant.
Also, the other post-operative parameters such as nausea, fever, vomiting, odor, bleeding, otalgia and trismus were not statistically different between the two groups.
There were no complications associated with ropivacaine hydrochloride, and no patients in this study suffered systemic side effects related to the use of this medication.

In a retrospective immunohistochemical study of paraffin-embedded biopsies from 125 patients with HBV infection (25 patients each with mild, moderate or severe hepatitis, cirrhosis or HCC) using an anti c-kit monoclonal antibody, the greatest number of c-kit-positive cases and the higher intensity of staining were found in the livers of patients with severe hepatitis and HCC, and in chronic hepatitis B infection the staining intensity was parallel with the grade and stage of the disease.
In cirrhotic liver, a lower intensity of staining and rarely c-kit positivity were present, and in the areas where fibrosis was seen c-kit positivity was rare or absent.

In the HCC specimens, c-kit positivity appeared both inside and around the cancerous nodes, and c-kit expression was observed in 62 of 75 HCC tissue specimens (82%) (p<0.001); in addition, 50 further HCC specimens formed on an HBV basis were studied to determine the prevalence of c-kit overexpression.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: diagnostic accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, or clinical utility of c-kit expression.

Yes — this study reports that higher Supplemental Security Income (SSI) benefits are linked to lower disability rates among the elderly, based on an analysis of the 1990 and 2000 censuses using state and year fixed-effect models to test whether within-state changes in maximum SSI benefits lead to changes in disability among people aged 65 and older.

Among all single elderly individuals, 30% had mobility limitations, and an increase of $100 per month in the maximum SSI benefit caused the rate of mobility limitations to fall by 0.46 percentage points.

The findings were robust to sensitivity analyses: analyses limited to those most likely to receive SSI produced larger effects, but analyses limited to those least likely to receive SSI produced no measurable effect.

Because the evidence comes from an observational, census-based comparison of within-state changes in maximum SSI benefits with changes in disability rather than a randomized intervention, the reported benefit-disability relationship is an association and does not by itself establish that raising benefits would cause disability to decline.
Yes: among older patients from a Dutch outpatient clinic invited to a self-management intervention, those who refused differed from those who agreed on some characteristics but not others.
Of the 361 patients invited, 267 (74%) refused participation.
Refusers were more restricted in their mobility, lived further away from the location of the intervention, and had a partner more often than did the participants.
No differences were found between refusers and participants in level of education, age or gender.

The comparison is a cross-sectional contrast of characteristics assessed at invitation, so the reported differences between refusers and participants cannot establish that any of these characteristics caused refusal.

In a secondary analysis of an ongoing prospective multicenter cohort of 1,036 blunt-injured adults with hemorrhagic shock, separate Cox proportional hazard regression models based on all patients evaluated the effects of gender on mortality, multiple organ failure, and nosocomial infection after controlling for all important confounders.
For the entire cohort of 1,036 patients, overall mortality was 20%, multiple organ failure 40%, and nosocomial infection 45%.

Men (n = 680) and women (n = 356) were clinically similar except that men required higher crystalloid volumes, more often had a history of alcoholism and liver disease, and had greater ventilatory and intensive care unit requirements.
Female gender was independently associated with a 43% lower risk of multiple organ failure and a 23% lower risk of nosocomial infection.

The study was designed to characterize the gender dimorphism after injury with specific reference to the reproductive age of the women (young, <48 years, vs old, >52 years) in a cohort of severely injured trauma patients in which significant variation in postinjury care was minimized.

The regression models were then used to characterize the effect of gender in the young and old age groups, and gender remained an independent risk factor in both subgroup analyses, with the protection afforded by female gender remaining unchanged.

Because the dimorphism was characterized by comparing young (<48 years) with old (>52 years) women rather than by reporting measured hormone levels, the analysis as designed cannot establish that hormonal differences are responsible for the observed protection.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: Direct evidence that hormonal differences mediate the gender dimorphism.

The retrieved evidence does not establish whether vaginal intraepithelial neoplasia (VAIN) has the same evolution as cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN): no cited source directly compared the natural history of the two conditions, and the available data come from separate studies with different designs (a post-hysterectomy cohort reporting VAIN/recurrence, and a matched comparison of women with CIN2-3 recurrence versus controls), so the requested head-to-head comparison is unsupported.
In a post-hysterectomy patient series, 15.0% (22/147) developed VAIN or recurrence, including two recurrent carcinomas and eight high-grade VAINs.

Those high-grade VAINs or recurrent carcinomas were detected only in patients with cervical squamous cell carcinoma within the first two years after hysterectomy, and not in patients with cervical adenocarcinoma.

Among 47 patients, 11 (23.4%) had at least one positive high-risk HPV test during follow-up, and VAIN was detected in 54.5% (6/11) of patients with an hrHPV-positive result compared with 16.7% (6/36) of those with an hrHPV-negative result.

In a separate study, women with CIN2-3 treated for dysplasia who had recurrence of CIN2+ more than 2 years after treatment were compared with controls without recurrence, matched for age and date of treatment; high-risk HPV-DNA was analysed by PCR from two archival smears per woman, and mean follow-up time was 14.6 years.
VAIN is described as a little known disease that could be related to risk factors different from simple HPV infections.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: a direct comparison of the natural history/evolution of VAIN versus CIN (whether they are the same).

Quantitative left ventricular regional wall motion did not change after fibrous tissue resection in endomyocardial fibrosis: wall motion in the five analyzed left ventricular regions did not differ between pre- and postoperative measurements.

In that study, regional left ventricular motion was measured by the centerline method, five left ventricular segments were analyzed pre- and postoperatively, and abnormality was expressed in units of standard deviation from the mean motion in a normal reference population.

The investigators compared left ventricular regional wall motion, global left ventricular ejection fraction, and New York Heart Association functional class pre- and postoperatively in 30 prospectively studied patients (20 female, age 30+/-10 years) assessed before and 5+/-8 months after surgery.

In a survey of UK radiology departments on skeletal surveys for physical abuse, 61% of departments had a named radiologist to report their skeletal surveys, 16% assigned surveys to a random radiologist, and 23% referred them elsewhere.

Only 52% of departments had a dedicated paediatric radiologist, so in 25% of departments the initial reports on skeletal surveys for physical abuse were provided by non-paediatric radiologists, and 15% did not have ready access to a paediatric radiology opinion.
Sixty-one percent of respondents thought that the service could be improved.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: UK radiologists' satisfaction with the training received in suspected child abuse.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: a direct measure of UK radiologists' satisfaction with support received in suspected child abuse.

In an experimental rat model of intestinal anastomosis, ethyl-2-cyanoacrylate glue performed comparably to polyglactin 910 sutures: there was no significant difference between bursting pressures of the suture (A) and glue (B) subgroup pairs on postoperative day 2 or day 6, while hydroxyproline levels and anastomosis performance time (AT) were significantly better in the B (glue) subgroups.

In that study, bursting pressures and hydroxyproline levels were measured on the second postoperative day in group E and on the sixth postoperative day in group L; 96 Sprague-Dawley rats were divided into groups E and L, each subdivided into 6 subgroups of 8 rats (EA1-EA3, EB1-EB3, LA1-LA3, LB1-LB3), with A subgroups receiving polyglactin 910 sutures and B subgroups ethyl-2-cyanoacrylate, and anastomoses constructed end to end (A1/B1), side to side (A2/B2) and end to side (A3/B3).

Because these findings come from an experimental animal (rat) study of intestinal anastomoses rather than from human patients, they support equivalence of the glue and suture techniques only in that experimental setting and cannot establish that cyanoacrylate is a good and reliable alternative for clinical intestinal anastomosis in humans.

No consensus exists among breast surgeons on attaining negative margins in breast-conservation operations; a survey of 1,000 surgeons interested in treating breast cancer, of whom 351 responses were analyzed (38% response rate), found a large variety in clinical practices across the country rather than a uniform approach.
Intraoperative margin analysis was infrequent in that survey: only 48% of surgeons examined the margins grossly with a pathologist, and even fewer used frozen sections or imprint cytology.
Decisions to reexcise specific margins varied greatly, for example 57% of surgeons would never reexcise for a positive deep margin whereas 53% would always reexcise for a positive anterior margin.

There was a large range in the margins surgeons reported as acceptable for ductal carcinoma in situ and invasive carcinoma: 15% would accept any negative margin, 28% a 1-mm negative margin, 50% a 2-mm negative margin, 12% a 5-mm negative margin, and 3% a 10-mm negative margin.

Because these findings come from a mailed survey of self-reported practices rather than observed operations or patient outcomes, the reported variation describes surgeons' stated margin practices and preferences and cannot by itself establish what is done intraoperatively or how it affects patient outcomes.

The retrieved evidence does not establish whether prescription data accurately identify children with asthma, so it does not show that prescriptions are a valid proxy for pediatric asthma; the only reported result is that Stock et al. (Eur Respir J 25:47-53, 2005) estimated asthma prevalence in Germany using claims data on prescriptions and hospital diagnoses and found high prevalence peaks in infants.

The objective of the citing paper was to critically assess and discuss various aspects of identifying children with asthma using prescription data, indicating that the accuracy of prescription-based identification of pediatric asthma was under critical review rather than established.

Because the reported German estimate is a population-level prevalence derived from claims data, it cannot by itself demonstrate that prescriptions identify individual children with asthma; this is an interpretation of the study design, not a reported validity measure.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: prescription data accurately identify children with asthma (validity as a proxy).

The cited evidence is mixed on acceptability: the National Infarct Angioplasty Project found overall satisfaction with care was high and statistically similar at angioplasty-based intervention sites and thrombolysis-based control sites (78% vs.
71% of patients rated care as 'excellent', P = 0.074), but carers rated convenience of visiting lower at intervention sites.

Patient satisfaction was higher at intervention sites offering angioplasty-based care than at control sites offering thrombolysis-based care for some aspects of care, such as speed of treatment (80% vs.
67% rated 'excellent', P = 0.001).
Carers rated convenience of visiting lower at intervention (angioplasty) sites than at control (thrombolysis) sites (12% vs.
1% rated it 'poor', P = 0.001).
In interviews, carers reported that they accepted the added inconvenience of visiting primary angioplasty sites in the context of this life-saving treatment.

The satisfaction findings come from a mixed-methods study using a postal survey of patients and their carers supported by semi-structured interviews, conducted in eight English hospitals with 682 patients and 486 carers surveyed and 33 patients and carers interviewed.
Survey responses were received from 595/682 patients (87%) and 418/486 carers (86%).
Patient satisfaction with discharge and aftercare was lower in both treatment groups than for other aspects of care.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: Comparative clinical outcomes (e.g., death, reinfarction, stroke) of primary angioplasty versus thrombolysis.

The cited evidence is insufficient to conclude that repeatedly fluctuating PSA (flu-PSA) levels are reassuring enough to avoid biopsy; PSA levels can show wide fluctuations when repeatedly measured, and in the study flu-PSA was defined as a PSA series with at least one PSA value lower than the one immediately preceding it, among 211 patients who underwent at least a second biopsy after a first negative prostate biopsy, 82 had flu-PSA levels and 129 had steadily increasing PSA (si-PSA) levels.

In the same study, there were no significant differences between the flu-PSA and si-PSA groups in terms of cancer detection, clinical or pathological stage, but the si-PSA group with cancer had a higher Gleason score; no difference was found for PSA slope between flu-PSA patients with cancer and those without.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: safety of avoiding biopsy.

Yes — among UHR patients seen at the PACE clinic, Orygen Youth Health between January 2000 and November 2008 and followed for 6 months, the risk of transition to psychosis differed across UHR criteria: when the two intermediate groups (APS alone and APS+Trait) were combined, the risk of transition increased in the order Trait alone < APS < BLIPS (p=0.024, adjusted analysis).

Yes — the EQ-5D showed construct validity in patients with acute coronary syndrome: in a cross-sectional study conducted at Trakya University Hospital between February and May 2008, 122 patients completed the Turkish version of the EQ-5D and the MacNew heart-related quality of life scale, and construct validity of the EQ-5D was assessed through its relationships with MacNew subscales using Spearman rank correlation and multiple linear regression analyses.

In that acute coronary syndrome sample, the mean EQ-5D index score was 0.79±0.32 and the MacNew global score was 5.01±1.16; EQ-5D index scores correlated with MacNew subscales at 0.557 to 0.721 and EQ-5D VAS scores at 0.297 to 0.484 (p<0.001 for all), and in the stepwise regression model the MacNew global score was a significant factor for the EQ-5D index score (β=0.188; 95% CI 0.152-0.224; p<0.001).

Because the evidence comes from a cross-sectional design, these correlations support construct validity at a single assessment but cannot establish the EQ-5D's responsiveness or sensitivity to change over time in acute coronary syndrome patients.

Yes: in a retrospective case-control, multiyear study of 412 students in the classes of 2005 to 2010 at a midwestern medical school, students' low performances relative to their class on the year 2 clinical performance examinations (CPEs) were a strong predictor that they would fail the senior (year 4) CPE.
Students' USMLE Step 1 scores also correlated with their performance on the senior CPE, but the predictive values for those scores were considerably weaker than for year 2 CPE performance.

During their second year, the students took four CPEs that each used three standardized patient (SP) cases, for a total of 12 cases, and the authors correlated each student's average year 2 case score with that student's average case score on the senior (year 4) CPE.

Contingency table analysis was carried out using performance on the year 2 CPEs and passing or failing the senior CPE, with sensitivity, specificity, odds ratio and relative risk calculated for two year 2 performance standards.

Because the design was a retrospective case-control, multiyear study with contingency table analyses, the reported sensitivity, specificity, odds ratio and relative risk describe retrospective classification of year 2 CPE performance against senior CPE pass/fail rather than a prospectively validated prediction rule.

Yes — endometrial polyp formation is associated with increased expression of both VEGF and TGF-β1: in a prospective study of 70 premenopausal women, VEGF and TGF-β1 scores were significantly higher in endometrial polyps than in adjacent endometrial tissue, with the pattern of significance differing by cell type (glandular vs stromal) and by menstrual phase.

The study compared VEGF and TGF-β1 expression between endometrial polyps and adjacent endometrial tissue in 70 premenopausal women, and the comparison was made separately for endometrium specimens obtained in the proliferative and secretory phases.

The VEGF score in glandular cells of endometrial polyps was significantly higher than in adjacent endometrium in both the proliferative phase (P<0.001) and the secretory phase (P=0.03), whereas the VEGF score in stromal cells of polyps was significantly higher than in adjacent endometrium only in the proliferative phase (P=0.006).

The TGF-β1 score in glandular cells of endometrial polyps was significantly higher than in adjacent endometrium in the proliferative phase (P=0.02), while the TGF-β1 score in stromal cells of polyps was significantly higher than in adjacent endometrium in both the proliferative phase (P=0.006) and the secretory phase (P=0.008).
The authors sought to compare the surgical results of laminoplasty in the treatment of cervical stenosis with myelopathy due to either degenerative changes or segmental OPLL.
The authors conducted a retrospective review of 40 instrumented laminoplasty cases performed at a single institution over a 4-year period to treat cervical myelopathy without kyphosis.
Twelve of these patients had degenerative cervical stenotic myelopathy (CSM; degenerative group), and the remaining 28 had segmental OPLL (OPLL group).
The 2 groups had statistically similar demographic characteristics and number of treated levels (mean 3.9 surgically treated levels; p>0.05).
There were no significant differences in the estimated blood loss (EBL) or length of hospital stay (LOS) between the groups (p>0.05).
The mean EBL and LOS for the degenerative group were 206 ml and 3.7 days, respectively, while the mean EBL and LOS for the OPLL group were 155 ml and 4 days, respectively.
There was a statistically significant improvement of more than one grade in the Nurick score for both groups following surgery (p<0.05).
The Nurick score improvement was not statistically different between the groups (p>0.05).
The visual analog scale (VAS) neck pain scores were similar between groups pre- and postoperatively (p>0.05).
The complication rates were not statistically different between groups (p>0.05).
Radiographically, both groups lost extension range of motion (ROM) following laminoplasty, but this change was not statistically significant (p>0.05).

The overall clinical follow-up rate was 88%, and the mean clinical follow-up duration was 16.4 months; the mean radiographic follow-up rate was 83%, and the mean length of radiographic follow-up was 9.3 months.

Because the comparison comes from a retrospective review of cases at a single institution, the reported absence of differences between the degenerative and OPLL groups is an observed association in that case series rather than evidence from a randomized or prospective controlled comparison.

The present study aims at providing additional quantitative evidence on the potential of dogs to positively modulate the behavior of children with ASD, and it exposed a 12-year-old boy diagnosed with ASD, at his usual treatment location (the Portuguese Association for Developmental Disorders and Autism at Vila Nova de Gaia, Portugal), to (1) one-to-one structured activities with a therapist assisted by a certified therapy dog, and (2) one-to-one structured activities with the same therapist alone (as a control).
The behavior of the participant was continuously video-recorded during both treatment conditions for further analysis and comparison.

In the presence of the dog, the participant exhibited more frequent and longer durations of positive behaviors (such as smiling and positive physical contacting) as well as less frequent and shorter durations of negative behaviors (such as aggressive manifestations).

The comparison of behavior with the dog present versus the same therapist alone does not establish whether the dog's presence primes or enhances subsequent therapy outcomes, engagement, or response to later therapist-led intervention.

The retrieved evidence does not establish: the dog's presence primes or enhances subsequent therapy outcomes, engagement, or response to later therapist-led intervention (a carry-over/preparatory effect beyond the concurrent sessions).

The retrieved evidence is insufficient to establish whether remote postischemic conditioning protects against ischemic damage in percutaneous coronary revascularization: the cited report describes the trial design, population and outcome definitions but does not report the comparative effect of remote postischemic conditioning versus placebo on ischemic damage.

The study was a randomized, single-blinded, single-center clinical trial of 320 patients undergoing elective PCI, who were randomized to receive three 5-min cycles of ischemia by inflation of a cuff on the non-dominant arm to 200 mm Hg (remote postischemic conditioning) or to placebo (uninflated cuff).

The stated aim was to evaluate the protective effect of remote postischemic conditioning in patients undergoing elective PCI for stable angina or non-ST elevation acute coronary syndrome with troponin <1 ng/ml at the time of randomization.

The primary outcome variable was the maximum increase in troponin in the first 24 h, and the secondary outcome variable was readmission due to heart failure or cardiovascular mortality after 1 year of follow-up.
In addition to the overall PCI population, a diabetic population was studied.

The cited report frames the question as a hypothesis, noting that remote postischemic conditioning might reduce the myocardial lesions associated with PCI, but perhaps less so in diabetics, and that PCI-associated myocardial damage is related to medium-term cardiovascular death.
The retrieved passages only partly cover this requested aspect: Whether remote ischemic postconditioning protects against ischemic damage in percutaneous coronary revascularization.

Yes — a pilot study of new recruits to the three British Armed Forces Services found a differential, with recruits in the Army sample having a significantly greater prevalence of dental decay and greater treatment resource need than either of the other two Services (PMID:22075911).

In that study, Army recruits had a mean of 2.59 (2.08, 3.09) decayed teeth per recruit, compared with 1.93 (1.49, 2.39; p<0.01) in Royal Navy recruits and 1.26 (0.98, 1.53; p<0.001) in Royal Air Force recruits (PMID:22075911).
Data for 432 participants were entered into the analysis (PMID:22075911).

Yes — serum can be used to analyze EGFR mutation status in patients with advanced NSCLC: among paired tumor and serum samples from 57 patients with advanced NSCLC, EGFR mutation status was consistent in 50 of the 57 pairs (87.7%), with a correlation index of 0.62 (P<0.001) between mutations detected in serum and in the matched tumor sample.

In that paired-sample study, EGFR mutation status in tumor samples was analyzed by genomic polymerase chain reaction and direct sequencing, whereas serum EGFR mutation status was determined by the peptide nucleic acid locked nucleic acid polymerase chain reaction clamp.
EGFR mutations were detected in the serum samples of 11 patients and in the tumor samples of 12 patients.

Among the 57 patients, 22 (38.5%) received EGFR-tyrosine kinase inhibitors as any line therapy, and response to these inhibitors was significantly associated with EGFR mutations in both tumor samples and serum samples (P<0.05).

Yes — in an in vivo animal study, serum levels of lidocaine and its metabolite monoethylglycinexylidide (MEGX) were undetectable in untreated skin, whereas following laser treatment both lidocaine and MEGX were detectable, indicating that laser pretreatment enhanced transdermal absorption of topical lidocaine.
The aim of this study was to demonstrate in vivo firstly that laser enhances transdermal drug absorption and secondly that this can be manipulated by altering laser settings.
Four pigs were used in the IACUC approved animal study.
On day 0, 5 g of 4% topical lidocaine was applied under occlusion for 60 minutes to a 400 cm(2) area on the abdomen.
On day 7, the Er:YAG laser was used at 500, 250, 50, and 25 µm ablative depth, respectively, over a 400 cm(2) area on the abdomen.
Five grams of 4% topical lidocaine was applied immediately with occlusion for 60 minutes, and then removed.
Blood was drawn at 0, 60, 90, 120, 180, and 240 minutes.
The serum was extracted and analyzed for lidocaine and its metabolite monoethylglycinexylidide (MEGX).
Peak levels of lidocaine were significantly higher (P = 0.0002) at 250 µm (0.62 mg/L), compared to 500 µm (0.45 mg/L), 50 µm (0.48 mg/L), and 25 µm (0.3 mg/L).
Peak levels of MEGX were significantly higher (P ≤ 0.0001) at 250 µm (0.048 mg/L), compared to 500 µm (0.018 mg/L), 50 µm (0.036 mg/L), and 25 µm (0.0144 mg/L).

Because these findings come from an animal model, they establish enhanced transdermal absorption of topical lidocaine under the experimental conditions tested rather than a demonstrated clinical benefit in patients.

Yes — a PET study of amoxapine in seven healthy volunteers found it matched the receptor-occupancy profile used to define currently available atypical antipsychotics, with 5-HT2 occupancy near saturation at 100 mg/day and above and 5-HT2 occupancy exceeding D2 occupancy at all doses tested.

The comparator profile applied to currently available atypical antipsychotics at clinically relevant doses is high serotonin (5-HT)2 occupancy, greater 5-HT2 than dopamine (D)2 occupancy, and a higher incidence of extrapyramidal side effects when D2 occupancy exceeds 80%.
A review of pharmacologic and behavioral data suggested amoxapine should conform to that atypical profile, which prompted the PET study of its 5-HT2 and D2 occupancy.
In that study, seven healthy volunteers received 50–250 mg/day of amoxapine for 5 days and then underwent [11C]-raclopride and [18F]-setoperone PET scans.

5-HT2 receptors showed near saturation at amoxapine doses of 100 mg/day and above, while D2 receptor occupancies increased dose-dependently and never exceeded 80%, so 5-HT2 occupancy exceeded D2 occupancy at all doses.

Because the criterion for elevated extrapyramidal side-effect risk is tied to D2 occupancy exceeding 80%, and D2 occupancy in this PET study never exceeded 80%, the reported data address receptor occupancy rather than directly demonstrating clinical atypical antipsychotic efficacy or tolerability in patients.

The evidence on whether a dedicated discharge coordinator improves the quality of hospital discharge is mixed: in an intervention study assessing the quality of discharge planning before and after the introduction of a discharge coordinator, the coordinator improved the discharge planning process and reduced problems patients experienced after discharge and their perceived need for medical and healthcare services, but there was no evidence of a more timely or effective provision of community services after discharge, or of improved appropriateness or efficiency of bed use.

The intervention evaluated was a discharge coordinator whose sole responsibility was to plan and coordinate the discharge of patients from medical wards, and the study was conducted in the three medical wards at the Homerton Hospital in Hackney, East London.

The study comprised 600 randomly sampled adult patients admitted to the medical wards of the study hospital who were resident in the district (but not in institutions), were under the care of physicians (excluding psychiatry), and were discharged home from one of the medical wards; sampling was conducted in three study phases over 18 months.

Phase I comprised base line data collection; in phase II data were collected after the introduction of the district discharge planning policy and a discharge form (checklist) for all patients; in phase III data were collected after the introduction of the discharge coordinator.

Outcomes assessed were readmission rates, duration of stay, appropriateness of days of care, patients' health and satisfaction, problems after discharge, and receipt of services; patients were interviewed on the ward before discharge and seven to 10 days after being discharged home.

The discharge coordinator resulted in an improved discharge planning process, a reduction in problems experienced by patients after discharge, and a reduction in perceived need for medical and healthcare services; however, there was no evidence that the coordinator resulted in a more timely or effective provision of community services after discharge, or that the appropriateness or efficiency of bed use was improved.

Variations in the use of carotid endarterectomy (CEA) across district populations in two English health regions were not explained by population need: utilisation rates were not associated with district stroke mortality (r=-0.06, 95% CI -0.41 to 0.30) or with admission rates for stroke (r=0.17, 95% CI -0.2 to 0.49).
Utilisation of CEA varied considerably, with a 14-fold difference across district populations.

Instead of need, use was related to service location and to area affluence: there was a strong relationship between residence in districts where services were located and higher utilisation, while rates of CEA were lowest in the regions' most affluent wards.

The analysis compared CEA utilisation at a population level with district stroke mortality, hospital admissions and material deprivation, an ecological cross-sectional design that cannot establish that changing service provision or need factors would alter CEA utilisation.
Yes — laparoscopic techniques can be used to treat patients whose antireflux surgery has failed, according to a case series conducted at two academic medical centers.
In that series of 46 consecutive patients, the previous antireflux procedures were laparoscopic in 21 patients, laparotomy in 21, thoracotomy in 3, and thoracoscopy in 1.

The laparoscopic reoperative procedures performed were Nissen fundoplication (n = 22), Toupet fundoplication (n = 13), paraesophageal hernia repair (n = 4), Dor procedure (n = 2), Angelchik prosthesis removal (n = 2), Heller myotomy (n = 2), and takedown of a wrap (n = 1).
Operative complications reported were fundus tear (n = 8), significant bleeding (n = 4), bougie perforation (n = 1), small bowel enterotomy (n = 1), and tension pneumothorax (n = 1).
The conversion rate from laparoscopy to an open procedure was 20% overall (9 patients) but 0% in the last 10 patients, and mortality was 0%.
The mean +/- SEM hospital stay was 2.3+/-0.9 days for operations completed laparoscopically, and the mean +/- SEM duration of surgery was 3.5+/-1.1 hours.
The well-being score (1 best; 10 worst) was 8.6+/-2.1 before and 2.9+/-2.4 after surgery (P<.001), and 31 (89%) of 35 patients were satisfied with their decision to have reoperation.
Follow-up was possible in 35 patients (76%) at a mean of 17.2+/-11.8 months.

Because the evidence comes from an uncontrolled case series rather than a comparative trial, it cannot establish that laparoscopic reoperation is superior to open reoperation for failed antireflux surgery.

Patients with sickle cell disease (SCD) presenting to the emergency department and hematology clinic with temperature greater than or equal to 38 degrees C were prospectively evaluated using a physician-completed questionnaire.
Seventy-three patients with SCD with 96 febrile events were evaluated over a 1-year period.
The questionnaire was completed before obtaining chest radiography (CXR) results in all patients.
Twenty-four percent (23/96) of the patients had CXR evidence of acute chest syndrome (ACS).
On the basis of the questionnaire data, 61% (14/23) of ACS cases were not clinically suspected by the evaluating physician before obtaining CXR.

Comparing the patients with and without ACS revealed that, with the exception of splinting (4/23 [17%] versus 0/73 [0%]), no symptom or physical examination finding helped to identify which patients had ACS.
Fifty-seven percent of patients with ACS had completely normal findings on physical examination.
The presentation of patients with clinically detected versus clinically unsuspected ACS also did not differ significantly.
Overall physician sensitivity for predicting ACS was only 39%, and diagnostic accuracy did not improve significantly with increasing levels of pediatric training.

When desflurane was used to control surgically induced hypertension, it restored blood pressure without altering left ventricular systolic function: in the 16 of 50 vascular surgery patients who developed hypertension at incision, systolic arterial pressure was controlled by desflurane in all 16, and no change in heart rate, cardiac index, mean pulmonary arterial pressure, stroke volume, end-diastolic and end-systolic cross-sectional areas, fractional area change or left ventricular circumferential fiber shortening was noted when desflurane was added to restore blood pressure.

Afterload indices — systemic vascular resistance index, end-systolic wall-stress and left-ventricular stroke work index — increased with incision and returned to post-induction values with a mean end-tidal desflurane concentration of 5.1+/-0.7%, so the LV findings concern unchanged contractile/volumetric indices alongside reversal of the incision-related afterload increase.

The LV-function findings come from 50 patients scheduled for vascular surgery, not a population defined as undergoing aortic surgery, so the evidence cannot establish the LV response to desflurane specifically during aortic surgery.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: LV function response to desflurane specifically in patients undergoing aortic surgery.

The retrieved evidence does not establish that profound hypotensive events cause myocardial ischaemic events in patients with coronary disease; the single observational study reports only that ST events were significantly associated with preceding hypotensive events (chi(2) = 40.2, p<0.0001).

In that observational study of patients with ischaemic heart disease attending an urban tertiary referral cardiology centre, 25 suitable patients were enrolled and 107 hypotensive events were documented; 40 ST events occurred in 14 patients, of which a quarter were symptomatic.

Hypotension induced ischaemic (HII) events were defined as episodes of ST segment ischaemia occurring at least one minute after an ambulatory blood pressure measurement (systolic/diastolic) below 100/65 mm Hg during the day, or 90/50 mm Hg at night.

Fourteen HII events occurred in eight patients; 13 of the 14 were preceded by a fall in diastolic pressure (median diastolic pressure 57.5 mm Hg, interquartile range 11, maximum 72 mm Hg, minimum 45 mm Hg) and six were preceded by a fall in systolic pressure (chi(2) = 11.9, p<0.001).

Because the data come from an observational study design, the reported temporal association between ST events and preceding hypotensive events cannot by itself establish that profound hypotension causes myocardial ischaemic events.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: causal relationship.

Yes — the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) can favor left hemisphere strokes, because it can award more points for tests of presumed left-hemisphere function, such as language, than for tests of right-hemisphere function, such as neglect.

In a retrospective study of 153 patients with acute stroke seen at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center between January 1995 and March 2000 who underwent MRI and NIHSS within 24 hours of stroke onset, the relationship between acute NIHSS score and stroke volume differed by side.
For patients with NIHSS scores of 0 to 5, the DWI volume of right cerebral lesions was greater than that of left-sided lesions (mean volume 8.8 versus 3.2 cm3; P=0.04).
Among patients with DWI lesions larger than the median volume (9 cm3), 8 of 37 with right-sided stroke had an NIHSS score of 0 to 5 compared with 1 of 39 patients with left-sided stroke (P=0.01).
Multiple linear regression analysis revealed a significantly lower acute NIHSS on the right compared with the left side when adjusted for stroke volume on chronic T2 imaging (P=0.03).

In the placebo arm of the NINDS t-PA stroke trial, the volume for right hemisphere stroke was statistically greater than the volume for left hemisphere stroke when adjusting for the baseline NIHSS (P<0.001).
For each 5-point category of the NIHSS score below 20, the median volume of right hemisphere strokes was approximately double the median volume of left hemisphere strokes.

For patients with a left hemisphere stroke and a 24-hour NIHSS score of 16 to 20, the median volume of cerebral infarction was 48 mL (interquartile range 14 to 111 mL), compared with 133 mL (interquartile range 81 to 208 mL) for patients with a right hemisphere stroke (P<0.001).
