The median volume of a right hemisphere stroke was roughly equal to the median volume of a left hemisphere stroke in the next highest 5-point category of the NIHSS.

In North Carolina, all mammography facilities were inspected during 1993-1994 and again in 1995, and both inspections evaluated mean glandular radiation dose, phantom image evaluation, darkroom fog, and developer temperature; the retrieved context does not report a comparative result for mean glandular radiation dose between the two inspections.

The percentage of facilities that met quality standards increased from the first inspection to the second inspection, indicating that measured mammography quality in North Carolina improved over the period when the Mammography Quality Standards Act was first implemented in 1995.

Among the specific quality measures, passing rates from the first to the second inspection were 31.6% versus 78.2% for phantom image scores, 74.3% versus 88.5% for darkroom fog, and 62.4% versus 86.9% for developer temperature difference.

The retrieved evidence is mixed/insufficient for recommending thrombosis prophylaxis in all hospitalised medical patients: no source directly compares universal prophylaxis with selective or risk-stratified prophylaxis for clinical outcomes, and the cited sources instead support targeting prophylaxis to higher-risk patients.
In medical wards, thrombosis prophylaxis is generally restricted to patients who are immobilised.

Among patients hospitalised on a general internal ward from 1992 to 1996, the incidence of symptomatic venous thrombosis during hospitalisation was 39/6332 (0.6%); 24 of these 39 patients had a malignancy, whereas 876 of all 6332 patients had a known malignancy.
The incidence of venous thrombosis in the cancer group was 2.7% compared with 0.3% (15/5456) in the non-cancer group, giving a relative risk for venous thrombosis due to malignancy of 10.0 (95% C.I.

Because that internal-ward study reported incidence in a retrospective patient series without comparing prophylactic strategies, its design cannot establish whether giving prophylaxis to all medical inpatients improves clinical outcomes.

Hospital-acquired venous thromboembolism (VTE) is described as a common and preventable adverse event that most patients are at risk of developing during their hospital stay, and VTE prophylactic anticoagulation (chemoprophylaxis) is the preferred pharmacological assignment for reducing VTE risk, although it is underused in current practices involving risk stratification (RS) for VTE prevention.
A non-risk-stratification protocol reduces complexity by assuming that the risk of VTE is present and uses contraindications to determine appropriate VTE assignment.

In cancer patients with long-term central venous catheters, thrombotic complications are potentially severe, but it is difficult to prescribe a prophylactic treatment systematically, so it is necessary to identify the higher-risk patients who need prophylaxis.

The retrieved evidence does not establish: Direct comparison of universal prophylaxis versus selective or risk-stratified prophylaxis in hospitalised medical patients for clinical outcomes such as VTE, bleeding, or mortality.

Yes, head positioning influenced anterior chamber depth in pseudoexfoliation syndrome: in 39 patients with clinically apparent unilateral pseudoexfoliation and elevated intraocular pressure, mean anterior chamber depth in the pseudoexfoliation eyes fell from 3.08 mm supine to 2.95 mm prone, and the decrease when facing down was significantly greater in the pseudoexfoliation eyes than in the fellow eyes.

Central anterior chamber depth was measured in these 39 patients after they were placed face-up for 5 minutes, when anterior chamber depth and axial length were measured by A scan and intraocular pressure was measured by Tonopen in both eyes; the measurements were then repeated on both eyes after 5 minutes in a face-down position.
In the same comparison, mean anterior chamber depth in the fellow eyes decreased only from 3.01 mm supine to 2.97 mm prone.
No significant differences in intraocular pressure or axial length between the prone and supine positions were found in either eye.

The study was designed to test whether increased lens mobility in pseudoexfoliation affects anterior chamber depth in the prone position, so its measurements describe positional change in anterior chamber depth rather than the effect of any treatment on that change.
The single retrieved study of this question reviewed medical records of all blunt trauma patients admitted to the trauma service from January 1, 1992, to March 31, 1998.

Physical examination for the detection of abdominal injuries has been considered unreliable in alcohol-intoxicated trauma patients, and computed tomography (CT) has been described as playing the primary role in these abdominal evaluations.
The patients studied had a blood alcohol level of at least 80 mg/dL, a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15, and an unremarkable abdominal examination.
Of 324 patients studied, 317 (98%) had CT scans negative for abdominal injury.
Abdominal injuries were identified in 7 patients (2%), with only 2 (0.6%) requiring abdominal exploration.
A significant association was found between major chest injury and abdominal injury.

Because these data come from a retrospective medical record review of patients who underwent CT, the findings describe the yield of abdominal CT in this intoxicated population but do not compare a selective-CT or no-CT strategy against universal scanning, so they do not establish that omitting or limiting abdominal CT in such patients is safe or misses no clinically significant injuries.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: Safety and missed-injury rate of selective or no abdominal CT.

In the analysis of risk factors for avascular necrosis of bone (AVN) in systemic lupus erythematosus, a cohort of 265 patients receiving long term follow up in an SLE clinic from 1978 to 1998 was analysed; 11 patients had AVN, giving a point prevalence of 4%, patients with AVN were matched for age, sex, ethnicity, duration of disease, and organ disease with two other patients with SLE, and a further 31 patients were chosen at random for the analysis.

The study investigated the role of antiphospholipid antibody status (IgM and IgG anticardiolipin antibodies and lupus anticoagulant) with adjustment for corticosteroid use as risk factors for the development of AVN; there were no significant differences demonstrable in the presence of individual antiphospholipid antibodies (aPL) or their combination between the group with AVN or the two control groups.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: significant associations of non-aPL risk factors with AVN.

Visual loss in amblyopia is not necessarily permanent: reported cases in which acuity improved in an eye with a history of amblyopia, and treated amblyopic eyes that gained acuity, indicate that visual loss can improve rather than being irreversible.
Twelve cases of acuity improvement were detected, and in nine of these the eye showing improvement of acuity had a history of amblyopia.

In amblyopic eyes, the mean improvement in distance and near acuity by 12 months was 3.3 and 1.9 lines logMAR respectively, with the improvement generally occurring between 1 and 12 months from baseline and remaining stable over the period of follow up.

In a prospective study of 32 anisometropic hyperopic children with unilateral amblyopia, the mean visual acuity of the amblyopic eyes significantly increased from 0.35 ± 0.3 to 0.16 ± 0.2 logMAR after treatment consisting of full refractive correction with eyeglasses, a refractive adaptation phase and occlusion by patching the fellow eye (p < 0.001).

The cited case-control evidence does not indicate an increased risk of bleeding complications in Werlhof's disease patients undergoing cardiac surgery: total mediastinal chest-tube drainage was almost identical (1140 ml in the WD group vs 1197 ml in the no-WD group) and one patient in each group had a bleeding complication requiring reexploration.

Between 05/95 and 07/98, ten patients with Werlhof's disease (eight males, two females) underwent cardiac surgery with extracorporeal circulation; each WD patient was matched to five patients without WD on diagnosis, age, gender, ejection fraction, number of distal anastomoses and body-mass index.

Mean platelet counts were significantly lower in the WD group than in the no-WD group despite a significant rise after preoperative immunoglobulin treatment in five WD patients with counts below 80/nl (54/nl to 112/nl, P=0.018); counts on the day before, directly after and on the first day after surgery were 141/nl vs 215/nl (P=0.012), 75/nl vs 147/nl (P=0.001) and 93/nl vs 136/nl (P=0.009).
WD patients received significantly more platelet concentrates than no-WD patients (mean 2.3 versus 0.7, P=0.007).
Postoperative mortality was three patients (6%) in the no-WD group and one patient (10%) in the WD group, and these deaths were unrelated to Werlhof's disease.

As a matched case-control study of only ten WD patients, this design describes the observed perioperative course in that cohort and cannot by itself establish that Werlhof's disease alters the risk of bleeding complications.

Open access endoscopy was associated with less pre-procedure information than subspecialty clinic referral: in PMID:10922093, patients referred for open access endoscopy reported receiving significantly less information to help them identify the procedure (p<0.01) and less explanation concerning the nature of the procedure (p<0.005) than patients referred from a gastrointestinal subspecialty clinic.
In the same study, there was no difference between the open access and GI clinic groups in satisfaction scores for examinations performed under conscious sedation.
For flexible sigmoidoscopy performed without sedation, the GI clinic patient group were more satisfied with their procedure than the open access group.
The majority of patients, regardless of access route, were more likely to receive their endoscopic results from a gastroenterologist than from the referring physician.
Patients in the GI clinic group who underwent colonoscopy felt significantly better at follow-up than the corresponding open access patients.

These comparisons rest on patient-reported data: information was obtained from all patients presenting for outpatient upper and lower endoscopy using a 1-page questionnaire, and patients in both groups who had an outpatient upper/lower endoscopic procedure were contacted by phone afterwards with a standardized questionnaire, so the reported differences reflect patients' recalled preknowledge, explanation and satisfaction rather than a directly observed consent process.

In UK rheumatoid arthritis patients established on methotrexate <20 mg weekly and folic acid 5 mg daily, the evidence on stopping folic acid long term is mixed: withdrawal was associated with more early study discontinuation and more nausea, but not with worse methotrexate efficacy.

In a prospective, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study, 75 patients established on methotrexate <20 mg weekly and folic acid 5 mg daily were asked to stop their folic acid and were randomized to placebo or folic acid 5 mg daily, with toxicity and efficacy evaluated before entry and then at 3-month intervals for 1 year.

Overall 25 (33%) patients concluded the study early, 8 (21%) in the group remaining on folic acid versus 17 (46%) in the placebo group (P = 0.02), and two patients in the placebo group discontinued because of neutropenia.
At 9 months the placebo group had an increased incidence of nausea (45 vs.
7%, P = 0.001), while the placebo group had significantly lower disease activity on a few of the variables measured, which was probably not of clinical significance.

The available evidence does not establish alexithymia as a risk factor for unexplained physical symptoms in general medical outpatients: in a cross-sectional study of 321 patients attending an internal medicine outpatient clinic, those with medically unexplained symptoms more often had a mental disorder but overall were not more alexithymic than patients with explained symptoms.
In that cross-sectional study, 169 of 321 patients were rated as having unexplained physical symptoms after complete physical examinations, according to two independent raters.

A subgroup finding in the same study was that patients with both unexplained symptoms and a mental disorder who also denied any possible connection between emotional problems and their physical symptoms did have more alexithymic traits.
Among patients with unexplained physical symptoms in that study, alexithymia was not associated with subjective health experience or use of medical services.
Because the cited study was cross-sectional, it cannot establish that alexithymia predicts the later development of unexplained physical symptoms in general medical outpatients.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: prospective evidence that alexithymia predicts later unexplained physical symptoms.

In an inception cohort of 85 consecutive emergency surgical patients admitted to a surgical ICU at a secondary referral center in 1999, the APACHE II score was calculated before surgery, after admission to the ICU, and on postoperative days 3, 7, and 10.

The mean +/- SD APACHE II score of 24.2 +/- 8.3 at admission to the ICU was approximately 36% greater than the initial (preoperative) score of 17.8 +/- 7.7, a difference that was highly statistically significant (P<.001).

The overall observed mortality of 32% favorably corresponded with the 34% mortality predicted by the initial APACHE II score, but the 50% mortality predicted by the APACHE II score at admission to the ICU was significantly different from the observed mortality rate (P=.02).
In the 40 long-term patients (>/=10 days in the ICU), the difference between the APACHE II scores of survivors and of patients who died was statistically significant on day 10 (P=.04).

The APACHE II score used as an ICU admission score in emergency surgical patients is not independent of the effects of treatment, which may lead to considerable bias in the comparability of defined groups of patients and in the evaluation of treatment policies, and postoperative monitoring with the APACHE II score is clinically irrelevant.

In the same cohort, the score at ICU admission was 24.2 +/- 8.3 versus 17.8 +/- 7.7 before surgery (P<.001), and the 50% mortality predicted by the ICU admission score differed significantly from the observed mortality rate (P=.02), indicating that the ICU admission APACHE II score did not reliably reflect physiological impairment or predict outcome in these emergency surgical patients.

Managed care does not enable more low-income persons to identify a usual source of care: in a cross-sectional 1996-1997 national household survey of 14,271 low-income persons, high community managed care penetration was associated with a lower likelihood of having a usual source of care among uninsured persons, 54.8% versus 62.2% in low penetration areas, and with a lower likelihood of having a usual physician, 60% versus 72.8%.
For privately insured and Medicaid beneficiaries, managed care had only marginal effects on the likelihood of having a usual source of care.

Yes — outcome could be predicted in children with malignancy and ARDS in a retrospective chart review of 17 children with ARDS and malignancy (mean age 10.5 +/- 5.1 years) who required mechanical ventilation in a pediatric intensive care unit between January 1987 and January 1997: peak inspiratory pressure, positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP), and ventilation index values could distinguish outcome by day 3.

In the same cohort, a significant relationship between respiratory data and outcome related to efficiency of oxygenation, as determined by PaO(2)/FIO(2) and P(A-a)O(2), was present from day 8 after onset of mechanical ventilation.

Because the evidence comes from a retrospective chart review rather than a prospective study, the reported respiratory predictors are associations with outcome and do not establish that altering peak inspiratory pressure, PEEP, ventilation index, or oxygenation parameters would change survival.

Yes — in a retrospective review of rattlesnake bites, aggressive polyvalent antivenin use produced acute side effects in 12 of the 65 patients treated (18%; 95% confidence interval, 10%-30%), but these reactions consisted solely of urticaria in all but 1 patient, so serious acute reactions were rare.

Acute side effects were counted as those occurring within the first 6 hours after antivenin administration; the single patient whose reaction was not limited to urticaria (2%; 95% confidence interval, 0%-8%) had a history of previous antivenin reaction and required a short course of intravenous epinephrine for blood pressure support.
No other complications occurred in this series.

The review identified 73 patients with rattlesnake bites during an 11-year period, of whom 65 received antivenin; doses ranged from 1 to 30 vials per patient (mean, 12.0 +/- 6.0), totaling 777 vials, and 43 patients (66%) received 10 or more vials, indicating a relatively aggressive dosing practice.

Because the data came from a retrospective record review and serum sickness data were not collected, the reported rates describe immediate (within 6 hours) hypersensitivity reactions only and cannot address delayed reactions.

Increasing the nerve length within the treatment volume did not improve pain relief in trigeminal neuralgia radiosurgery: in 87 patients with typical trigeminal neuralgia randomized to retrogasserian gamma knife radiosurgery (75 Gy maximal dose, 4-mm collimators) with one isocenter (n = 44) or two isocenters (n = 43), pain relief was identical for one- and two-isocenter radiosurgery.

Facial numbness and mild and severe paresthesias developed in 8, 5, and 1 two-isocenter patients versus 3, 4, and 0 one-isocenter patients, respectively (p = 0.23), and complications (numbness or paresthesias) correlated with the nerve length irradiated (p = 0.018), so the longer irradiated nerve length was associated with greater toxicity rather than better pain relief.

In a prospective convenience sample of children with a first episode of wheezing, clinical variables did not reliably identify pathologic radiographs: the discriminant analysis correctly predicted 90% of nonpathologic radiographs but only 15% of pathologic radiographs.

Pathologic radiographs were identified in 61 patients (9%); data collected included demographics, baseline and post-treatment clinical score and physical examination, number of aerosols, requirement for supplemental oxygen, and disposition, and patients were divided into 2 groups based on pathologic versus nonpathologic radiograph interpretation.

Chi2 testing was used for categoric variables and the student t test for continuous variables; between groups a significant difference was noted for pretreatment oxygen saturation only, whereas clinical score, respiratory rate, and presence of rales both pretreatment and posttreatment were not significantly different between groups.

A discriminant analysis was used to develop the model, and the study objective was to determine whether clinical variables assessed in relation to albuterol aerosol treatments accurately identify children with pathologic radiographs during their initial episode of bronchospasm.

An observational study in a district general hospital of all patients admitted to hospital aged over 75 years with fracture of the proximal femur over 3 1/2 years found that delay in transfer to a rehabilitation ward was associated with a longer total hospital length of stay of 0.64 (95% CI 0.23-1.05) days per day of delay in transfer.

Outcome data collected included the number of patients discharged back to their usual residence and total hospital length of stay, related to age, gender, usual residence and delay in transfer to a rehabilitation ward.
58% of 455 patients were transferred to a rehabilitation ward.

For those patients who were transferred to a rehabilitation ward, only age predicted discharge to a more dependent residence; the relative risk for discharge to a more dependent residence for people aged over 85 years compared to younger people was 1.47 (95% CI 1.15-1.88).

Because the evidence comes from an observational study design, it can demonstrate an association between delay in transfer and longer hospital stay but cannot establish that reducing the delay would itself improve outcomes.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: Antral follicle assessment as a tool for predicting outcome in IVF.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: direct comparison of predictive accuracy vs age and FSH.

The study was undertaken to show the results of treating posterior uveal melanomas with 106Ru plaque beta-ray radiotherapy and to review and discuss the literature concerning the optimal apical dose prescription (100 vs.
Forty-eight patients with uveal melanomas (median height 3.85 mm plus 1 mm sclera) were treated with ruthenium plaques; the median apical dose was 120 Gy and the median scleral dose was 546 Gy.
Local control was achieved in 90% of the patients with conservative therapy alone; 6% received a second ruthenium application and 10% of the eyes had to be enucleated.
After 5.8 years of follow-up, the overall 5-year survival rate was 90% and the disease-specific 5-year survival rate was 92%, with 3 patients alive with metastasis.
Central or paracentral tumors showed 50% of the pretherapeutic vision after 4 years, and 80% of the vision was preserved in those with peripheral tumors.
The main side effects were mostly an uncomplicated retinopathy (30%), and macular degeneration or scarring led to poor central vision in 30% of cases.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: Comparison of treatment outcomes between escalated and standard apical doses.

Bottom line: the cited evidence supports looking further when retinal haemorrhage is found after convulsions — in a prospective study of 153 children seen in the emergency department after a convulsive episode, one child had unilateral retinal haemorrhages following a simple febrile convulsion, and a thorough investigation uncovered no other reason for this finding.

The prevalence of retinal haemorrhages after convulsions is not well established, and because these haemorrhages are considered characteristic of child abuse, the study investigated their occurrence after convulsive episodes to see whether the finding of haemorrhage should prompt further investigation.

The study was a prospective study of 153 children aged 2 months to 2 years who were seen in the emergency department after a convulsive episode; after a thorough history and physical examination, a retinal examination was performed by an ophthalmologist, and when findings were positive, further investigation was undertaken to rule out systemic disorder or child abuse.

Only one child was found with unilateral retinal haemorrhages following an episode of a simple febrile convulsion, and a thorough investigation uncovered no other reason for this finding, so this single case in 153 children does not establish the prevalence of retinal haemorrhage after convulsions.
Hepatitis G virus-RNA was detected in 4 out of 23 patients with cryptogenic chronic hepatitis and in 6 out of 40 with hepatitis C virus chronic hepatitis (17.4% vs 15% p=ns).

At least one marker of hepatitis G virus infection (hepatitis G virus-RNA and/or anti-hepatitis G virus, mostly mutually exclusive) was present in 6 out of 23 patients with cryptogenic hepatitis and 16 out of 40 with hepatitis C virus liver disease (26.
Demographic and clinical features, including stage and grade of liver histology, were comparable between hepatitis G virus-infected and uninfected subjects.
T virus-DNA was present in serum in 3 subjects, 1 with cryptogenic and 2 with hepatitis C virus-related chronic liver disease.
The study included a total of 23 subjects with chronically raised alanine transaminase and a liver biopsy in whom all known causes of liver disease had been excluded.
The study also included 40 subjects with hepatitis C virus-related chronic liver disease.
TT virus-DNA was present in serum in only 3 subjects, 1 with cryptogenic and 2 with hepatitis C virus-related chronic liver disease.

The cited evidence is insufficient to establish that the inter-arm blood pressure difference predicts the severity of steal in subclavian steal syndrome (SSS); it reports only a retrospective comparison in which the systolic blood pressure difference was significantly higher in the complete reversal and alternating waveform groups than in the systolic deceleration group (P<.001).

The records of 1860 patients from the Neuroultrasound Laboratory between January 2000 and December 2000 were screened for a final ultrasound report diagnosis of SSS, which was found in 51 of 1860 (2.7%) ultrasonography studies of 49 patients (17 men, 32 women; mean age 65.3 +/- 10.5 years).

In all patients, bilateral brachial arterial blood pressure was measured in a sitting position prior to the ultrasound examination, and the blood pressure difference calculated as normal-side blood pressure minus lesion-side blood pressure was compared with 3 Doppler vertebral artery waveform types classified as (1) systolic deceleration, (2) alternating flow, and (3) complete reversal at rest.
Waveform analysis showed a completely reversed flow in 16 (31%), an alternating flow in 24 (47%), and a systolic deceleration in 11 (22%) cases.

Because the source reports a retrospective comparison of inter-arm systolic blood pressure difference against Doppler waveform type rather than a prospective predictive model, no predictive accuracy or prospective prediction of steal severity from the inter-arm blood pressure difference is established.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: Predictive accuracy or prospective prediction of steal severity from the inter-arm blood pressure difference.

Admission to a hospital with onsite coronary revascularization services was not associated with improved survival among elderly patients with acute myocardial infarction complicated by cardiogenic shock: after adjustment for demographic, clinical, hospital, and treatment strategies, onsite revascularization services were not associated with a significantly lower 30-day mortality (odds ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.47, 1.45) or 1-year mortality (odds ratio 0.91, 95% CI 0.49, 1.72).

In the same retrospective medical record review of Cooperative Cardiovascular Project Medicare patients aged 65 years or older, patients admitted to hospitals with revascularization services were more likely to undergo coronary revascularization during the index hospitalization and during the first month after acute myocardial infarction, although clinical characteristics were similar across the subgroups.

Of the 601 patients with cardiogenic shock, 287 (47.8%) were admitted to hospitals without revascularization services and 314 (52.2%) were admitted to hospitals with coronary angioplasty and coronary artery bypass surgery facilities.

Because the comparison rests on a retrospective medical record review of patients grouped by the admitting hospital's available services rather than on randomized allocation to a tertiary center, the finding of no significant adjusted mortality difference is an observational association and cannot establish that transferring or admitting such patients to a revascularization-capable hospital would improve survival.

No — in a tonsillectomy audit, postoperative antibiotics had no role in pain control, postoperative fever, secondary hemorrhage or reduction in hospital stay, indicating they did not decrease morbidity after tonsillectomy.
That audit comprised 185 patients who underwent tonsillectomy with or without adenoidectomy, with ages ranging from 2 to 53 years and a majority of children.
The same audit found no difference in surgical outcome according to grade of surgeon or method of hemostasis, and reported that as-required analgesic administration gave poor pain control.

In a review of 400 patients with renal cell carcinoma treated between January 1988 and February 2001, the cited evidence suggests pelvic CT adds little to routine evaluation, because only 14 patients (3.5%) had any abnormality on pelvic CT and all of those pelvic abnormalities had already been detected before CT by other investigations (ultrasonography or plain x-ray); the study was explicitly designed to determine the necessity of pelvic CT in RCC.

Of the 400 RCC patients, 14 (3.5%) had an abnormality on pelvic CT: 5 (1.25%) had a category 1 abnormality (benign and likely insignificant), 3 (0.75%) a category 2 abnormality (benign and likely significant), and 6 (1.5%) a category 3 (malignant) abnormality.
Of the six patients with malignant pelvic findings, two had superficial bladder cancer, one had RCC in a pelvic kidney, and three had bone metastases in the pelvis.

Because this was a retrospective record review in which every pelvic abnormality had been identified by ultrasonography or plain x-ray before pelvic CT, the design supports the interpretation that pelvic CT provided no unique diagnostic yield in this cohort, though it does not by itself establish that omitting pelvic CT would leave no abnormality undetected in other populations.

For lipids, serum cholesterol was a significant risk factor for both sexes, with hazard ratios decreasing with age, whereas triglyceride risk was significantly higher for women and decreased significantly with age, so lipid-related risk was not equal between sexes.
For blood pressure, systolic blood pressure was a stronger risk factor for women, as was ECG-confirmed left ventricular hypertrophy (women HR 2.89, 95% CI 1.67-5.01; men HR 1.11, 95% CI 0.86-1.43).
For diabetes, fasting blood glucose of 6.7 mmol/L or greater identified significantly higher risk for women (HR 2.65) than for men (HR 2.08), as did self-reported diabetes.
For smoking, risk increased two- to five-fold with increasing dose for women, significantly higher than the doubling in risk for men.

The cited evidence indicates that these risk factors did not confer equal risk of myocardial infarction in women and men: in this study, systolic blood pressure, diabetes, triglycerides and smoking were each significantly stronger risk factors for women than for men.

Muscle power is only partly related to running speed with changes of direction: in 15 male participants timed in 8 m sprints, correlations between speed while changing direction and concentric leg power were generally low and non-significant, whereas some moderate and statistically significant (p<0.05) coefficients were found for reactive strength.
The 15 participants were male, required to be free of injury and to have recent experience competing in sports involving sprints with changes of direction.

Speed was assessed by timing the participants in 8 m sprints in a straight line and with various changes of direction, and muscle power was assessed as bilateral and unilateral leg extensor concentric power output by an isokinetic squat together with reactive strength by a drop jump.
Among these participants, those who turned faster to one side tended to show a reactive strength dominance in the leg responsible for the push-off action.

Because the study was designed to describe relationships between physical qualities and a component of sports performance, its reported correlations are associations and do not establish that changing muscle power would improve running speed with changes of direction.

Yes — the cited physiologic evidence supports that mossy fibers release GABA: mossy fiber terminals show intense immunoreactivity for the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA and for GAD67, and electrical stimuli that recruit dentate granule cells elicit monosynaptic GABAA receptor-mediated synaptic signals in CA3 pyramidal neurons.

The evidence for GABA release by mossy fibers comes from guinea pig hippocampal slices (3- to 5-week-old animals) with whole-cell voltage clamp recordings from CA3 pyramidal cells and stimulating electrodes placed in stratum granulosum and adjusted to recruit mossy fiber-to-CA3 projections, i.e., an ex vivo animal preparation rather than human tissue.

These inhibitory signals satisfy the criteria that distinguish mossy fiber-CA3 synapses: high sensitivity to metabotropic glutamate-receptor agonists, facilitation during repetitive stimulation, and N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor-independent long-term potentiation.
The review's stated purpose is to present physiologic evidence of GABA release by mossy fibers and its modulation by epileptic activity.
Yes: in the U.K.

Prospective Diabetes Study, among 5,088 of 5,102 participants grouped by fasting plasma glucose (FPG) at diagnosis (low <140 mg/dl [<7.8 mmol/l], intermediate 140 to <180 mg/dl [7.8 to <10.0 mmol/l], high >or =180 mg/dl [>or =10 mmol/l]), lower FPG at diagnosis was associated with reduced risk of several predefined clinical outcomes.
Fewer people with FPG in the lowest category had retinopathy, abnormal biothesiometer measurements, or reported erectile dysfunction.

Individuals in the low FPG group had a significantly reduced risk for each predefined clinical outcome except stroke, whereas those in the intermediate group had significantly reduced risk for each outcome except stroke and myocardial infarction.
The low and intermediate FPG groups had a significantly reduced risk for progression of retinopathy, reduction in vibration sensory threshold, or development of microalbuminuria.
The rate of increase in FPG and HbA(1c) during the study was identical in all three groups, although absolute differences persisted.

Because this was an observational comparison of groups defined by FPG at diagnosis, with type 2 diabetes potentially present for years before diagnosis and evidence supporting earlier detection and treatment described as lacking, the findings cannot establish that lowering FPG at diagnosis itself causes improved outcomes.

Anorectal endosonography appears valuable in dyschesia: in a prospective study it demonstrated paradoxical shortening and/or thickening during straining of the anal sphincter in 85% of patients versus 35% of healthy controls and of the m. puborectalis in 80% versus 30%, with both differences statistically significant (p<0.01, chi(2) test).
The prospective study was designed to demonstrate dysfunction of the anal sphincter and/or the musculus (m.) puborectalis in patients with dyschesia using anorectal endosonography.

Twenty consecutive patients with a medical history of dyschesia and a control group of 20 healthy subjects underwent linear anorectal endosonography (Toshiba models IUV 5060 and PVL-625 RT), with dimensions of the anal sphincter and m. puborectalis measured in both groups at rest and during voluntary squeezing and straining.

The anal sphincter became paradoxically shorter and/or thicker during straining compared with the resting state in 85% of patients but in only 35% of control subjects, and the changes in sphincter length were statistically significantly different between patients and controls (p<0.01, chi(2) test).

The m. puborectalis became paradoxically shorter and/or thicker during straining in 80% of patients but in only 30% of controls, and both the changes in its length and its thickness were significantly different in patients versus control subjects (p<0.01, chi(2) test).

The cited evidence does not establish that withdrawal-induced anxiety in alcoholism is based on beta-endorphin deficiency; it reports an association between lowered plasma beta-endorphin levels and self-rated anxiety during withdrawal, which cannot by itself demonstrate that a beta-endorphin deficit causes the anxiety.

In a consecutive sample of 60 alcoholics assessed on day 1 and day 14 after onset of withdrawal and in 30 healthy volunteers, plasma beta-endorphin (beta E), measured by RIA, was significantly lowered on both day 1 and day 14 of alcohol withdrawal relative to controls.
Self-rated anxiety, depression, and alcohol craving in these alcoholics decreased significantly between day 1 and day 14 of withdrawal.
Beta-endorphin levels were inversely correlated with anxiety on day 1 (r=-0.58) and on day 14 (r=-0.71) of withdrawal.
Partial correlation coefficients controlling for ACTH plasma levels indicated that the inverse beta-endorphin–anxiety correlation was largely independent of ACTH.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: causal determination that beta-endorphin deficiency underlies withdrawal-induced anxiety.

In a randomized trial of 260 women with measurable metastatic breast cancer fulfilling high-risk criteria who had not previously received chemotherapy for metastatic disease, first-line single-agent mitoxantrone 12 mg/m(2) did not differ significantly from the combination FEC (fluorouracil 500 mg/m(2), epirubicin 50 mg/m(2), cyclophosphamide 500 mg/m(2)), each given every 3 weeks, in terms of response, objective remission rate, remission duration, time to response, time to best response, time to progression or overall survival.

The same trial found a significant difference in gain from treatment, assessed with a modified Brunner's score composed of time to progression, patients' rating of treatment benefit, alopecia, vomiting and performance status, and this difference favored the single-agent mitoxantrone arm.
In this trial there was no evidence that any subgroup of high-risk metastatic breast cancer patients would fare better with the combination treatment than with single-agent mitoxantrone.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: Inflammatory markers or findings in pre-eclampsia/HELLP.

In a prospective randomized study conducted at a single community hospital in 240 adults undergoing general anesthesia, the right internal jugular vein was cannulated using either anatomic landmarks or prepuncture ultrasound (3.75/7.5 MHz) guidance.
In the landmark group, respiratory jugular venodilation was used as the primary landmark for locating the vein.

Respiratory jugular venodilation was identified in 188 patients (78.3%), in whom results of cannulation did not differ between the 2 techniques with respect to the venous access rate (cannulated at the first attempt: 83.5% in the landmark v 85.7% in the ultrasound group), the success rate (cannulated within 3 attempts: 96.9% v 95.6%), and the incidence of arterial puncture (1.0% v 3.3%).

In the remaining 52 respiratory jugular venodilation-unidentified patients, the access rate (30.4% v 86.2%, p<0.001) and the success rate (78.3 v 100%, p<0.05) were significantly better in the ultrasound group, and no arterial puncture was recorded in the ultrasound group, whereas the incidence was 13.0% in the landmark group.
The results were similar regardless of the ultrasound frequency used.

Taken together, prepuncture ultrasound did not improve cannulation results in the 188 patients in whom respiratory jugular venodilation was identified, but it did improve the venous access rate and success rate and reduced arterial puncture in the 52 patients in whom respiratory jugular venodilation was not identified.

Yes—among 50 patients scheduled for total hip replacement allocated to two groups in a double-blind, randomized manner, all patients were pretreated for 2 weeks before surgery: Group 1 with placebo drug, Group 2 with ibuprofen; perioperative blood loss increased by 45% in the ibuprofen group compared with placebo, and the total (+/-SD) blood loss in the ibuprofen group was 1161 (+/-472) mL versus 796 (+/-337) mL in the placebo group.
The presence of severe adverse effects caused eight patients in the ibuprofen group and six in the placebo group to terminate their participation in the trial.

Patients receiving written information scored significantly higher (48% correct answers) than patients receiving verbal information (38% correct answers), indicating that a written information sheet improves recall.
The test group was 126 patients undergoing revision or primary total hip arthroplasty; 65 patients were given information verbally, 61 patients were given written information.

Patients were divided into 4 groups, on the basis of their pattern of outpatient care over a 12-month period after discharge: 1) general medicine clinic visits only (GM-only); 2) cardiology clinic visits only (CARD-only); 3) general medicine and cardiology (MIXED) clinic visits; and 4) neither general medicine nor cardiology clinic visits (no-GM/CARD).

In a retrospective cohort study conducted with national Veterans Health Administration (VHA) databases, 11,661 patients discharged from VA hospitals between October 1, 1991, and September 30, 1992, with the primary diagnosis of CHF (cohort 1) were examined for the association between the pattern of outpatient care and survival; 1-year survival was evaluated with the Cox proportional hazards model, controlling for clinical and demographic factors.

The overall 1-year mortality rate was 23% in the primary cohort; the unadjusted mortality rate was highest for patients in the no-GM/CARD follow up (29%) and lowest for patients in the MIXED group (19%).

By use of the MIXED group as reference and adjusting for important clinical and demographic factors, the risk of death (risk ratio [95% CI]) was 1.12 (0.94-1.34) in the CARD-only group, 1.26 (1.15-1.38) in the GM-only group, and 1.48 (1.28-1.72) in the no-GM/CARD group.

Consistency of the results was examined by performing identical analysis on a cohort of patients discharged from VHA hospitals between October 1, 1994, and September 30, 1995 (cohort 2, n = 10,141); cohort-2 results were consistent with cohort 1 for most covariates, and significant survival differences were again found between the GM-only and the MIXED group (1.25 [1.14-1.37]).

Because the cited study is an observational retrospective cohort analysis of care patterns rather than a randomized comparison of care settings, its results establish an association between outpatient care pattern and 1-year survival and cannot establish that receiving specialty care itself causes improved survival.

In gastric cancer patients who had undergone gastrectomy with D2-lymphadenectomy, body mass index was associated with long-term survival, but the direction of the association differed by stage: a significantly longer mean survival rate was observed for the lower body mass index group (<0.185) in stage 2 (1667 vs.
1322 days, P = 0.0240), while a significantly longer mean survival rate was observed for the higher body mass index group (>0.210) in stage 3a (1431 vs.

The study's stated aim was to clarify the relationship between the degree of patients' body mass index and their long-term survival, and patients' morbidity and long-term survival rate were retrospectively compared between the lower and higher body mass index groups.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: actual morbidity comparison between lower and higher BMI groups.

Yes — in a case-control study, farming, occupational silica and solvent exposure, drug allergy and allergy overall were significantly associated with primary systemic vasculitis (PSV), so the cited evidence supports environmental factors being important in PSV.

The study interviewed 75 PSV cases and 273 controls (220 nonvasculitis, 19 secondary vasculitis, and 34 asthma controls) with a structured questionnaire, and investigated social class, occupational and residential history, smoking, pets, allergies, vaccinations, medications, hepatitis, tuberculosis, and farm exposure in the year before symptom onset (the index year).
Odds ratios (OR) and 95% confidence intervals (95% CI) adjusted for potential confounders were calculated using stepwise multiple logistic regression.

Farming in the index year was significantly associated with PSV (OR 2.3 [95% CI 1.2-4.6]), Wegener's granulomatosis (WG) (2.7 [1.2-5.8]), microscopic polyangiitis (MPA) (6.3 [1.9-21.6]), and perinuclear ANCA (pANCA) (4.3 [1.5-12.7]).
Farming during working lifetime was associated with PSV (2.2 [1.2-3.8]) and with WG (2.7 [1.3-5.7]).

Significant associations were reported for high occupational silica exposure in the index year with PSV (3.0 [1.0-8.4]), Churg-Strauss syndrome (CSS) (5.6 [1.3-23.5]) and ANCA (4.9 [1.3-18.6]); for high occupational solvent exposure in the index year with PSV (3.4 [0.9-12.5]), WG (4.8 [1.2-19.8]) and classic ANCA (cANCA) (3.9 [1.6-9.5]); for high occupational solvent exposure during working lifetime with PSV (2.7 [1.1-6.6]), WG (3.4 [1.3-8.9]) and cANCA (3.3 [1.0-10.8]); for drug allergy with PSV (3.6 [1.8-7.0]), WG (4.0 [1.8-8.7]) and cANCA (4.7 [1.9-11.7]); and for allergy overall with PSV (2.2 [1.2-3.9]) and WG (2.7 [1.4-5.7]).
No other significant associations were found among the factors investigated.

Because these findings come from a case-control comparison of self-reported exposures between PSV cases and controls, they establish associations between the reported environmental exposures and PSV rather than demonstrating that changing these exposures prevents or improves the disease.

Socioeconomic status did matter for quality of life in newly diagnosed lung cancer patients at baseline, but not at the three-month follow-up assessment: lower-status patients reported more health problems, less functioning and more symptoms than affluent patients initially, yet at follow-up there was no significant difference between the groups and no consistent pattern emerged.

In this prospective study, 129 lung cancer patients entered, and complete data at both baseline and follow-up were available for 82 patients; 57% of patients were of lower socioeconomic status, and these patients had more health problems, less functioning and more symptoms compared with affluent patients.

Socioeconomic status was derived for each patient using the Carstairs and Morris Deprivation Category ranging from 1 (least deprived) to 7 (most deprived) on the basis of the postcode sector of their address.

At baseline, the differences between socioeconomic groups were statistically significant for physical mobility (P = 0.05), energy (P = 0.01), role functioning (P = 0.04), physical functioning (P = 0.03) and breathlessness (P = 0.02); quality of life was measured with the Nottingham Health Profile, the EORTC QLQ-C30 and its lung cancer supplement QLQ-LC13 at baseline and three months after initial treatment.

At the follow-up assessment three months after initial treatment, there was no significant difference in quality of life between the socioeconomic patient groups, nor did any consistent pattern emerge.

Studies on experimental models and patients with intractable epilepsy suggest that apoptosis may be involved in neuronal death induced by recurrent seizures. the authors searched evidence for apoptotic cell death in temporal lobes resected from drug-resistant epilepsy patients with MTS by using the terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) and digoxigenin-11-dUTP (TUNEL) method and immunohistochemistry for Bcl-2, Bax, and caspase-cleaved actin fragment, fractin.
The temporal lobe specimens were obtained from 15 patients (six women and nine men; mean age, 29 +/- 8 years).

Unlike that in normal adult brain, the authors observed Bcl-2 immunoreactivity in some of the remaining neurons dispersed throughout the hippocampus proper as well as in most of the reactive astroglia.
Bax immunopositivity was increased in almost all neurons.
Fractin immunostaining, an indicator of caspase activity, was detected in approximately 10% of these neurons.

The study found no evidence for apoptotic cell death in these MTS specimens: despite increased Bax expression and activation of caspases, the authors could not find evidence for DNA fragmentation by TUNEL staining, and the authors also could not detect typical apoptotic changes in nuclear morphology by Hoechst-33258 or hematoxylin counterstaining.
In the absence of data from a clinical trial, the authors used a decision-analysis model to compare the expected values of 2 treatment strategies-warfarin and no anticoagulation-for such patients.
For patients with prior lobar ICH, withholding anticoagulation therapy was strongly preferred, improving quality-adjusted life expectancy by 1.9 QALYs.
For patients with prior deep hemispheric ICH, withholding anticoagulation resulted in a smaller gain of 0.3 QALYs.
In sensitivity analyses for patients with deep ICH, anticoagulation could be preferred if the risk of thromboembolic stroke is particularly high.

Warfarin increases both the likelihood and the mortality of intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH), particularly in patients with a history of prior ICH. the authors used a Markov state transition decision model stratified by location of hemorrhage (lobar or deep hemispheric).

Yes — the cited prospective randomized trial supports a 9-month anti-tuberculous regimen as sufficient in tuberculous enterocolitis, since complete response was obtained in all patients in both the 9-month and 15-month groups and no recurrence of active intestinal tuberculosis occurred during the follow-up period in either group.
Forty patients with tuberculous enterocolitis were randomized prospectively, 22 into a 9-month and 18 into a 15-month treatment group.
Complete response, defined as resolution of symptoms and of active tuberculosis by colonoscopy, was obtained in all patients in both the 9-month and the 15-month groups.
No recurrence of active intestinal tuberculosis occurred during the follow-up period in either the 9-month or the 15-month group.
Two patients in the 9-month group and one patient in the 15-month group underwent operation, for intestinal obstruction and perianal fistula respectively.

In a study in CD Fischer rats, Nd:YAG laser-induced thermo therapy (LITT) of the left forebrain was associated with blood-brain barrier (BBB) permeability changes; BBB disruption was analyzed using Evans blue and immunohistochemistry, and LITT induced locoregional opening of the BBB as demonstrated by extravasation of Evans blue, C3C, fibrinogen, and IgM.

In the same rat experiments, animals were perfused with paclitaxel and high-pressure liquid chromatography (HPLC) was used to measure paclitaxel content in brain and plasma samples; HPLC demonstrated passage of paclitaxel across the disrupted BBB.

The study addressed the question of whether LITT-induced locoregional disruption of the BBB could allow locoregional passage of chemotherapeutic agents into brain tissue to treat malignant glioma; the retrieved evidence supports this as a proposed concept only, and does not report an actual adjuvant glioma therapeutic effect such as tumor response or survival.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: actual adjuvant glioma therapeutic effect (e.g., tumor response or survival).

The cited evidence does not support that progression of valvar aortic stenosis can be predicted with a quantitative measure of accuracy, because the study reports determinants and catheterization-based thresholds of hemodynamic progression rather than discrimination, calibration, sensitivity, or specificity for progression.

In a study whose aim was to elaborate criteria for assessing rapid hemodynamic progression of valvar aortic stenosis, hemodynamic, echocardiographic, and clinical data were analyzed for 169 men and 88 women with aortic stenosis, aged 55.2 +/- 15.7 years at their first and 63.4 +/- 15.6 years at their second cardiac catheterization.

The progression rate of aortic valve obstruction was found to be dependent on the degree of valvar calcification (VC scoring 0 to III) and to be exponentially correlated with the aortic valve opening area (AVA) at initial catheterization.
Neither age nor sex of the patient nor etiology of the valvar obstruction significantly influenced the progression of aortic stenosis.

The study proposed threshold values at which operation in the following years was considered probable: AVA below 0.75 cm(2) with a present degree of VC = 0, AVA of 0.8 with VC of I, AVA of 0.9 with VC of II, or AVA of 1.0 with VC of III.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: a quantitative measure of predictive accuracy for progression of valvar aortic stenosis.

Yes — the cited evidence indicates that communication with terminally ill patients can be taught: models of courses that resulted in improvements in participants' communicative skills have been published mainly in the Anglo-American literature, and a 2-day course model based on the first three courses of this kind in Rhineland-Palatinate, attended by 31 participants, was described and analyzed for changes in participants' communication behavior.

In that German course evaluation, participants gave high satisfaction scores for the methods and for the clarity and relevance of the contents; participants' self-assessment on a visual analog scale across seven communication settings showed a growing sense of security, with important increases for communicating a cancer diagnosis with good or less good prognosis, recurrence of cancer, or far advanced cancer without a curative approach, and 3 months after the course participants described multiple changes indicating increased sensibility and professionalism in their communication behavior.

As a limitation entailed by the study design, these reported improvements rest on satisfaction evaluation forms completed after each course and on participants' own ratings of their sense of security and perceived changes in communication behavior, so the study does not provide an objective or external measure that the course improved actual communication with terminally ill patients.

The cited evidence does not establish an effect of nurse home visits on the adequacy of newborn metabolic screening: the single relevant study compared early newborn discharge (defined as discharge between 24 and 47 hours of age) with traditional stay and reported no nurse home visit intervention.

In that study, metabolic screening tests included phenylketonuria (PKU), hypothyroidism, and congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH), and results were matched from the Alabama State Lab for infants born 8/1/97-1/31/99, yielding specimens from 3860 infants: 1324 early discharge newborns and 2536 traditional stay infants.
At least one filter paper test (PKU, hypothyroidism, or CAH) was collected on 99.2% of early discharge infants versus 96.0% of traditional stay infants (P<.0001).

Early discharge infants had a higher rate of initial filter paper specimens being inadequate (22.9%) than traditional stay infants (14.3%, P<.0001), but a higher rate of repeat specimens when the initial specimen was inadequate (85.0% early discharge vs 75.3% traditional stay, P=.002).
The early discharge group was more likely to have an adequate specimen within the first 9 days of life: 1001 infants (98.8%) versus 2016 infants (96.7%) in the traditional stay group (P=.0005).
The retrieved evidence does not establish: effect of nurse home visits on adequacy of newborn metabolic screening.

The randomised evidence indicates that the sequence of clamp application during open abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) repair does not influence distal embolisation: among 40 patients randomised to first clamping of the proximal aorta or of the iliac vessels, there was no difference between the two groups in the number of emboli detected (p=0.49), and no significant correlation between the number of emboli and dissection time (r=0.0008).
Reports have suggested that preferential clamping of the distal vessel(s) before the proximal aorta may decrease the number of emboli passing distally and hence reduce complications.
In that randomised study of 40 patients undergoing AAA repair, emboli passing through the superficial femoral arteries were detected with a transcranial Doppler ultrasound system.

The cited evidence on whether breast cancer survival is improving is mixed: survival improved significantly in unadjusted analyses of recurrent breast cancer and prognosis improved considerably for patients diagnosed before age 50 years, but in the adjusted analysis of recurrent disease the improvement was only a trend.

Among 834 women who developed recurrent breast cancer between November 1974 and December 2000 and were divided into five consecutive groups by year of recurrence, the unadjusted analysis showed a statistically significant improvement in survival across the five groups, with the more recent cohorts having longer survival (P<0.001).

In the multivariate model of that recurrent breast cancer cohort, which adjusted for prognostic factors including initial tumor size, stage, lymph node involvement, disease-free interval, estrogen receptor status and dominant site of recurrence, year of recurrence was associated with only a trend toward improved survival, with a 1% reduction in risk for each increasing year.
In a large population-based sample of patients diagnosed with breast cancer before age 50 years, prognosis has considerably improved during the past decades.

According to the latest estimates from period analysis in that study, cumulative 40-year relative survival is now approximately 43% for all cancers combined, 57% for localized cancers, and 24% for cancers with regional tumor spread.

Despite the improvement, patients diagnosed with breast cancer before age 50 years continue to have increased mortality throughout at least four decades after diagnosis, including when the cancer is diagnosed in a localized stage and in the absence of a second primary breast cancer.

Because the reported improvement in the recurrent breast cancer cohort was statistically significant only in the unadjusted comparison and was reduced to a trend after adjustment for prognostic factors, that study design does not by itself establish that later year of recurrence independently improves survival.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: breast cancer survival improvement for all breast cancer patients overall.

Yes — among prostate cancer patients who developed metastases, a favorable subset appears to exist by metastatic lesion number: patients with ≤5 metastatic lesions had superior survival rates compared with those with >5 lesions (73% and 36% at 5 and 10 years vs 45% and 18% at 5 and 10 years, respectively; p = 0.02).

This finding comes from a retrospective analysis of 369 eligible patients with Stage T1-T3aN0-NXM0 prostate cancer treated with curative-intent external beam radiotherapy and followed for a minimum of 10 years, of whom 74 (20%) developed metastases; survival among those who developed metastases was significantly reduced at both 5 and 10 years (p < 0.0001) relative to patients who never developed metastases.

Both the metastasis-free survival rate and the interval from initial prostate cancer diagnosis to the development of bone metastasis were statistically superior for patients with ≤5 lesions compared with those with >5 lesions (p = 0.01 and 0.02, respectively).
However, once bone metastasis was diagnosed, the two groups did not differ significantly in survival rate or in the interval from bone metastasis diagnosis to death (p = 0.17 and 0.27, respectively).

Because the reported analysis was retrospective, the superior outcomes observed in patients with ≤5 metastatic lesions represent an association within the documented cohort rather than evidence that any treatment of oligometastatic disease causes improved survival.

The cited evidence does not establish whether a practicing surgeon can reliably detect early lymphedema; the only relevant data report the sensitivity and specificity of circumference-based criteria compared against an academic trial standard, so the reliability of surgeon detection itself remains unsupported.

In that prospective academic trial, 90 breast cancer patients were enrolled and seven upper extremity circumferences were measured quarterly for 3 years, yielding 39 cases of lymphedema identified by the trial.

The report states that lymphedema may be identified by simpler circumference changes compared with changes in limb volume, and that a 10% volume increase or a greater than 1 cm increase in arm circumference identified lymphedema with verification by a lymphedema specialist.

Using a 10% increase in circumference at two sites as the criterion, half the lymphedema cases were detected, giving a sensitivity of 37%, whereas a 10% increase at any site detected 74.4% of cases (sensitivity 49%).
Detection by a 5% increase in circumference at any site was 91% sensitive.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: reliability of a practicing surgeon in detecting early lymphedema.

Yes — pain appears to be a clinically relevant problem in general adult psychiatry: in a cross-sectional questionnaire study of 106 patients primarily diagnosed with a psychiatric disorder in the field of general adult psychiatry, the point prevalence of pain was about 50%, the 6-month prevalence was 75.5% and the 12-month prevalence was 76.5%.
The most frequent pain complaints among these patients were low back pain, headache, and shoulder and neck pain.

Patients with affective disorders most frequently had pain complaints, followed by those with neurotic, stress-related and somatoform disorders, and then those with psychotic disorders such as schizophrenia, schizotypic and delusional disorders.
Almost 10% of all patients reported pain that continued at least 3 months in the past year, and impairment and unfitness for work were related to the specific psychiatric diagnosis.
Statistically significant risk factors for pain were depression (OR=6.05) and the number of past admissions to psychiatric hospitals (OR=3.609).

Because the study used a cross-sectional questionnaire design, it can establish the prevalence of pain, its duration, associated impairment and unfitness for work, and statistical associations with potential risk factors, but it cannot establish that pain causes, or is caused by, psychiatric disorders.

Cranial CT can distinguish communicating from non-communicating hydrocephalus in tuberculous meningitis only to a limited degree: the sole CT finding that correlated with the type of hydrocephalus was the shape of the third ventricle, so CT does not predict the CSF block level through multiple independent indices.

In that study, a number of CT indices were measured in 50 children with communicating and 34 children with non-communicating hydrocephalus, with the type of hydrocephalus defined according to air-encephalographic findings.
Significantly more children with non-communicating hydrocephalus had a rounded third ventricle than children with communicating hydrocephalus.

In 17 hypertensive patients (mean age 59 +/- 9 years), acute increases in heart rate produced by isoproterenol did not significantly affect aortic stiffness: when percent changes in the aortic stiffness parameters (deltaPWV, deltaC and deltaCi) were grouped by every 10% increase in deltaHR, there was no significant difference among the groups (p>0.05 for each).

In that study, carotid-to-femoral pulse wave velocity was measured by the foot-to-foot method, pulse waves were recorded at baseline and at every 5 to 10 bpm increase in heart rate achieved by gradually increasing the isoproterenol dose, blood pressure and heart rate were measured simultaneously, and heart rate, PWV, compliance (C) and compliance index (Ci) were converted to percent changes (delta) from baseline values for analysis.

Regression analysis in the same 17 hypertensive patients showed no significant correlation of deltaHR with deltaPWV (r = 0.18) or deltaC (r = 0.13) (p>0.05 for each), whereas deltaCi had only a poor correlation with deltaHR (r = 0.22, p<0.05), with just 4.6% of deltaCi attributable to deltaHR (r2 = 0.046).

The message patients with diabetes receive is not identical across professions: in a mailed survey of 366 certified diabetes educators in the southern United States (207 registered nurses and 159 registered dietitians), no statistically significant differences were found between RNs and RDs in typical carbohydrate recommendations for the treatment of diabetes.

In that same survey of certified diabetes educators, RDs were more likely than RNs to make recommendations for fiber intake or use of the glycemic index, whereas RNs were more likely than RDs to recommend consuming a carbohydrate source with protein to treat hypoglycemia.
The women were divided into those who received RT around the time of pregnancy and those who were not pregnant.
Comparisons of the overall incidence, actuarial rates, and latency to breast cancer between the two groups were made.
Of the 382 women, 14 developed breast cancer (3.7%).
The increase in the overall incidence (16.0% vs.
2.3%, p = 0.0001) and the actuarial rate of breast cancer among the women in the pregnant group (p = 0.011) was statistically significant.
The women treated around the time of pregnancy had a 10- and 15-year actuarial rate of breast cancer of 6.7% and 32.6%, respectively.
The 10-year and 15-year actuarial rate for the nonpregnant women was 0.4% and 1.7%, respectively.
The median latency from RT to the diagnosis of breast cancer was 13.1 and 18.9 years for women in the pregnant and nonpregnant groups, respectively.
In the multivariate analysis, pregnancy around the time of RT was the only variable associated with an increased risk of breast cancer.

The risk was dependent on the length of time from pregnancy to RT, with women receiving RT during pregnancy and within 1 month of pregnancy having an increased risk of breast cancer compared with nonpregnant women and women irradiated later than 1 month after pregnancy (hazard ratio, 22.49; 95% confidence interval, 5.56-90.88; p<0.001).

In uveal melanoma, c-kit expression was found in 84 of 134 paraffin-embedded tumour samples by immunohistochemistry and in six of eight fresh-frozen samples by Western blot analysis. c-Kit was strongly expressed and tyrosine phosphorylated in cultured uveal melanoma cells (OCM-1, OCM-3 and 92-1) compared with cutaneous melanoma cells, and in contrast to cutaneous melanoma cell lines it maintained a high phosphorylation level in serum-depleted uveal melanoma cells.

Expression of the stem cell growth factor (c-kit ligand) was detected in all three uveal melanoma cell lines, suggesting autocrine (paracrine) stimulation pathways, while no activation-related mutations were found in exon 11 of the KIT gene.

Treatment of uveal melanoma cell lines with STI571, which blocks c-kit autophosphorylation, resulted in cell death, and the IC(50) of the inhibitory effects on c-kit phosphorylation and on cell proliferation was of equal size and less than 2.5 microM, indicating that c-kit is a potential therapeutic target in uveal melanoma.
This therapeutic-target evidence derives from in vitro cell-line experiments, so the design does not establish that inhibiting c-kit improves clinical outcomes in patients with uveal melanoma.

The Omega-3 Index is defined as the red blood cell (RBC) content of eicosapentaenoic plus docosahexaenoic acid (EPA + DHA), a measure proposed on the basis that RBC fatty acid composition reflects long-term intake of EPA + DHA.
The authors proposed that this RBC EPA + DHA measure be considered a new risk factor for death from coronary heart disease (CHD).

Low intakes or blood levels of eicosapentaenoic and docosahexaenoic acids (EPA + DHA) are independently associated with increased risk of death from coronary heart disease (CHD), and in randomized secondary prevention trials, fish or fish oil have been demonstrated to reduce total and CHD mortality at intakes of about 1 g/day. the authors conducted clinical and laboratory experiments to generate data necessary for the validation of the Omega-3 Index as a CHD risk predictor.
The relationship between this putative marker and risk for CHD death, especially sudden cardiac death (SCD), was then evaluated in several published primary and secondary prevention studies.

In those studies, the Omega-3 Index was inversely associated with risk for CHD mortality, with an index of 8% or greater associated with the greatest cardioprotection and an index of 4% or less associated with the least.

The evidence presented supports an association between the Omega-3 Index and CHD mortality; because it derives from independent associations and secondary prevention trials of fish or fish oil rather than a demonstrated effect of changing the index itself, it does not by itself establish that raising the Omega-3 Index reduces death from CHD.

The evidence that reducing spasticity translates into functional benefit is mixed: an exploratory meta-analysis pooling individual stroke-patient data from two randomised controlled trials of intramuscular botulinum toxin reported a definite relationship between the maximum change in spasticity and the maximum change in arm function independent of treatment (rho = -0.2822, p = 0.0008, n = 137), yet noted that although botulinum toxin is used to reduce spasticity, its functional benefits are less easily demonstrated.

In that pooled analysis, maximum changes in both the composite spasticity and composite functional measures occurred concurrently in 47 patients, whereas in 26 patients the improvement in spasticity preceded the improvement in function and 18 showed the reverse.

The relationship between change in spasticity and change in arm function was clear in patients treated with botulinum toxin (Dysport) at 500 or 1000 units (rho = -0.5679, p = 0.0090, n = 22; rho = -0.4430, p = 0.0018, n = 47), but was not present in those treated with placebo or 1500 units.

In a separate trial, both groups showed significant improvement of spasticity with a median Modified Ashworth Scale of 1+ (range, 0.0-2.0) at eight weeks, yet compared with baseline no significant differences between the two groups were detected in any of the surface electromyography and clinical parameters at week 8 (P>0.05).

As an exploratory meta-analysis of change scores and their timing from pooled trial data, this design can describe an association between reductions in spasticity and changes in arm function but cannot establish that reducing spasticity causes functional benefit.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: causal demonstration and consistent functional benefit across treatments.

This was a classification study of original research articles, short reports, and case reports published in four major sport and exercise medicine journals, classified according to the main topic of study and the type of subjects used.
In that classification study, the most common topic was sports science, and very few studies related to the treatment of injuries and medical conditions.
The majority of published articles used healthy subjects sampled from the sedentary population, and few studies were carried out on injured participants.
The study's stated objective was to examine the evidence base of sports medicine research and assess how relevant and applicable it is to everyday practice.

This source addresses relevance and applicability to everyday practice (practitioners) but does not establish relevance or applicability to athletes; the reported topic and subject distributions should not be interpreted as evidence of athlete applicability.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: relevance and applicability to athletes.

Early adopters of club/psychostimulant drugs do exist as a defined group: a study of the relationship between mephedrone, ecstasy pills, cocaine and MDMA powder was conducted amongst club-goers considered to be 'early adopters' of psychostimulant/club drug trends, using in situ surveys of 308 customers in two south London gay dance clubs across 3 weekend nights in July 2010.

Among those surveyed club-goers, mephedrone was added to existing drug repertoires and acted to supplement more established club drugs including ecstasy pills, cocaine and MDMA powder, rather than replacing or displacing those drugs.

In an analysis testing the hypothesis that physicians' early adoption of new drugs is a personal trait independent of drug groups, general practitioners' adoption of one group of drugs was poorly associated with adoption of others (r ≤ 0.49), indicating that early adoption of one type of drugs is not associated with early adoption of another.
Consistently, for all drug groups, adoption time adjusted for practice size was only weakly associated with other indicators (r: -0.56 to -0.27).

The retrieved evidence does not establish that combining 2-methoxyestradiol with chemotherapeutics reduces chemotherapeutic dosages in the treatment of human ovarian cancer; it reports only an in vitro additive antiproliferative effect.

In two different human ovary cancer cell lines, a significant additive effect of 2-methoxyestradiol with epirubicine and with carboplatin was observed at the lower concentration range of these chemotherapeutic substances.

In that in vitro model, all cell lines were incubated with equimolar concentrations of 2-methoxyestradiol (0.8-25 microM) and the chemotherapeutics epirubicine, doxorubicine, paclitaxel, docetaxel, carboplatin, vinorelbine, 5-fluorouracil and mafosfamide, with proliferation measured after four days using the ATP-chemosensitivity test.
Because the reported combination testing was performed in human ovary cancer cell lines in vitro, the design cannot demonstrate that chemotherapeutic dosages given to patients can be reduced.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: reduction of chemotherapeutic dosages in patients with ovarian cancer.

Yes—in a single-surgeon series, patients who had undergone at least one prior benign prostate biopsy before radical perineal prostatectomy for prostate cancer had more favorable pathologic findings and a lower probability of biochemical failure than patients with no prior biopsy, indicating that prior benign biopsy was associated with outcome in this cohort.

The study comprised 1369 patients with clinically localized prostate cancer treated by a single surgeon between 1991 and 2001; the study population was the 203 patients (14.9%) who had at least one prior benign prostate biopsy performed for a rising prostate-specific antigen level and/or abnormal digital rectal examination, and the control group was the 1115 patients with no prior biopsy.
Patients with a prior benign biopsy had more favorable pathologic features: organ-confined disease in 74% versus 64% of controls (P<0.001), and margin-positive disease in 9.8% versus 18% of controls.

Biochemical failure (prostate-specific antigen 0.5 ng/mL or greater, assessed after prostatectomy at 6-month intervals) occurred in only 24 study-group patients (12%) versus 20% of the control group (P = 0.01).

Kaplan-Meier analyses suggested improved biochemical disease-free survival for patients with prior benign biopsies, especially among those with more aggressive disease (Gleason sum 7 or greater; P<0.01).
Overall, study-group patients had a lower probability of biochemical failure than controls (odds ratio 0.57, P<0.001).

Because the comparison was between non-randomized patient groups defined by whether a prior benign biopsy had been performed, the reported associations cannot establish that undergoing a prior benign biopsy itself improves oncologic outcome.

Yes, socioeconomic status mattered for postpartum learning needs: although few differences in identified concerns were evident, women of low socioeconomic status were significantly more likely than women of higher socioeconomic status to report unmet learning needs related to 9 of 10 topics.
The main unmet learning needs identified by postpartum women were signs of infant illness and infant care/behavior.

For most topics, significantly more women in both socioeconomic groups identified learning needs at 4 weeks after hospital discharge than had identified corresponding concerns while still in hospital.
The findings come from recruitment of 250 women from each of 5 hospitals in Ontario, Canada (n = 1,250), of whom approximately 17 percent were of low socioeconomic status.

The retrieved evidence does not establish that increased use of private health care reduces demand on the NHS; the one relevant finding points in the opposite direction, since NHS referral rates were highest where private referral rates were highest.

In a prospective survey of general practitioner referrals to private and NHS consultant-led services between 1 January and 31 December 2001 from 10 general practices in the Trent Focus Collaborative Research Network, United Kingdom, 90.4% (15,495) of 17,137 referrals were to the NHS and 9.6% (1,642) were to the private sector, with referrals aggregated to private and NHS referral rates for each electoral ward in each practice.

The NHS referral rate was significantly higher in wards whose private referral rates were in the top fifth compared with wards in the bottom fifth (rate ratio 1.40, 95% CI 1.15 to 1.71, p = 0.001) after adjustment for deprivation and practice; private referral rates were lower in the most deprived fifth of wards than in the least deprived fifth (rate ratio 0.25, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.41, p<0.001), while NHS referral rates were slightly higher in the most deprived fifth (rate ratio 1.18, 95% CI 0.98 to 1.42, p = 0.08), both after age standardisation and adjustment for practice.

Because this evidence comes from ward-level referral rates measured within a single year rather than from repeated measures over time, it cannot show whether an increase in private health care use over time reduces NHS demand.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: an increase in private health care use over time reduces NHS demand.

Annual data on children aged under 16 y treated for asthma, including consumption of regular medication for asthma, numbers of hospital periods, lengths of hospitalizations and annual proportions of readmissions, were collected using patient-specific medical records from 1995 to 1999.

In the Kuopio province, on average, 35.6-36.7/1000 children were on maintenance for asthma, of which 23% were receiving cromones, 51% were taking inhaled steroids and 26% were treated with cromones plus intermittent steroids; in the Oulu province, the respective prevalence was 32.7-34.9/1000, and the respective proportions were 5%, 93% and 2%.
Total and first admissions, as well as hospital days were clearly less in the Oulu province.

In the children aged >or = 6y, the average annual total admissions were 0.3/1000 (Oulu) vs 1.2/1000 (Kuopio) (p<0.001); the first admissions were 0.2/1000 vs 1.0/1000 (p<0.001), proportions of readmissions 6.3% vs 19.3% (p<0.05), and numbers of hospital days 0.7/1000 vs 3.8/1000 (p<0.001).
The differences were in the same direction, though less prominent, also among children 2-5 y of age.

The study compared two geographic provinces (Oulu and Kuopio) whose paediatric asthma maintenance-medication profiles differed, rather than directly comparing hospital admission rates between children receiving inhaled steroids and children receiving cromones; the admission-rate difference therefore cannot be attributed to the choice between inhaled steroids and cromones.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: direct comparison of hospital admission rates between children receiving inhaled steroids and children receiving cromones.
