The cited evidence does not support adjuvant radiation as necessary for stage III thymoma: in a retrospective review of 45 stage III thymoma patients, adjuvant radiotherapy did not alter recurrence rates or disease-specific survival, and in a separate analysis of 969 patients with sufficient staging data, overall survival did not differ statistically between surgery alone and surgery plus adjuvant radiotherapy in stage III disease.

Among the 45 stage III patients who underwent resection in the Massachusetts General Hospital review, baseline prognostic factors were similar between the radiated and nonradiated groups, and adding adjuvant radiotherapy did not alter local or distant recurrence rates.

Disease-specific survival at 10 years for stage III patients who did not receive radiation was 75% (95% confidence interval, 32% to 100%) versus 79% (95% confidence interval, 64% to 94%) for those who did receive radiation therapy (p = 0.21).

In the analysis of 969 patients with sufficient staging data, comparing surgery with surgery plus adjuvant radiotherapy showed no statistical difference in overall survival when stratifying for stage I (P =.57), stage II (P =.37), stage III (P =.25), and stage IV (P =.24) tumors.

Interpretation: the Massachusetts General Hospital findings come from a retrospective review of case records (1972-2004), a design that can describe associations between radiation use and outcomes but cannot by itself establish that withholding radiation is safe or that giving it is causally ineffective.

Yes—injury mortality rates differ across U.S. states: among the 12 states with the highest and lowest road traffic death rates, 74% of the six states with the highest road traffic death rates (group 1) also had above-average rates of other forms of injury such as falling, poisoning, drowning, fire, suffocation, homicide, and suicide (and for the retail trade and construction industries), while 85% of the six states with the lowest road traffic death rates (group 2) conformed to the converse hypothesis.
The comparison drew on data for these 12 states for the period 1983 to 1995, comprising nine categories of unintentional injury and four categories of intentional injury.

Serum pancreatic lipase may improve the diagnosis of pancreatitis compared to serum amylase; both enzymes have been measured simultaneously at their hospital allowing for a comparison of their diagnostic accuracy, and receiver operator characteristic analysis of the initial sample from patients received in the Emergency Department showed improved diagnostic accuracy for serum pancreatic lipase (area under the curve (AUC) 0.948) compared with serum amylase (AUC, 0.906, P<0.05).

Seventeen thousand five hundred and thirty-one measurements of either serum amylase and or serum pancreatic lipase were made on 10 931 patients treated at a metropolitan teaching hospital between January 2001 and May 2003.

At diagnostic-threshold cut-off points of 208 U/L for serum pancreatic lipase (normal <190 U/L) and 114 U/L for serum amylase (normal 27-100 U/L), sensitivity was 90.3% for lipase versus 76.8% for amylase, and specificity was 93% for lipase versus 92.6% for amylase.
On the first emergency department measurement, 18.8% of acute pancreatitis patients did not have elevated serum amylase, whereas only 2.9% did not have elevated serum pancreatic lipase.

In a comparison of pancreatitis aetiologies, serum amylase and lipase levels supported the diagnosis in 26% and 58% of patients with hypertriglyceridemic acute pancreatitis versus 58% and 79% of patients with lithiasic acute pancreatitis, respectively; the authors note that lipemic serum may interfere with accurate pancreatic enzyme measurement and may hinder the diagnosis of acute pancreatitis.

Yes — grandmultiparity was an independent risk factor for adverse perinatal outcomes in a California record-linkage study of singleton deliveries, where grandmultiparous women remained at significantly higher risk after controlling for potential confounding factors.

Maternal and neonatal pregnancy outcomes of grandmultiparous women were compared with those of multiparous women who were 30 years or older at the time of their last birth, in a database of maternal and newborn hospital discharge records linked to birth/death certificates covering all multiparous women with a singleton delivery in California from January 1, 1997 through December 31, 1998.
The study population comprised 25,512 grandmultiparous women and 265,060 multiparous women 30 years or older as controls; grandmultiparous women were predominantly Hispanic (56%).

Adjusted odds ratios for grandmultiparous versus multiparous women 30 years or older were 1.3 (95% CI 1.2–1.5) for abruptio placentae, 1.3 (95% CI 1.2–1.4) for preterm delivery, 1.5 (95% CI 1.4–1.6) for fetal macrosomia, 1.5 (95% CI 1.3–1.8) for neonatal death, 1.2 (95% CI 1.1–1.3) for postpartum hemorrhage and 1.5 (95% CI 1.3–1.8) for blood transfusion.

As an observational analysis of linked discharge and vital-records data, this design can establish an association that persists after adjustment for the measured confounding factors examined, but it cannot by itself demonstrate causation or exclude residual confounding by unmeasured factors.

Yes, fast food consumption was reported as an independent risk factor for asthma symptoms: in an ISAAC cross-sectional prevalence study of 1321 children (mean age 11.4 years, range 10.1-12.5) in Hastings, New Zealand, hamburger consumption was independently associated with having a history of wheeze (less than once a week OR = 1.44, 95% CI: 1.06-1.96; 1+ times a week OR = 1.65, 95% CI: 1.07-2.52) compared with children who never ate hamburgers, after adjusting for lifestyle factors including other diet and BMI variables.

For current wheeze in the same cohort, the association was present only at the higher intake level: hamburger consumption 1+ times a week was associated with current wheeze (OR = 1.81, 95% CI: 1.10-2.98), whereas consumption less than once a week was not (OR = 1.17, 95% CI: 0.80-1.70), relative to children who never ate hamburgers.
Takeaway consumption 1+ times a week was marginally significantly related to exercise-induced bronchial hyperresponsiveness in this sample (OR = 2.41, 95% CI: 0.99-5.91).

Because the Hastings, New Zealand data came from a cross-sectional prevalence study of 1321 children, the reported associations between fast food and asthma symptoms cannot establish that fast food consumption causes asthma or that changing intake alters asthma risk.

No: among 83 children with a prepubertal and early adolescent bipolar disorder phenotype (PEA-BP) from an ongoing controlled study, preferential transmission of AVPR1A GATA or complex microsatellite repeats to hypersexual or uninhibited people-seeking probands was not significant by the transmission disequilibrium test, and case-control analyses likewise found no significant associations between hypersexuality or uninhibited people-seeking and the number of AVPR1A GATA or complex repeats.

In that study, hypersexuality and uninhibited people-seeking were assessed from the corresponding WASH-U-KSADS items; microsatellite genotyping of the AVPR1A repeats used fluorescently labeled primers detected by laser-induced fluorescence; and the data were analyzed with case-control and family-based association methods.
There were 32 complete biological trios (28 informative families) for the GATA repeat and 34 complete biological trios (30 informative families) for the complex repeat.

The reported power of this sample was limited: at p<0.05 there was about 80% power to detect odds ratios of 5.0 and 4.0 in the family-based analyses and 3.5 and 2.6 in the case-control analyses, for allele frequencies of 0.1 and 0.5, respectively, so the null results do not exclude smaller effects.

In the comparison of Snellen E acuity (SE) with Landolt C acuity (LR), differences were small; the mean decimal values were 0.25 for LR and 0.29 for SE in the entire group, and 0.14 for LR and 0.16 for SE in the eyes with strabismus amblyopia, and the mean difference between LR and SE was 0.55 lines in the entire group and 0.55 lines for the eyes with strabismus amblyopia, with higher SE values in both groups.
The results of the other groups tested were similar, again with only small differences between LR and SE.
The study tested 100 patients (age 8-90 years, median 60.5 years) with various eye disorders, including 39 with amblyopia due to strabismus, along with 13 healthy volunteers.

In a series of 125 peripheral PTA procedures in which a conventional guidewire was used first and a hydrophilic guidewire only if needed, hydrophilic guidewire use was associated with significantly improved technical success for SFA stenosis and for iliac and SFA occlusions, but not for iliac stenosis, where no significant difference was found.

Reported technical success rates with conventional versus hydrophilic wires were: iliac stenosis 96% (24/25) versus 100%; iliac occlusions 60% (15/25) versus 96%; femoral (SFA) stenosis 84% (21/25) versus 100%; and among occlusions, lesions <10 cm 64% (16/25) versus 96% and lesions >10 cm 48% (12/25) versus 88%.

The study population comprised 25 stenosed and 25 occluded iliac arteries and 25 stenosed and 50 occluded femoral arteries, and technical success was defined as the lesion being crossed by a guidewire and balloon and dilated with restoration of vessel lumen, less than 30% residual stenosis, and a rise in ABI of at least 0.15 after 24 hours.

Because the design used the conventional guidewire first and the hydrophilic guidewire only when needed, the higher hydrophilic-wire success rates reflect a sequential, non-randomized comparison within the same lesions rather than a randomized comparison of the two wire types, so the design alone does not establish the magnitude of benefit that would be expected if hydrophilic wires were used first.

Yes: in ventilated extremely low birth weight infants in the first week of life, the study assessed correlation and agreement between end-tidal carbon dioxide (EtCO2) and arterial carbon dioxide (PaCO2), and the intraclass correlation coefficient was 0.81.
It was a retrospective chart review of all ELBW (<1,000 g) infants admitted to a level III NICU from January 2003 to December 2003.
There were 754 end-tidal and arterial CO2 pairs from 31 ELBW infants (21 male and 10 female).
Data collected included demographic details and simultaneous EtCO2 (mainstream capnography) and arterial blood gas values (pH, PaCO2, PaO2).
The correlation coefficient and degree of bias with 95% confidence interval between EtCO2 and PaCO2 were assessed.
The overall bias was 5.6 +/- 6.9 mmHg (95% C.I.
The overall EtCO2 values were significantly lower than PaCO2 value.
In only 89/754 (11.8%) pairs, the EtCO2 was higher than the PaCO2.
Using EtCO2 ranges of 30 to 50 mmHg, the capnographic method was able to identify 84% of instances where PaCO2 was between 35 (<35 = hypocarbia) and 55 mmHg (>55 = hypercapnia).

The retrospective chart review design describes correlation and agreement between EtCO2 and PaCO2, but an observational association does not establish that intervening on EtCO2 (such as EtCO2-guided management) improves clinical outcomes.

Yes: in a retrospective data analysis of 353 consecutive OSA patients who had a successful manual CPAP titration in a sleep disorders unit, greater OSA severity was associated with a greater likelihood of requiring high CPAP.

The mean optimal CPAP in this cohort was 9.5 +/- 2.4 cm H2O, and optimal CPAP pressure rose with OSA severity, from 7.79 +/- 2.2 cm H2O in the mild group to 8.7 +/- 1.8 cm H2O in the moderate group and 10.1 +/- 2.3 cm H2O in the severe OSA group.

High CPAP was defined as the mean plus 1 standard deviation (>/=12 cm H2O), and the variables tested as predictors were apnea-hypopnea index (AHI), age, sex, body mass index (BMI), Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS) and the Multiple Sleep Latency Test (MSLT).
High CPAP was required by 2 (6.9%) patients with mild OSA, 6 (5.8%) with moderate OSA and 63 (28.6%) with severe OSA.
On univariate analysis, AHI, BMI, ESS score and the proportion of males were significantly higher among patients needing high CPAP, who also had a lower mean MSLT.

On logistic regression adjusted for the other variables, the use of high CPAP was 5.90 times more frequent (95% confidence interval 2.67-13.1) in severe OSA patients, and the area under the receiver operator curve was 72.4%, indicating the model was adequate.

Because the underlying design was a retrospective data analysis, these findings describe associations between OSA severity and the need for high CPAP rather than demonstrating that a change in OSA severity causes a change in the required CPAP pressure.

Yes for interleukin-8: in patients with abdominal pain compatible with pancreatic origin, multivariate analysis revealed that only interleukin-8 in pancreatic juice was able to discriminate between normal pancreas and chronic pancreatitis (P =.011), pancreatic cancer (P =.044), and the presence of pancreatic diseases (P =.007).

Pancreatic juice levels of interleukin-8, interleukin-6, intercellular adhesion molecule 1, and transforming growth factor-beta 1 were measured by modified enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays; individual cytokine concentrations were not significantly different in chronic pancreatitis compared with pancreatic cancer.

From January 2003 to December 2004, consecutive patients with abdominal pain compatible with pancreatic origin were enrolled; of 130 patients screened, 118 met the inclusion criteria, and the final diagnosis was made by the primary gastroenterologist on the basis of medical history; laboratory, endoscopic, and imaging studies; and clinical follow-up.

The reported discrimination is an association between pancreatic juice interleukin-8 concentration and the presence of pancreatic diseases; it does not establish the effect of intervening on interleukin-8 concentration.

In a prospective cohort study at the University of British Columbia during January 2005, 159 vascular procedure cases were included (65% elective same-day admission, 20% elective previously admitted, 15% emergent), and resident involvement in each patient's care was recorded along with case type (emergent, outpatient, inpatient) and resident demographic data; the overall rates were 67% for preoperative assessment, 17% for involvement in the decision to operate, 79% for postoperative assessment on the ward, and 3% for patient follow-up in clinic, while the rate of complete in-hospital continuity of care (assessing the patient preoperatively and postoperatively) was 57%.

Emergent cases were associated with a significantly higher rate of preoperative assessment (92% vs 63%, P<.05), and among elective cases those admitted before the day of surgery had significantly higher rates of preoperative assessment (78% vs 58%, P<.05) and involvement in the decision to operate (16% vs 4%, P<.05) than same-day admission patients.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: trainees are learning complete surgical care.

Preoperative TBS changed the diagnosis in a subset of newborns with esophageal atresia: among 62 patients who underwent preoperative TBS between 1997 and 2003, the pre-TBS Gross classification was type A in 9, type B in none and type C in 51, yet at TBS 3 of the 9 type A patients were found to have an unsuspected proximal fistula (type B).
TBS also detected respiratory tree malformations that had not been identified previously in 4 patients (2 aberrant right upper bronchus and 2 hypoplastic bronchi).

TBS findings directly altered the surgical approach: when a wide carinal fistula was found it was mechanically occluded with a Fogarty catheter and cannulated with rigid bronchoscopy, and the 3 patients with an unsuspected proximal fistula plus the 2 with an H-type fistula were repaired through a cervical approach.

Carinal fistulas in 14 type C patients were occluded by Fogarty catheter to improve ventilation during repair, and overall TBS was judged clinically useful in 28 of 62 patients (45.2%), including 15 of 62 (24.2%) in whom it was crucial in modifying the surgical approach.
No complications of preoperative TBS were observed in this series of 62 newborns with esophageal atresia.

This study provides the first large-volume (1000 implant) comparison of the deflation rates of Poly Implant Prosthesis prefilled textured saline breast implants versus a control group of Mentor Siltex textured saline implants; a consecutive series of 500 Poly Implant Prosthesis prefilled textured saline breast implants was compared with a consecutive series of 500 Mentor Siltex breast implants, and each breast implant was evaluated for a 4-year period.
The cumulative deflation rates of the Poly Implant Prosthesis implants were: year 1, 1.2 percent; year 2, 5.6 percent; year 3, 11.4 percent; and year 4, 15.4 percent.
The cumulative deflation rates of the Mentor implants were: year 1, 0.2 percent; year 2, 0.6 percent; year 3, 1.6 percent; and year 4, 4.4 percent.

Because the study compared two consecutive series rather than randomly assigning implants, the observed difference in deflation rates represents an association and does not establish the effect of intervening on the exposure (i.e., choosing one implant type over the other).

Statistical significance was calculated with Fisher's exact test at year 1 and chi-square analysis at years 2 through 4; the difference in deflation rates was not statistically significant at year 1 (Fisher's exact test, p>0.05), but was statistically significant at year 2 (chi-square, 13.29; p<0.001), year 3 (chi-square, 37.91; p<0.001) and year 4 (chi-square, 32.69; p<0.001).
The retrieved evidence does not establish: comparison results for presenting symptoms and clinical features between groups.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: comparison results for outcome between groups.

Among 107 patients diagnosed with uterine myomas during pregnancy who had two or more obstetrical ultrasounds, myoma volume did not grow uniformly: between the first half of pregnancy (up to 19 weeks) and the third quarter (20-30 weeks), 55.1% (95% CI: 43-66) of myomas decreased in size with a mean decrease in volume of 35%±4%, while 44.9% (95% CI: 34-56) enlarged with a mean increase in volume of 69%±11%.

Between the second study period (20-30 weeks) and the third study period (31 weeks to term), 75% (95% CI: 56-87) of the myomas became smaller with a mean decrease in volume of 30%±3%, while 25% (95% CI: 13-43) enlarged with a mean increase in volume of 102%±62%.

These volume changes were derived from a retrospective review of a departmental electronic perinatal database and medical records rather than a prospective interventional design, so the reported direction and magnitude of myoma volume change describe observed associations across pregnancy periods and cannot establish that any exposure or intervention alters myoma growth.

On the reported comparison, decisional algorithms cannot replace WHO global introspection (GI) for individual causality assessment of spontaneously reported ADRs, because the algorithms tested showed a high average sensitivity of 93% and positive predictive value of 89% but a low average specificity of 7% with a negative predictive value of 31%.
In that study, an expert panel assessed the causality of 500 adverse reports using the WHO global introspection method, and the same reports were independently assessed using 15 published algorithms.

For the comparison, the causality assessment level 'possible' was considered the lower limit for a report to be considered drug related, with sensitivity defined as the proportion of reports classified as drug related by both the algorithm and the GI method and specificity as the proportion simultaneously considered non-drug related; the analysis was performed for the total sample and within serious or unexpected events.

Yes — complex coronary lesions were more frequent in patients with diabetes mellitus: among 1,014 consecutive patients (mean age 61.3 ± 10.7 years) classified as diabetic (n=281) or nondiabetic (n=733), the prevalence of bifurcation lesions was 9.8% in the diabetic group versus 4.3% in the nondiabetic group (P=0.001) and the prevalence of ostial lesions was 38.4% versus 29.2% (P=0.003).
In that study, coronary angiograms were examined for bifurcation and ostial lesions using a digital quantitative system.

In multivariate analysis, the presence of diabetes mellitus and greater age were independent predictors of bifurcation lesions (OR=2.27, P=0.004 for DM; OR=1.03, P=0.01 for age) and of ostial lesions (OR=1.40, P=0.027 for DM; OR=1.02, P=0.001 for age).

Yes - in 391 advanced NSCLC patients whose pretreatment health-related quality of life was measured with the EORTC QLQ-C30 and the EORTC Lung Cancer module QLQ-LC13, self-reported HRQOL provided independent prognostic information for survival.
Survival analyses used the Cox proportional hazards regression model for both univariate and multivariate analysis, with a bootstrap validation technique to assess the stability of the outcomes.

The final multivariate Cox regression model retained four independent prognostic factors for survival: male gender (HR 1.32, 95% CI 1.03-1.69; P = 0.03), performance status (0 to 1 versus 2; HR 1.63, 95% CI 1.04-2.54; P = 0.032), the patient's self-reported pain score (HR 1.11, 95% CI 1.07-1.16; P < 0.001) and dysphagia (HR 1.12, 95% CI 1.04-1.21; P = 0.003).
A 10-point shift worse on the scale measuring pain and dysphagia translated into an 11% and 12% increased likelihood of death, respectively.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: explicit recommendation on whether routine chest radiography after transbronchial biopsy is necessary.

No: in a case-control study of liveborn Down syndrome children, first-trimester folic acid use did not protect against congenital heart anomalies, with an adjusted odds ratio of 0.95 (95% CI 0.61-1.47) for heart anomalies overall.

The study used case-control analyses within Down syndrome children, comparing those with heart anomalies (cases) against those without heart anomalies (controls); the population was women with liveborn Down syndrome children in the Slone Epidemiology Center Birth Defects Study, 1976-1997.
Exposure was any folic acid-containing product used an average of at least 4 days per week during the first 12 weeks of pregnancy, and no exposure meant no folic acid use in those 12 weeks.
Exposure frequency was similar between groups: 110 of 223 cases (49%) were exposed versus 84 of 184 controls (46%).

After adjustment for possible confounders, no protective effect of folic acid was found separately for conotruncal defects, ventricular septal defects, ostium secundum atrial septal defects, or endocardial cushion defects.

Because the evidence comes from an observational case-control comparison of exposure frequency rather than a trial, it cannot establish that folic acid use changes the risk of heart anomalies in Down syndrome children.

Frozen section did not alter surgical management of multinodular thyroid disease: in none of the 135 patients who underwent intra-operative frozen section did the result change the intraoperative management.

The finding comes from a series of 236 patients with multinodular goiter who underwent thyroidectomy at one institution between May 1994 and November 2004, of whom 135 (57%) had an intra-operative frozen section.

Among the 135 patients who had frozen section, 4 (3%) were subsequently diagnosed with thyroid cancer on permanent histology; three of those frozen sections had been misread as benign, so the sensitivity of frozen section for diagnosing thyroid cancer was only 25%.

The evidence is a retrospective review of patient records to determine whether a frozen section was performed and whether it changed the patient's outcome, so it reports observed practice in the reviewed records rather than a randomized comparison of management strategies.

Occlusion of the atherosclerotic ascending aorta with an endoaortic inflatable balloon has been proposed as an alternative to conventional cross-clamping to prevent injury to the vessel and distal embolization of debris; in the reported series the surgeon's choice was based on preoperative identification of aortic calcifications or intraoperative epiaortic ultrasonographic scanning, and endoaortic occlusion was employed in 52 of 2,172 consecutive patients.

In the single cited series of endoaortic balloon occlusion used for the atherosclerotic ascending aorta, the evidence indicates the technique was not safe: in-hospital death occurred in 13 of the 52 treated patients (25%), a rate significantly higher than among all other patients (4.2%, p<0.0001) and higher than the expected European System for Cardiac Operative Risk Evaluation estimate (10.5%, p=0.05).
Use of endoaortic occlusion was independently associated with in-hospital death on multivariable analysis (odds ratio 5.609, 95% confidence interval 2.684 to 11.719).
In 10 patients (19.2%) the endoaortic balloon had to be replaced by the ordinary cross-clamp because of incomplete occlusion (n = 5), hindered exposure (n = 2), or balloon rupture (n = 3).

Stroke on awakening from anesthesia occurred in 2 patients (3.8%); the stroke rate was higher in the endoaortic occlusion group than among all other patients, but the difference was only possibly significant (3.8% versus 0.8%, p = 0.067).

The cited evidence is mixed rather than showing equality: overall post-pull-through scores were similar between the transanal endorectal pull-through (TERPT) and conventional transabdominal (ABD) pull-through groups, but the continence score was significantly better in the ABD group while the stool pattern score was better in the TERPT group.

This comparison came from a review of records of 41 patients more than 3 years old who underwent a pull-through for Hirschsprung disease (TERPT, n = 20; ABD, n = 21), whose families were interviewed and scored using a 15-item post-pull-through long-term outcome questionnaire.
A significant difference in age at interview between the two groups was noted, and after reanalysis controlling for age, age did not significantly affect the long-term scoring outcome between groups.

As a limitation entailed by the reported design, this was a retrospective record review in which the authors' group transitioned from the ABD to the TERPT technique while patients were operated on between 1995 and 2003, so the two procedures were not compared in a randomized or contemporaneous fashion.

Between June 2001 and January 2005, a total of 110 patients with a mean age of 33.5 years (range 12-65) suffering from lower ureteral calculi (below the upper margin of the sacroiliac joint) prospectively underwent ureteroscopic removal.

In that prospective series, complete clearance without the use of fluoroscopy was achieved in 99 patients (94.2%), and fluoroscopy was required in 6 patients (4%) for calcified stricture (n = 1), duplex system (n = 1), narrow and tortuous meatus causing difficulty in passing the 5-Fr balloon dilator (n = 3), and confirmation of spontaneous passage of the stone (n = 1); of the 13 patients who required balloon dilatation, it was successfully achieved without fluoroscopy.

In a separate retrospective evaluation, between 2010 and 2011, 93 patients with ureteral calculi who underwent ureteroscopic treatment by experienced urologists were evaluated; the stones were localized in the proximal, middle, and distal segments in 11, 30, and 52 patients, respectively.

In that retrospective series, stone-free status was achieved for 90 patients (96.77%), and manipulations such as guidewire, ureteral stent insertion, and balloon dilatation were performed with visual and tactile cues.

In the same retrospective series, fluoroscopic imaging was required for 7 patients with a mean fluoroscopy time of 9 ± 4.72 seconds (range, 4-16 seconds) for the following reasons: stone migration to the kidney (3 patients), double collecting system with 2 ureters (1 patient), and ureteral orifice stricture extending to the upper segment (1 patient).

Taken together, these reports show that ureteroscopic retrieval of lower ureteric stones can be completed without fluoroscopy in the large majority of patients, with fluoroscopy needed only in a small proportion for defined anatomical or intraoperative indications, so fluoroscopy is not universally essential but remains necessary in selected circumstances.

Both reports are single-arm case series without a comparator group managed with routine fluoroscopy, so they describe how frequently fluoroscopy was needed during attempted fluoro-less ureteroscopy rather than establishing comparative outcomes of fluoroscopic versus fluoro-less retrieval.

Among 61 patients with metastatic carcinoma to cervical lymph nodes from an unknown head and neck primary treated curatively with radiotherapy, the addition of neck dissection did not produce a statistically significant difference in 8-year actuarial overall survival (biopsy 64.8% vs neck dissection 67.6%, p =.64) or in local relapse-free survival (75% vs 74.5%, respectively, p =.57), indicating that neck dissection was not shown to improve these outcomes in this series.

The series comprised 61 patients referred to the McGill University Hospital Centers between 1987 and 2002; 20 underwent neck dissection (11 radical, 9 functional) and 41 had a biopsy only (9 fine-needle aspiration and 32 excisional biopsy), and all patients received radiotherapy.

Because the reported comparison of outcomes between patients who had biopsy versus those who had neck dissection was not described as a randomized comparison of treatment strategies, the absence of a statistically significant survival or local control difference does not by itself establish that neck dissection is unnecessary.

The cited evidence supports the existence of a stretch-sensitive KCNQ1 mutation: mutation screening of KCNQ1, KCNE1, KCNE2, and KCNE3 in 50 families with atrial fibrillation identified one missense KCNQ1 mutation, R14C, in a single family with a high prevalence of hypertension.

Patch-clamp studies of wild-type or R14C KCNQ1 co-expressed with KCNE1 in CHO cells showed no statistically significant differences between wild-type and mutant channel kinetics at baseline or after activation of adenylate cyclase with forskolin, but after exposure to hypotonic solution to elicit cell swelling/stretch, mutant channels showed a marked increase in current, a leftward shift in the voltage dependence of activation, altered channel kinetics, and shortening of the modeled atrial action potential duration.

The report links a genetic defect to an acquired factor by noting that although atrial fibrillation can have a genetic etiology, links between inherited gene defects and acquired factors such as atrial stretch had not been explored; in the family carrying R14C, atrial fibrillation was present only in older individuals who had developed atrial dilation and who were genotype positive, and the mutant channel's marked current increase, leftward shift in the voltage dependence of activation, altered kinetics and shortened modeled atrial action potential duration appeared specifically after hypotonic solution-induced swelling/stretch.

For pathogenesis of atrial fibrillation, the study reports that the R14C KCNQ1 mutation was found in 1 family with a high prevalence of hypertension, that atrial fibrillation occurred only in older genotype-positive individuals who had developed atrial dilation, and that after stretch the mutant shortened the modeled atrial action potential duration — a combination the authors present as a mechanism in which the inherited channel defect and the acquired factor of atrial dilation/stretch act together.

As a limitation entailed by the design, the functional support for this mechanism comes from heterologous CHO-cell patch-clamp experiments and human atrial action potential modeling rather than patient atrial tissue, so the findings indicate a proposed mechanism rather than establishing that the mutation causes atrial fibrillation in patients.

The clinical significance of bile duct sludge does not clearly differ from that of common bile duct stones with respect to recurrence after endoscopic therapy: among 228 patients who underwent therapeutic ERCP for suspected choledocholithiasis, CBD stones recurred in 17% (33/197) of patients with CBD stones versus 16% (5/31) of patients with bile duct sludge (p = 0.99).

Bile duct sludge occurred in 14% (31/228) of these patients and was more common in females; common bile duct dilation was less common in the sludge group, and the other known risk factors for recurrent CBD stones (age, previous open cholecystectomy, bile duct angulation, and the presence of a peripampullary diverticulum) were not statistically different between the sludge and stone groups.

The significance of bile duct sludge is poorly defined, and this study was designed to compare bile duct sludge with bile duct stones in terms of frequency, associated risk factors, and clinical outcome after endoscopic therapy.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: ambulatory process of care predicts health-related quality of life outcomes for patients with chronic disease.

The antismoking advertisement had a mixed effect on young cinema patrons' perception of smoking in the movie they viewed: among non-smokers, 47.8% of intervention subjects thought the smoking in the viewed movie was not OK compared with 43.8% of controls (p = 0.04).
Among smokers, however, there was no significant difference in this perception between the intervention (16.5%) and control (14.5%) groups (p = 0.4).

These findings come from a quasi-experimental survey of cinema patrons, with the control group surveyed in week 1 and the intervention group in weeks 2 and 3, so the design entails that the reported differences in perceptions and intentions cannot by itself establish that the advertisement caused them.

For intention to smoke, a higher percentage of smokers in the intervention group indicated that they were likely to be smoking in 12 months' time (38.6%) than smokers in the control group (25.6%; p<0.001).

Among non-smokers there was no significant difference in smoking intentions between groups, with 1.2% of intervention subjects and 1.6% of controls saying they would probably be smoking in 12 months' time (p = 0.54).

Yes—breast cancer prognosis appears to be inherited: in a population-based Swedish cohort, daughters and sisters of a proband with poor 5-year prognosis had a 60% higher 5-year breast cancer mortality than relatives of a proband with good prognosis (hazard ratio 1.6; 95% CI 1.2 to 2.2; p for trend 0.002), after adjustment for potential confounders.

The same cohort, drawn from the nationwide Swedish Multi-Generation Register, comprised 2,787 mother-daughter pairs and 831 sister pairs with breast cancer diagnosed from 1961 to 2001, with complete follow-up and proband 5-year prognosis classified into poor, intermediary, or good tertiles.

The 5-year survival proportion was 87% among daughters whose mothers died within 5 years versus 91% if the mother was alive (p = 0.03), and among sisters the corresponding proportions were 70% versus 88% (p = 0.001).

The association between a proband's poor prognosis and a relative's 5-year breast cancer mortality was slightly stronger among sisters (HR 1.8; 95% CI 1.0 to 3.4) than among daughters (HR 1.6; 95% CI 1.1 to 2.3).

Because this is an observational population-based cohort study of familial aggregation, it documents that a proband's prognosis predicts breast cancer mortality in daughters and sisters, but the design alone cannot separate inherited traits from shared non-genetic factors as the explanation for the familial clustering.

Reduction aortoplasty can be an optional therapy; however, indications regarding the diameter of the aorta, the history of dilatation (poststenosis, bicuspid aortic valve), or the intraoperative management (wall excision, reduction suture, external reinforcement) are not established.
External reinforcement with a non-coated dacron prosthesis was added in order to stabilize the aortic wall.

In a retrospective study between 1997 and 2005, 531 patients were investigated who were operated for aneurysm or ectasia of the ascending aorta (diameter: 45-76mm), and of these, in 50 patients, size-reducing ascending aortoplasty was performed.
The procedure was performed with low hospital mortality (2%) and a low postoperative morbidity.

Computertomographic and echocardiographic diameters were significantly smaller after reduction (55.8+/-9mm down to 40.51+/-6.2mm (CT), p<0.002; 54.1+/-6.7mm preoperatively down to 38.7+/-7.1mm (echocardiography), p<0.002), with stable performance in long-term follow-up (mean follow-up time: 70 months).
There were no ascending aortic reoperations after previous reduction aortoplasties or supracoronary ascending aortic grafts, and there were no late aortic dissections.

Operations included isolated aortic valve repair/replacement in 63 patients, combined aortic valve replacement and reduction aortoplasty in 9, aortic root replacement in 7, and isolated ascending aortic replacement in 2.

The supporting experience for size-reducing ascending aortoplasty with external reinforcement comes from retrospective single-centre series, so it documents feasibility, operative mortality and postoperative diameter reduction, but this observational design does not establish the effect of intervening with reduction aortoplasty plus external reinforcement, rather than not intervening, on late aortic outcomes.

Working in a rural location did not change midwives' overall self-reported competence: the proportion of rural and urban midwives reporting that they were competent was broadly similar, although there were significant differences for specific competencies.

In a comparative questionnaire survey of midwives in remote/rural maternity units versus three urban maternity units in Scotland, midwives in the rural group were more likely to report competence for breech delivery (p = 0.001), whereas more urban midwives reported competence in intravenous fluid replacement (p<0.001) and initial and discharge examination of the newborn (p<0.001).

The comparison rests on midwives' own questionnaire responses about their competence and confidence in rural versus urban settings, so the differences reported describe self-assessed competence rather than directly observed clinical performance.

Yes — in a study of 114 formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded specimens from locally advanced urothelial carcinoma patients treated with surgery alone or adjuvant M-VEC, HER2 immunoreactivity was a significant prognostic factor for progression-free survival (p = 0.03) and disease-specific overall survival (p = 0.02) among patients receiving adjuvant M-VEC, based on univariate analysis.

The prognostic value of HER2 immunoreactivity in the adjuvant M-VEC group did not persist in multivariate analysis, and HER2 immunoreactivity was not prognostic in patients receiving watchful waiting, so the reported prognostic information is confined to the univariate analysis of the adjuvant M-VEC subgroup.

Family history was not reliable for selecting school children for cholesterol screening: among 2096 school children in Ankara, 64.4% reported a family history of hyperlipidemia, yet no relation was found between family history and serum lipid levels.

The study population comprised 2096 school children (1043 male, 1053 female) in Ankara, with a mean age of 9.03 years; demographic properties of the children and their families were recorded and the children's serum lipid levels were measured.

The relation between these demographic properties and the children's lipid levels was investigated, and among the participants 135 had a serum cholesterol level of 200 mg/dL or greater while 83 had a serum LDL-cholesterol level of 130 mg/dL or greater.

Because the study examined relations between reported demographic properties and lipid levels measured in the same school children, it can demonstrate an association only and cannot establish whether using family history to select children for screening would change clinical outcomes.
The study was designed to identify gender differences in delay time and the reasons why African Americans delay in seeking medical care for symptoms of acute myocardial infarction (AMI).
It was conducted at five hospitals in the San Francisco and East Bay areas and included 61 African American men and women diagnosed with an AMI; the outcome examined was prehospital delay time.
Median prehospital delay time was longer for women than men (4.4 hours vs 3.5 hours), but the difference was not statistically significant.

Single women delayed longer than single men (P =.03), which is a direct comparison between genders; in contrast, being alone when symptoms began was examined within women only, with women who were alone delaying longer than women who had someone with them (P =.03).
Among women, those who received advice to seek help or call 911 upon symptom onset had shorter delays than women who were not advised to call 911 (P =.01).
Among men, those who were at home delayed longer than men who experienced their symptoms outside the home (P =.01).

Among men, those with emergency room insurance delayed longer than men without emergency room insurance (P =.03), and men who took an ambulance to the hospital had shorter delay times than men who took other means of transportation (P =.04).

Because the study is cross-sectional, the reported associations between patient characteristics (such as marital status, being alone, advice received, location, insurance, and transportation) and delay time do not establish that intervening on these factors would change delay times.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: Direct gender comparisons of most reasons for delay.

The analysis used data from facility-based maternal mortality audits in three African hospitals together with data from the latest confidential enquiry in the Netherlands, covering Kalabo district in Zambia, Farafenni division in The Gambia, Onandjokwe district in Namibia, and nationwide data from the Netherlands (rural populations in Zambia and The Gambia, a peri-urban population in Namibia).
Across these audited settings the maternal mortality ratio ranged from 10 per 100,000 in the Netherlands to 1540 per 100,000 in The Gambia.

The audit identified different cause profiles: deaths were characterized by HIV/AIDS in Namibia, by sepsis and HIV/AIDS in Zambia, by (pre-)eclampsia in the Netherlands, and by obstructed labour in The Gambia.

The audit findings indicate that the mortality differences between these low- and high-income settings were not simply a rich-versus-poor gap: the 10 per 100,000 (Netherlands) to 1540 per 100,000 (The Gambia) range was accompanied by distinct cause patterns, with HIV/AIDS in Namibia, sepsis and HIV/AIDS in Zambia, (pre-)eclampsia in the Netherlands and obstructed labour in The Gambia.

The audit approach is presented as identifying different causes of and contributing factors to maternal deaths in different settings, which the authors link to locally tailored solutions for reducing maternal deaths.

As a descriptive study of maternal mortality from different settings combined with a review of historical data from what are now high-income countries, this design can describe differing causes and ratios but cannot quantify how much of the difference in maternal mortality is attributable to economic level.
Yes — the study searched for factors present preoperatively which could be used to predict the intensity of postoperative pain.
The study was a prospective study among all patients aged over 18 years who underwent shoulder surgery from January to September 2004 in the authors' unit.

It included 86 patients, for whom the following data were noted preoperatively: past history of pain, intensity and duration of prior pain, triggering factors, localization, and psychological context.
The intensity of postoperative pain was measured on a visual analog scale (VAS), with measurements noted up to 24 hours postoperatively and then at one month.
Significant postoperative pain was correlated with a prior history of surgical pain, with the duration of prior pain, with the intensity of preoperative pain, and with depression.

Because these are reported correlations between preoperative variables and postoperative pain, they identify preoperative predictors of pain intensity but do not establish that intervening on those factors would change postoperative pain levels.

In a retrospective review of 56 patients aged 11 to 216 months who underwent exploration for a nonpalpable testis at two institutions between 1994 and 2006 and had removal of the testicular remnant, viable germ cell elements were identified in 8 of the specimens (14%), and an additional 4 patients (7%) had seminiferous tubules without germ cell elements.

The optimal management of the testicular remnant associated with the vanishing testes syndrome is controversial, with some urologists advocating surgical exploration and others considering it unnecessary, the differing opinions being based on variable reports of viable germ cell elements found within the testicular remnants; the authors reviewed their experience to better understand the pathology of the syndrome and the need for surgical management.

The retrieved report does not state a direct conclusion or recommendation on whether surgical management is necessary, and because the evidence comes from a retrospective review, that design cannot by itself establish whether removal of the remnant is required.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: a direct conclusion or recommendation on whether surgical management is necessary.

Compared with tamoxifen for early breast cancer, aromatase inhibitors were associated with an unexpectedly greater number of grade 3 and 4 cardiovascular events (CVAEs), as defined by National Cancer Institute of Canada-Common Toxicity Criteria version 2.0.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: increase in cardiovascular events specifically in postmenopausal women on adjuvant AIs.

Yes — in winter oil-seed rape (Brassica napus subsp. oleifera), pectins are implicated in cold acclimation: in leaves of two double-haploid lines differing in winter survival and blackleg (Leptosphaeria maculans) resistance, acclimation at 2 degrees C retarded leaf expansion while freezing resistance developed, and these effects were associated with increases in leaf tensile stiffness, cell wall and pectin contents, pectin methylesterase (EC 3.1.1.11) activity and low-methylated pectin content, independently of genotype.
The cold-induced modifications in cell wall properties were more pronounced in the leaves of the more pathogen-resistant genotype.

Pectins are also implicated in de-acclimation of winter oil-seed rape: de-acclimation promoted leaf expansion and reversed most of the cold-induced effects, with the exception of pectin methylesterase activity, which remained altered.

In a prospective study 218 preschool children were enrolled (stratified in 2 training programs, one specialized for phonologic awareness in order to prevent dyslexia, the other consisting in training of general perception) during the last year of kindergarten.
After finishing the first grade 131 children were compared in their reading and writing abilities.

In the whole group only a slight difference was found between both training modalities concerning their writing abilities, so the whole-group comparison does not indicate that specialized phonological awareness training is warranted for every preschool child.

The indication appears to differ across children: those with a history of hearing loss, actual hearing loss or pathologic middle ear findings profited most from the specialized training program compared with the control group in their reading abilities.

In a retrospective review of liver biopsies from a 10-year period at one hospital, routine laboratory markers were useful for distinguishing nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) from alcoholic steatohepatitis (ASH): a multivariate model combining MCV, the AST/ALT ratio and sex achieved an area under the ROC curve of 0.92.

Of the 95 patients with steatohepatitis identified, NASH was diagnosed in 58 (61%; 30 female) and ASH in 37 (39%; 9 female), with the diagnosis assigned on the basis of biopsy and history of alcohol consumption (<140 g/week) after other liver diseases were excluded.

An AST/ALT ratio >1 was more common in ASH than in NASH (54.1% vs 20.7%, P = 0.0008), as was high-grade fibrosis (59% vs 19%, P < 0.0001); the AST/ALT ratio (P < 0.0001) and age (P = 0.00049) were independent predictors of high-grade fibrosis.
MCV was elevated in 53% of ASH patients and was normal in all NASH patients (P < 0.0001), and differences in MCV were more marked in high-grade fibrosis.
On multivariate analysis, MCV (P = 0.0013), the AST/ALT ratio (P = 0.011) and sex (P = 0.0029) were identified as relevant regressors, giving an aROC of 0.92.

Because the study was a retrospective re-evaluation of data collected prior to biopsy, with diagnoses assigned from histology and reported alcohol intake, it supports an association between these routine parameters and the type of steatohepatitis rather than demonstrating that acting on them alters clinical outcomes.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: Effect of chest wall irradiation on recurrence or survival in node-negative post-mastectomy patients.

Low-tone sudden deafness (SD) does not inevitably progress to Meniere's disease: in a retrospective case review, 83 of 177 patients with low-tone SD unaccompanied by vertigo had recurrent hearing loss, of whom 15 developed vertiginous attacks, while the remaining 94 patients had a single episode.

Among seven patients with low-tone SD accompanied by vertigo, three had recurrent hearing loss and two of those three were subsequently confirmed to have Meniere's disease, whereas the other four had a single episode.
No difference in the rate of progress from SD to Meniere's disease was observed between the low-tone and the high-tone SD groups.

This was a retrospective case review in a university hospital in which 184 patients with low-tone SD were divided into two groups with single and recurrent episodes, and their progress, follow-up audiograms and ECochG results were reviewed and compared with those of patients with high-tone SD and Meniere's disease.
On ECochG, the average -SP/AP of each group with a single episode was smaller than that of the other groups with recurrent episodes and Meniere's disease.

In a Dutch multi-centre retrospective analysis of karyotype results from chorionic villus sampling performed for advanced maternal age (at least 36 years at 18 weeks of gestation) between 1995 and 2005, 20 885 CVS results drawn from 322 246 pregnancies were analysed, comprising 235 IVF/ICSI pregnancies and 20 650 control pregnancies.

When missing data were taken into account, the incidence of confined placental mosaicism was lower in the IVF/ICSI group than in the control group, 1.3% versus 2.2% (odds ratio 0.59, 95% CI 0.19-1.85), whereas the incidence of fetal chromosomal anomalies was higher in the IVF/ICSI group, 4.3% versus 2.4% (odds ratio 1.81, 95% CI 0.95-3.42); neither difference was statistically significant.
IVF singletons have poorer perinatal outcomes than singletons from spontaneous conceptions.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: confined placental mosaicism mediates or causally explains adverse perinatal outcomes in IVF pregnancies.

Yes — in a retrospective series of 154 adults undergoing major foregut surgery, laparoscopic surgery was associated with a lower risk of new-onset atrial fibrillation (univariate p = 0.004), and the association persisted in multivariate analysis after adjusting for surgery type (OR 0.09, 95% CI 0.01-0.95, p = 0.04).

The cohort comprised 154 adult patients who underwent major foregut surgery including esophagectomy, partial or total gastrectomy, redo Heller myotomy, and redo or transthoracic fundoplications; 14 of the 154 developed new-onset atrial fibrillation, nonthoracic surgery was also associated with lower risk of atrial fibrillation (p = 0.01), atrial fibrillation was associated with age (OR 1.08, 95% CI 1.02-1.14, p = 0.01), and patients with atrial fibrillation were older (67.1 +/- 8.8 years versus 56.4 +/- 14.1 years, p = 0.006).

Because the data came from a retrospective record review rather than a randomized comparison, the reported lower risk of atrial fibrillation with laparoscopic surgery is an association and cannot establish that performing laparoscopic rather than open surgery itself reduces the incidence of this complication.

The cited evidence indicates that wandering and physically nonaggressive agitation (PNA) are not equivalent concepts: in a cross-sectional correlational study of ambulatory residents meeting DSM-IV criteria for dementia, factor analysis produced a one-factor solution for wandering (explained variance = 43.66%) but a two-factor solution for PNA (explained variance = 53.45%), so the two constructs did not share the same factor structure.
In that sample of 181 participants, 73.5% wandered whereas all showed PNA behaviors, indicating that the behaviors were not co-extensive within the same individuals.

Overall wandering correlated significantly with PNA Factor 1 (df = 179, r = 0.68, p < 0.001) and with PNA Factor 2 at a lower value (df = 179, r = 0.26, p < 0.01), showing a strong association with one PNA factor but only a weak association with the other.

Wandering was coded from video-tapes of up to twelve 20-minute observations per participant using an empirically derived taxonomy of ambulation patterns, while separate raters coded the same tapes for six PNA behaviors on the agitation behavior mapping instrument, so the two constructs were measured on different instruments and rating streams.
Because the design was cross-sectional and correlational, it can describe the relationship between wandering and PNA but cannot establish that one behavior causes or leads to the other.

In a prospective comparative study of acute-phase response markers, robotically assisted laparoscopic prostatectomy (RALP) provoked a smaller surgical inflammatory response than radical retropubic prostatectomy (RRP), the marker the investigators used to judge whether RALP is less invasive.

Between May and November 2006, all patients in the department undergoing RRP or RALP were prospectively assessed; 35 patients were assessed for RALP and 26 for RRP, with a median (interquartile range) age of 62 (56-68) versus 68.5 (59.2-71.2) years (P < 0.009).
Baseline (T0) levels of IL-1, IL-6, CRP and lactate were comparable between the two arms, and IL-6, CRP and lactate levels increased during both kinds of surgery.
Mean IL-6 and CRP values were higher for RRP than RALP at T1 (P = 0.01 and 0.001), T2 (P = 0.001 and <0.001), T3 (P = 0.002 and <0.001) and T4 (P < 0.001 and 0.02), respectively.
Lactate was higher for RRP at T2 (P = 0.001), T3 (P = 0.001) and T4 (P = 0.004), although remaining within the normal ranges, while IL-1 alpha did not change at the different sample times.

As a limitation of this design, invasiveness was assessed indirectly through blood acute-phase and inflammatory markers rather than by a direct clinical measure of surgical invasiveness, so the comparison rests on the assumption that the acute-phase reaction is proportional to surgery-induced tissue damage.

In a retrospective cohort of 42 pregnancies with severe Kell alloimmunization in which fetal platelet counts were obtained before the first intrauterine transfusion, the cited evidence indicates that Kell alloimmunization was not associated with clinically significant fetal thrombocytopenia, since none of the Kell fetuses, including 15 with severe hydrops, had a platelet count below 50 x 10(9)/l.

Fetal thrombocytopenia defined as a platelet count below 150 x 10(9)/l was found in 4/42 (10%) of the Kell alloimmunized pregnancies versus 84/318 (26%) of the RhD alloimmunized control pregnancies, whose platelet counts came from 318 first intrauterine transfusions.

Among the RhD alloimmunized pregnancies, clinically significant thrombocytopenia (platelet count below 50 x 10(9)/l) occurred in 2/230 (1%) of non-hydropic fetuses and 7/30 (23%) of severely hydropic fetuses, the comparison group against which the Kell findings were assessed.

Yes: in a cohort of 1,796 men with prostate cancer treated with radiotherapy alone between April 1989 and November 2004, a larger share of nontreatment days (i.e., longer elapsed treatment time) was associated with worse biochemical control.

Treatment duration was expressed as the nontreatment day ratio (NTDR), defined as the number of nontreatment days divided by the total elapsed days of radiotherapy, a ratio used to account for the relationship between treatment duration and total radiotherapy dose.
The 10-year freedom from biochemical failure (FFBF) rate was 68% for NTDR<33% versus 58% for NTDR>/=33% (p = 0.02), with biochemical failure defined as a prostate-specific antigen nadir + 2 ng/mL.
Within the low-risk group, the 10-year FFBF rate was 82% for NTDR<33% versus 57% for NTDR>/=33% (p = 0.0019).

On multivariate analysis including Gleason score and radiation dose, NTDR was independently predictive for FFBF (p = 0.03), along with T stage (p = 0.005) and initial prostate-specific antigen level (p<0.0001).
NTDR was not a significant predictor of FFBF when examined in the intermediate-risk group, the high-risk group, or all risk groups combined.

Because the reported finding is an evaluation of elapsed treatment time against outcome in an already treated cohort, the association between a higher nontreatment day ratio and poorer FFBF does not by itself establish that shortening treatment duration would improve biochemical control.

Specialty pharmaceuticals have evolved beyond niche drugs for rare conditions and are now positioned to become the standard of care across a wide variety of common chronic illnesses, with their promise described as increased life expectancy, improved quality of life, enhanced workplace productivity, decreased burden of disease, and reduced health care spending.

That promise comes at a significant cost: specialty agents require special handling, administration, patient education, clinical support, and risk mitigation, and they require distribution systems that ensure appropriate patient selection and data collection; with an overflowing specialty pipeline and an aging population relying on these treatments for common diseases, the challenge of managing the associated costs can be daunting.

Partly because of the cost of these therapies, payers are increasingly demanding evidence of their value, but determining that value is hampered by a lack of robust pharmacoeconomic data; the source states that with sophisticated pharmacoeconomic models to assess value, the cost impacts of specialty drugs can be appropriately controlled.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: definitive conclusion on whether benefits justify price.

Yes — in a cross-sectional assessment at a 900-bed teaching hospital in Ibadan, Nigeria, physicians' specialties significantly influenced both the depth and the frequency of medication history documentation across the nine specialties studied (P<0.0001 for each).

The study was a cross-sectional assessment of the frequency and depth of medication history information documented by 123 physicians for 900 randomly selected patients stratified across Cardiology, Chest, Dermatology, Endocrine, Gastroenterology, Haematology, Neurology, Psychiatry and Renal specialties.

Post hoc pair-wise comparisons using Tukey's HSD test showed the highest mean scores for adverse drug reactions and adherence to medicines in the Cardiology specialty, and the highest mean scores for allergy to drugs, food, chemicals and cigarette smoking in the Chest specialty.
Mean scores for use of alcohol, illicit drugs and dietary restrictions were highest in the Gastroenterology, Psychiatry and Endocrine specialties respectively.

Because the design was cross-sectional, the reported differences by specialty describe an association between specialty and documentation practice and cannot establish that changing a physician's specialty or practice would cause a change in documentation.

Yes — in a case-control study, polymorphisms in the beta-adrenergic receptor genes were associated with transient tachypnea of the newborn (TTN), based on the finding that the beta1Ser49Gly polymorphism differed significantly between cases and controls.
The study population comprised 73 term newborns with TTN and 55 healthy controls, all from a Caucasian cohort, with DNA collected for genotyping.
In multivariate analysis, beta1Gly49 homozygotes had a higher risk for TTN than beta1Ser49 allele carriers (OR 18.5; 95% CI 1.5–229; p = 0.023).
Further analysis showed a significant association between the T-47C, A46G, C79G and C491T (TACC) haplotype of the ADRB2 gene and TTN (p = 0.048).

Because the cited evidence comes from a case-control comparison of newborns with TTN against healthy controls, it can establish an association between ADRB variants and TTN but not that these variants cause TTN.

For tissue microarrays, although pathologists frequently feel better if larger core sizes are used, there is no evidence in the literature showing that large cores are better (or worse) than small cores for assessment of TMAs; measurement of a single random 0.6-mm spot was comparable to analysis of the whole 1-mm or 1.5-mm spot, with a Pearson R coefficient varying from 0.87 to 0.98 for all markers tested.
Evidence from surgery shows that high volume is often associated with better outcomes.

In the study of boys and girls, overweight and obese girls selected larger ideal body figures than the others (trend test: P<0.001); compared with those with middle ideal body figures, girls who selected smaller ones were twice as likely to have an unhealthy diet as indicated by less fruit and milk consumption, with odds ratios (95% CIs) of 2.40 (1.15-5.02) for fruit intake less than once per week and 2.13 (1.06-4.29) for milk consumption less than once per day.

Boys with larger IBI were less likely to eat snack often [≥once/day; OR = 0.11 (0.02-0.50)]; girls with larger IBI were less likely to spend more screen time [OR = 0.12 (0.02-0.70)] and reported better food choice intentions (P<0.05); overweight and obese boys and girls appeared to have better food choice intentions and food self-efficacy than their non-overweight peers (trend test: both P<0.01).

In a survey, two hundred and nine (57% female) adults completed the survey; thirty eight percent had a healthy BMI (18.5-24.9), 38% were overweight (BMI 25-29.9) and a further 22% were obese (BMI>30); over 80% thought being overweight was likely or very likely to be a risk factor for cardiovascular disease, hypertension, diabetes and stroke; however, 20% of overweight or obese individuals did not think their health would improve if they lost weight.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: A general answer to whether being big is better across all contexts.

Yes, in part: in 67 patients undergoing transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) without a video camera, randomized into three groups by urologist experience (Group I, 24 patients, urologist having done 25 TURPs; Group II, 24 patients, urologist having done 50 TURPs; Group III, 19 patients, senior urologist with vast TURP experience), the weight of resected tissue per minute was approximately four times higher in Group III than in Groups I and II, indicating that resection efficiency differed with the surgeon's previous experience.

The parameters recorded during the procedures in that trial were the weight of resected tissue, the duration of the resection procedure, the volume of irrigation used, the amount of irrigation absorbed, and the hemoglobin and sodium levels in serum during the procedure.

There were no differences between the three experience groups in the amount of irrigation fluid used per operation, the amount of irrigation fluid absorbed, or hematocrit and hemoglobin variation during the procedure; the mean absorbed irrigation fluid was similar between groups with no statistical difference (p=0.24).
Four patients (6%) presented with TUR syndrome, without a significant difference between the groups.

In the Bezafibrate Infarction Prevention (BIP) Study analysis, the effect of bezafibrate on colon cancer development in patients with coronary artery disease was investigated over a 6-year follow-up; the observed findings are suggestive of a possible preventive effect but do not establish that bezafibrate prevents colon cancer.
Development of colon cancer was recorded in 25 patients: in 8 (0.53%) patients from the bezafibrate group vs.
17 (1.13%) from the placebo group (Fisher's exact test: one side p = 0.05; two side p = 0.07).
On multivariable analysis the colon cancer risk in patients who received bezafibrate tended to be lower with a hazard ratio of 0.47 and 95% confidence interval 0.2-1.1.
In this analysis, a difference in the incidence of cancer was only detectable after a 4 year lag and progressively increased with continued follow-up.

The population included 3011 patients without any cancer diagnosis who were enrolled in the randomized, double blind Bezafibrate Infarction Prevention (BIP) Study and who received either 400 mg of bezafibrate retard (1506 patients) or placebo (1505 patients) once a day, with cancer incidence data obtained by matching a subject's identification numbers with the National Cancer Registry.

Yes — in a study of 45 end-stage renal disease patients on regular hemodialysis, intradialytic endothelin-1 (ET-1) changes paralleled hemodynamic status: ET-1 fell significantly in the dialysis-induced hypotension group (8.56 +/- 1.44 vs.
11.75 +/- 2.51 pg/ml) and rose significantly in the rebound hypertension group (16.39 +/- 3.12 vs.
11.93 +/- 2.11 pg/ml), both P<0.001 versus pre-dialysis values, whereas it was unchanged in the stable-hemodynamics group (14.49 +/- 2.04 vs.

Pre-dialysis ET-1 levels were significantly higher in the 45 dialysis patients than in the 15 healthy volunteer controls (P<0.001), but were comparable across the three hemodialysis groups, which were defined by stable intradialytic hemodynamics, dialysis-induced hypotension and rebound hypertension during hemodialysis.

The authors note that the etiology of hemodialysis-induced hypotension and hypertension remains speculative, and because the study compared intradialytic ET-1 concentrations with hemodynamic status rather than manipulating ET-1, it cannot establish that the observed ET-1 changes cause the hypotension or rebound hypertension.

Yes — severe macrosomia appears to be manifested already at 11-14 weeks' gestation in a case-control study of 30 term severely macrosomic neonates and 90 appropriate-for-gestational-age controls who all underwent nuchal translucency (NT) screening at 11-14 weeks: the difference between measured and expected crown-rump length (CRL) was significantly greater in the severely macrosomic group than in controls, both in millimetres (mean 6.66 +/- 4.78 mm vs.
1.17 +/- 4.6 mm, P<0.0001) and in days of gestation (3 +/- 2.2 days vs.

0.5 +/- 2.3 days, P<0.0001), and the extent of macrosomia correlated significantly with the discrepancy between expected and measured fetal size at the time of NT screening (r = 0.47, P<0.01 and r = 0.48, P<0.01).
Yes — a relationship is reported: mean serum homocysteine (Hcy) was significantly higher in patients with vitiligo than in age-matched healthy controls (21.61 +/- 13.28 vs.

That comparison came from a study of 26 patients of both sexes with vitiligo (age range 20-50 years, mean 31.4 +/- 8.09) and 26 age-matched healthy controls, in which, after excluding factors that may affect serum Hcy levels, blood samples from patients and controls were obtained for homocysteine determination by enzyme immunoassay.
The Hcy level was related to the activity of vitiligo and was significantly higher in patients with progressive disease than in controls (25.4 +/- 14.99 vs.
No — in a prospective cohort of participants with major affective disorders, the effects of risk factors for suicidal behavior did not differ by affective disorder polarity.

In the NIMH Collaborative Depression Study, mixed-effects, grouped-time survival analysis assessed the risk of suicidal behavior and the differential effects of risk factors for suicidal behavior by polarity, modeling in addition to polarity the main effects of age, gender, hopelessness, married status, prior suicide attempts and active substance abuse, with mood cycle as the unit of analysis.
Age, hopelessness and active substance abuse, but not polarity, predicted suicidal behavior.

The analysis followed 909 participants meeting prospective diagnostic criteria for major depressive and bipolar disorders through 4204 mood cycles, during which 40 cycles ended in suicide and 384 cycles contained at least one suicide attempt.
After controlling for age of onset, there were no differences in prior suicide attempts by polarity, although bipolar participants had more prior severe attempts.

Yes — a geriatric oncology consultation modified the cancer treatment plan: among 93 patients with an initial treatment decision, the treatment plan was modified in 38.7% of cases after the assessment.

In this study, oncology data and treatment decisions were recorded before and after the geriatric oncology consultation, and the analysis examined possible correlations between domains of the geriatric assessment and modification of the treatment plan.
Only body mass index and the absence of depressive symptoms were associated with a modification of the treatment plan.

The study included 105 patients aged 70 years or older referred to a geriatric oncology consultation at the Institut Curie cancer center between June 2004 and May 2005; their assessment covered functional status, nutritional status, mood, mobility, comorbidity, medication, social support and place of residence.

This study aimed to establish whether an easy and practical intervention, mailing out a summary of current evidence to surgeons, can change surgeons' practice to bring it more in line with current evidence; a one-page summary of recent evidence concerning prophylactic NG decompression was then mailed to all general surgeons at the Royal Alexandra Hospital.

The use of prophylactic nasogastric (NG) decompression in elective colonic resections was documented for the 2 consecutive months of October and November, 2004 at the Royal Alexandra Hospital (RAH), and a similar second review was carried out for the months of January and February, 2005.
Twenty two patients underwent elective colonic resections during the months of October and November, 2004, and twenty one patients underwent such procedures in January and February, 2005.
The two periods were compared with regards to prophylactic NG use.

Seven out of the 22 cases in the first group (the pre-intervention block) received prophylactic NG decompression, and five out of the 21 cases in the second group (the post-intervention block) received prophylactic NG decompression.
The difference in prophylactic NG use between the two groups was not statistically significant.
The observed difference in prophylactic NG use is an association and does not by itself establish that surgeon familiarization with the evidence caused any change in practice.

Yes — in a prospective series of 100 patients with epilepsy or new onset seizure, several cytokines were detectable in serum (IL-6 42, TNF-alpha 36, IL-2 22, IL-4 22, IFN-gamma 20, IL-1 11 patients) and in CSF of the 9 patients tested, and levels fell during the seizure-free period, indicating an association between cytokines and seizure activity in this cohort.

Serum samples were prospectively collected from 100 patients with epilepsy or new onset seizure in the immediate post-ictal phase and compared with 100 matched healthy controls, with serum TNF-alpha, IFN-gamma, IL-1beta, IL-2, IL-4 and IL-6 assessed by ELISA; CSF analysis was performed in 9 patients of this cohort when clinically indicated, and a second sample was collected during the seizure-free period in 16 patients.
In CSF, IL-6 was detectable in 4/9 patients and IL-1 in 2/9 patients, while IL-2, IL-4 and IFN-gamma were each detectable in 1 patient.

Correlations were noted between male gender and IL-1beta (p=0.04), positive family history and IL-1beta (p=0.001), no alcohol use and TNF-alpha (p=0.05), more than one year history of epilepsy and IL-1beta (p=0.02), and status epilepticus and IL-6 (p=0.04).
There was no difference between the new onset seizure group and the epilepsy group.

Serial analysis during the seizure-free period showed decreases in cytokine levels: TNF-alpha from 25% to 12.5%, IFN-gamma from 12.5% to 0%, IL-1 from 25% to 0%, IL-2 from 6.2% to 6.2%, IL-4 from 18.8% to 0%, and IL-6 from 18.8% to 6.2%.

Because this study prospectively measured cytokine levels and correlated them with clinical parameters rather than intervening, it can support an association between cytokines and epilepsy but cannot establish that cytokines cause seizures or that modifying cytokine levels alters clinical outcomes.

In a prospective study of 97 patients with ulcerative colitis (UC) and 65 with Crohn's disease (CD) in clinical remission, calprotectin testing was assessed for its role in predicting clinical relapse, with the cutoff set at 130 mg/kg of feces and patients followed for 1 year after the test or until relapse.

Among the UC patients, the calprotectin test was positive in 44 and 26 of them relapsed within a year, whereas 11 of the 53 UC patients with a negative test relapsed within the same time frame; a significant correlation emerged between a positive calprotectin test and the probability of relapse in UC patients (P= 0.000).

Among the CD patients, 30 had a positive calprotectin test and 13 of them relapsed within a year, as did 7 of the 35 with a negative test result; only cases of colonic CD showed a significant correlation between a positive calprotectin test and the probability of relapse, with 6 colonic CD patients positive for the test and 4 relapsing (P= 0.02).

The reported evidence for calprotectin as a relapse marker in this prospective remission cohort consists of correlations between test positivity and relapse probability within 1 year, so the design as reported does not establish that acting on calprotectin results alters clinical outcomes.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: Longitudinal evidence on the proportion or risk of overweight children who become overweight adults.

Myometrial electrical activity, assessed as electrical uterine myography (EUM), can help identify patients in preterm labor: in a prospective study of 87 women at gestational age less than 35 weeks, patients who delivered within 14 days of testing had a higher EUM index and higher mean RMS than those who did not (P =.000), and no patient with an EUM index score of 1-2 delivered within that time frame.

The EUM index score (1-5) for prediction of preterm delivery within 14 days of the test was developed from the period between contractions, the power of contraction peaks, and the movement of the center of electrical activity (RMS), and the score was compared with fetal fibronectin (fFN) and cervical length (CL).

Combining EUM with CL or fFN increased predictability of preterm delivery within 14 days, and logistic regression showed that a history of preterm delivery and the EUM index were associated with a 4- to 5-fold increased risk of preterm delivery.
In the same logistic regression, gestational age at testing, body mass index, fFN, and CL were nonsignificant contributors to preterm delivery risk.

In a prospective repeat-measures study of 82 newly diagnosed head and neck cancer patients (54 males, 28 females, mean age 60 years), path analyses demonstrated that fears of cancer recurrence after treatment were directly predicted by pre-treatment fears and optimism; participants completed measures of fears of recurrence, illness perceptions, coping, and anxiety and depression before treatment and again 6-8 months after treatment (fears of recurrence only).

In the same cohort, a third of head and neck cancer patients reported relatively high levels of fear of recurrence at diagnosis, and 12% still reported similar levels of fear 6-8 months after treatment.

Fears of recurrence in these head and neck cancer patients were not related to any socio-demographic factor (age, gender, ethnicity, marital status, and educational attainment) or to disease, treatment, or symptom-related factors.

The retrieved evidence does not establish that octogenarians are at high risk for carotid endarterectomy: the cited series reports only perioperative outcomes for octogenarians themselves (4 neurologic complications and no deaths among 103 operations) without a younger-patient comparator or a defined high-risk threshold.

In a 12-year series of 103 carotid endarterectomies performed in 95 octogenarians aged 80 to 89 years, there were 4 perioperative neurologic complications: 1 transient ischemic attack (0.97%), 2 minor strokes (1.94%), and 1 major stroke (0.97%), and there were no deaths.

The 103 procedures in that octogenarian series were performed on 59 men and 36 women, and the indications for operation were symptomatic carotid stenosis in 44 patients (43%) and asymptomatic carotid stenosis in 59 patients (57%).

Because this was a single-group series of octogenarians, the cited evidence cannot test the proposal that being an octogenarian places patients in a carotid stenting high-risk category, nor does it compare perioperative carotid endarterectomy risk against patients younger than 80 years, for whom randomized trials had shown the operation to be safe and effective.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: a direct comparison with younger patients or an explicit high-risk threshold.

Yes — home sampling kits for bacterial sexually transmitted infections were generally viewed as acceptable, that is, positively, by men who have sex with men in the cited qualitative study, which was conducted as a formative evaluation of HSKs using focus groups (n = 20) and one-to-one semi-structured interviews (n = 24).

The reported benefits of a HSK were increased access to testing, enhanced personal comfort and empowerment, while the concerns raised were the accuracy of the test, delays in receiving results, a possible lack of support and a potential negative impact on 'others'.

Because the evidence comes from focus group discussions of self-sampling materials and interviews with men who had used self-sampling in a pilot clinical study, the findings describe views and potential acceptability rather than measured uptake of home sampling kits; the reported perspectives cannot by themselves establish use or test performance.

The retrieved report of the French-German Military Trauma Group does not use the label 'Main Gate Syndrome' and does not explicitly designate the described approach as a new format for mass-casualty victim 'surge' management.
