In an observational cross-sectional study of 75 patients with chronic periodontitis (43 males and 32 females) divided into Group I and Group II, blood oozing from the gingival crevices of anterior teeth following periodontal probing was collected with the stick of a glucose self-monitoring device and the blood glucose levels were measured, while finger-prick blood was taken at the same time for glucometric analysis with the readings recorded.

In that chronic periodontitis population the patients' blood glucose values ranged from 74 to 256 mg/dl, and the comparison between gingival crevicular blood and finger-prick blood showed a very strong correlation, with a t value of 3.97 at a P value of 0.001.

Because the cited evidence comes from an observational cross-sectional design in which gingival crevicular and finger-prick glucose were measured at the same time, the reported correlation supports agreement between the two simultaneous readings but does not by itself establish that gingival crevicular blood can be relied upon for assessing blood glucose level, for example as a substitute diagnostic measurement.

A high-intelligence subgroup does exist among schizophrenia patients: although schizophrenia patients are typically found to have low IQ both pre- and post-onset relative to the general population, a subgroup displays above average IQ pre-onset.

In the study by PMID:25752725, 29 schizophrenia patients of exceptionally high pre-morbid intelligence were identified, with a mean estimated pre-morbid IQ of 120, and around half of them also showed minimal decline (less than 10 IQ points) from their estimated pre-morbid IQ.

The symptom scores of these high-IQ patients (SAPS, SANS, OPCRIT, MADRS, GAF, SAI-E) were compared with a comparison group of schizophrenia patients of typical IQ using multinomial logistic regression.

Patients with very high pre-morbid IQ had significantly lower scores on negative and disorganised symptoms than typical patients (RRR=0.019; 95% CI=0.001, 0.675, P=0.030) and showed better global functioning and insight (RRR=1.082; 95% CI=1.020, 1.148; P=0.009).
Among the high-IQ patients, those with a minimal post-onset IQ decline also showed higher levels of manic symptoms (RRR=8.213; 95% CI=1.042, 64.750, P=0.046).

In a population-based observational study in Paris and surrounding suburbs, the probability of prenatal diagnosis and of termination of pregnancy for fetal anomaly was not statistically different between ART-conceived and spontaneously conceived fetuses with congenital heart defects.

The probability of PND was 28.1% versus 34.6% (P = 0.077) and of TOPFA 36.2% versus 39.2% (P = 0.677) for ART-conceived (n = 171) versus spontaneously conceived (n = 4620) fetuses, and estimates were similar after adjustment for potential confounders (maternal characteristics, multiplicity and year of birth or TOPFA).
The retrieved evidence does not establish: Probability of PND or TOPFA for ART-conceived fetuses with congenital anomalies other than congenital heart defects.

The retrieved evidence does not establish whether clinical supervision sustains the workforce (e.g., retention, turnover, or workforce stability) in the current healthcare landscape; the available study measured clinical supervision effectiveness rather than workforce-sustainability outcomes.

In a cross-sectional study of community allied health workers (n = 82) conducted 8 months after implementation of structured clinical supervision, the outcome measure, clinical supervision effectiveness, was operationalised using the Manchester Clinical Supervision Scale-26 (MCSS-26).
Data were analysed with Pearson correlation (r) and independent sample t-tests (t) with significance set at 0.05 (ie the probability of significant difference set at P<0.05).

The length of the supervision sessions (r(s) ≥ 0.44), the number of sessions (r(s) ≥ 0.35) and the total period supervision had been received (r(s) ≥ 0.42) were all significantly positively correlated with the MCSS-26 domains of clinical supervision effectiveness.

Three individual variables, namely 'receiving clinical supervision', 'having some choice in the allocation of clinical supervisor' and 'having a completed clinical supervision agreement', were also significantly associated with higher total MCSS-26 scores (P(s)<0.014).

Because the design was a cross-sectional survey, these correlations and associations between supervision characteristics and MCSS-26 scores cannot establish that clinical supervision sustains the workforce, since no retention, turnover or workforce-stability outcome was measured.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: clinical supervision sustains the workforce (e.g., retention, turnover, or workforce stability) in the current healthcare landscape.

The cited evidence is mixed: gay men living with HIV recruited via the Web reported worse mean psychological symptom burden than those recruited in clinics, but a similar physical symptom burden, and recruitment setting was not significantly associated with a high physical symptom score.

The Web-based sample comprised 154 respondents to a UK-wide Web survey of gay men with diagnosed HIV who identified themselves as resident in London, while the clinic comparison group comprised 400 gay men recruited from five HIV outpatient clinics in London.

The Web-based sample was younger than the clinic sample (37.3 years, SD 7.0 vs 40.9 years, SD 8.3), more likely to be in paid employment (72.8%, 99/136 vs 60.1%, 227/378), and less likely to be on antiretroviral therapy (58.4%, 90/154 vs 68.0%, 266/391).

Mean psychological symptom burden was worse in the Web-based sample than in the clinic sample (1.61, SD 1.09 vs 1.36, SD 0.96), whereas mean physical symptom burden was similar between the two groups (0.78, SD 0.65 vs 0.70, SD 0.74).

In a multivariable logistic regression model for physical symptom burden adjusted for age, ethnicity, employment status, and ART use, recruitment setting (Web-based vs clinic) was not significantly associated with a high physical symptom score.
In the psychological symptom burden model, those recruited via the Web were significantly more likely to report being in the upper (worst) tertile (adjusted OR 2.20, 95% CI 1.41-3.44, P=.001).

Because these results come from a cross-sectional comparison of two separately recruited samples rather than a randomized or longitudinal design, the association between Web recruitment and a worse psychological symptom tertile cannot establish that recruitment setting itself causes greater psychological symptom burden.

Evidence on the accuracy of emergency physician (EP) assessment of acute vertigo is mixed: in a prospective single-center academic emergency department (ED) validation of the STANDING tool, EPs showed high sensitivity and specificity for central acute vertigo, but a separate review of routine ED nystagmus documentation found that the recorded descriptions rarely supported a meaningful inference and frequently conflicted with the EP diagnosis.

In the STANDING (SponTAneous Nystagmus, Direction, head Impulse test, standiNG) validation, a convenience sample of 98 adult patients with isolated vertigo (vertigo without other neurological deficits) presenting to a single academic ED was prospectively evaluated by five EPs with limited experience in nystagmus assessment, and central acute vertigo was suspected in 16 (16.3%) patients.

Using local standard practice of senior audiologist evaluation corroborated by neuroimaging when deemed appropriate as the reference standard, STANDING produced 13 true positives, three false positives, 81 true negatives and one false negative, giving a sensitivity of 92.9% (95% CI 70-100%) and specificity of 96.4% (95% CI 93-38%, as reported) for central acute vertigo according to senior audiologist evaluation.

Of 1,091 visits for dizziness, 887 (81.3%) documented a nystagmus assessment; nystagmus was present in 185 of those 887 (20.9%) visits, yet the documentation of nystagmus, including all recorded descriptors, allowed a meaningful inference about localization or cause in only 10 of those 185 visits (5.4%), and the nystagmus description conflicted with the EP diagnosis in 113 (80.7%) of the 140 visits that received a peripheral vestibular diagnosis.
On the first 30 patients, inter-observer agreement among EPs was also assessed.

Inter-observer agreement among EPs using STANDING was assessed on the first 30 patients, and the Cohen's kappas of the first, second, third and fourth steps (spontaneous nystagmus, direction of nystagmus, head impulse test, and gait) were 0.86, 0.93, 0.73 and 0.78, respectively.
For the whole STANDING test, inter-observer agreement was good, with k = 0.76 (95% CI 0.45-1).

Sensation does return to the nasal tip after microfat grafting: in a prospective study of 30 young women (mean age 20.04 ± 3.63 years), the preoperative mean touch threshold of 3.60 units decreased by 2.50 units one week after injection and then recovered gradually, reaching 1.51 units at week 2, 2.39 units at week 4, 3.01 units at week 8 and 3.35 units at week 12.

In the same cohort, significant differences were detected between multiple different measurement points (P<.05), and the percentage of women experiencing paresthesia after the microfat injections gradually diminished to none.

The study's objective was to suggest trial conditions adapted from the NF EN 13727 standard for evaluating antiseptics used in gynecology and dermatology, with the adaptation consisting of choosing the dilutions, solvent and interfering substances.

Under these adapted conditions the activity of the solutions was assessed on the recommended strains at concentrations of 97% (pure solution), 50%, 10% (diluted solution) and 1%, with a logarithmic reduction of at least 5 expected after 60 seconds of contact to meet the requirements of bactericidal activity.
Three antiseptic solutions were tested in vitro: a chlorhexidine-benzalkonium (CB) combination, a hexamidine-chlorhexidine-chlorocresol (HCC) combination, and povidone iodine (P).
HCC did not present any bactericidal activity except on P. aeruginosa at a concentration of 97%, and P was not bactericidal on E. hirae at any concentration and on S. aureus at 97%.
CB had the most homogeneous bactericidal activity with a reduction>5 log on the 4 bacterial strains at concentrations of 97%, 50% and 10%.

The authors state that there is no standard protocol for evaluating antiseptics used for skin and mucous membranes in the presence of interfering substances, and that adapting the trial conditions to the standard involved choosing dilutions, solvent and interfering substances.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: effect of selected interfering substances on bactericidal activity.

Yes, selected preresidency selection criteria correlated with subsequent measures of orthopaedic resident performance: in a review of 60 residents at one institution, ABOS Part I scores had a moderate linear correlation with USMLE Step 2 scores (r = 0.55, p<0.001) and with the number of clinical honors received in medical school (r = 0.45, p<0.001).
OITE scores had a weak linear correlation with the number of clinical honors (r = 0.35, p = 0.009) and with USMLE Step 2 scores (r = 0.29, p = 0.02).

For the subjective outcome, AOA honor medical society membership was associated with higher global evaluation scores (p = 0.005) and correlated with higher global evaluation scores (r = 0.60, p = 0.005), with the strongest correlation between AOA membership and the interpersonal and communication skills subsection of the global evaluations.

These findings come from a retrospective review of charts of 60 orthopaedic residents at a single institution in which associations between preresidency criteria and later performance metrics were tested with linear correlation analysis and Mann-Whitney tests, so the reported correlations describe associations rather than establishing that these selection criteria cause better resident performance.

Minimally invasive video-assisted mitral valve repair using artificial chords was reproducible in a single-centre retrospective series of 426 consecutive patients (mean age 55 ± 18 years) in which neochords were used in all patients, in association with leaflet resection in 47 patients; one patient was not repairable and underwent valve replacement, giving a repair rate of 99.8%.

In that series, 15 patients had Grade I regurgitation (3.5%) while the remainder had none, and over a follow-up of 3–60 months all patients remained with no or trace mitral regurgitation, with no de-insertion or rupture of any neochords and no patient requiring a reoperation.

Because the evidence comes from a retrospective review of consecutive patients without a comparison group, it supports within-series reproducibility of the technique but cannot by itself establish prospective, multi-centre reproducibility.

Applicability in routine surgery is supported by a retrospective review of all patients who underwent minimally invasive video-assisted mitral valve repair from 2008 to 2013, in which 426 consecutive patients were treated with neochords in all cases and a repair rate of 99.8% was achieved.

In the same routine-surgery setting, patients were fast-tracked, with 25% extubated in the operating theatre and the remainder within 6 h, 5 deaths occurred within 30 days (1.2%), and no patients required a reoperation.

The purpose of this study is to evaluate whether this rate reduction is sustainable for at least 1 year and to identify key determinants of this sustainability at the NICU of the Floating Hospital for Children at Tufts Medical Center. the authors reviewed the incidence of CLABSIs in the NICU temporally to the implementation of new practice policies and procedures, from July 2008 to December 2013.

Yes, a zero CLABSI rate was reported as sustained in that NICU: adoption of standardized care practices, including bundles and checklists, was associated with a significant reduction of the CLABSI rate to zero for >370 consecutive days in the NICU in 2012.
In the first quarter of 2013, there was a brief increase in CLABSI rate to 3.3 per 1000 line days; after a series of interventions, the CLABSI rate was maintained at zero for >600 days.

Overall, CLABSI rates decreased from 4.1 per 1000 line days in 2009 (13 infections; 3163 line days) to 0.94 in 2013 (2 infections; 2115 line days), which represents a 77% reduction over a 5-year period.
Ongoing training, surveillance, and vigilance with catheter insertion and maintenance practices and improved documentation were identified as key drivers for success.

These results come from a single-center temporal review of CLABSI incidence in one NICU alongside the implementation of new practice policies and procedures, so the reported sustainability is documented for that unit rather than establishing that zero rates are achieved or maintained in other NICUs.

In 230 Saudi patients whose pretreatment orthodontic casts were classified into tapered, ovoid or square mandibular arch forms from digitally scanned images, no association was observed between the presence of a significant Bolton tooth-size discrepancy and either sagittal molar relationship or arch form.

In that sample the Bolton ratio was calculated, sagittal molar relationship was defined according to Angle classification, and correlations were analyzed using ANOVA, chi-square and t-tests, with no single arch form being significantly more common than the others.

Because these findings come from a cross-sectional classification of casts with correlation analysis rather than a longitudinal or interventional design, they cannot establish that sagittal molar relationship or Bolton discrepancy causes or influences arch form.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: association between sagittal molar relationship and arch form.

In a retrospective study of patients who underwent emergency laparotomy from June 2010 to May 2012, 477 laparotomies were performed in 446 patients (57% aged <70 years and 43% aged >70 years); 30-day mortality was 12, 4% in those aged <70 years and 22% in those aged >70 years (p<0.001).
Recent studies suggest 30-day mortality to be 14-15%.
In the same series, 1-year mortality was 25, 15% in those aged under 70 years and 38% in those aged >70 years (p<0.001).
The primary end point of the study was 30-day mortality, age-related 30-day mortality and 1-year all-cause mortality.

In a retrospective study of 130 poor responders undergoing IVF, pretreatment with luteal estradiol plus GnRH antagonist before microdose leuprolide did not improve IVF outcomes relative to oral contraceptive pill pretreatment; ongoing pregnancy rates were significantly higher in the OCP/ML group (40% vs.
Between the OCP/ML and E2 + antagonist/ML groups there were no significant differences in gonadotropin requirement, cancellation rate, or number of embryos transferred.
Trends toward a greater number of oocytes retrieved (7.7 ± 3.4 vs.
5.9 ± 4.2) and improved implantation rates (20% vs.
12%) were also noted, but these did not reach statistical significance.

The comparison rests on a retrospective design in 130 poor responders, which is an observational comparison and does not by itself establish that changing the pretreatment protocol causes a change in IVF outcomes.
Yes — in an observational clinical study of 431 dental patients, an association was found between sublingual varices and hypertension (OR = 2.25, p<0.002).

In that study, mean systolic blood pressure was 123 mmHg in patients with grade 0 sublingual varices and 132 mmHg in those with grade 1 varices (p<0.0001, 95% CI), while mean diastolic blood pressure was 80 mmHg and 83 mmHg in the grade 0 and grade 1 groups, respectively (p<0.005, 95% CI).
Sublingual varices indicated hypertension with a positive predictive value of 0.5 and a negative predictive value of 0.80.

Tongue status was documented in the 431 dental patients using digital photographs of the lateral borders of the tongue, which two independent blinded observers graded as none/few (grade 0) or medium/severe (grade 1) presence of sublingual varices, alongside blood pressure measurement; Pearson's Chi-square test, Student's t-test and multiple regression analysis were applied.

Because the cited evidence comes from an observational clinical study, the reported association between sublingual varices and hypertension does not establish that sublingual varices cause hypertension or that treating one changes the other.

For the question of whether biofeedback training enhances athletes' sport performance, the cited evidence is insufficient: the 8-week experimental study in highly competent athletes reports greater psychophysiological control in the biofeedback (experimental) group than in controls, but the retrieved report describes only one-year follow-up questioning of the experimental group about any subsequent enhancement in athletic performance and presents no measured performance outcome.

The 8-week biofeedback study reported that a greater number of participants in the experimental group (18 athletes: 4 women, 14 men) were able to successfully control their psychophysiological parameters compared with the control group (21 athletes: 4 women, 17 men), based on the overall percentage of athletes in each group able to control respiration, skin conductance, heart rate, blood flow amplitude, heart rate variability, and heart-respiration coherence.

Significant results (p<0.05) were noted in regulation of GSR following short stress test conditions (p = 0.037), in regulation of HR after exposure to the STROOP stressor (p = 0.037), in regulation of GSR following the Math and GSR stressors (p = 0.033, p = 0.409), and in achieving HR-breathing coherence following the math stressor (p = 0.042).
The retrieved evidence does not establish: Measured enhancement of athletes' sport/athletic performance following biofeedback training.

Unenhanced fat-suppressed T1-weighted MRI did not reliably differentiate bone infarcts from acute osteomyelitis in children with sickle cell disease: bone marrow signal intensity on T1-W fat-saturated imaging was not significant for the differentiation between bone infarct and osteomyelitis (P = 0.56).

The study retrospectively reviewed the records of 31 children (20 boys, 11 girls; mean age 10.6 years, range 1.1-17.9 years) with sickle cell disease and acute bone pain who underwent MR imaging including unenhanced T1-W fat-saturated images from 2005 to 2010.

A clinical standard defining the presence or absence of osteomyelitis was established by a pediatric hematologist with training in infectious diseases who reviewed complete clinical charts, while a pediatric radiologist blinded to clinical information reviewed all MR imaging.

Children were classified on T1-W fat-saturated images as positive for osteomyelitis when bone marrow signal intensity was low and positive for bone infarct when it was high; by the clinical standard, 5 children were classified as positive for osteomyelitis and 26 as positive for bone infarct (negative for osteomyelitis).
None of the additional evaluated imaging parameters on unenhanced MRI proved reliable in differentiating bone infarct from osteomyelitis in this pediatric sickle cell disease cohort.

Yes: in a retrospective cohort of 522 singleton pregnancies with a history of spontaneous preterm birth, the risk of recurrent preterm birth differed significantly by the clinical presentation of the prior preterm birth, occurring in 55.2% of women with prior advanced cervical dilatation versus 27.2% of those with prior preterm premature rupture of membranes and 32.2% of those with prior preterm labor (P =.001).

Mean gestational age at delivery was significantly lower in women with a history of advanced cervical dilatation (34.0 weeks) than in women with prior preterm premature rupture of membranes (37.2 weeks) or prior preterm labor (37.0 weeks) (P =.001).

The lowest mean cervical length measured before 24 weeks was significantly shorter in women whose prior preterm birth involved advanced cervical dilatation than in women with the other prior clinical presentations.

Of the 522 patients analyzed, 96 (18.4%) had a prior preterm birth with advanced cervical dilatation, 246 (47.1%) had prior preterm premature rupture of membranes, and 180 (34.5%) had prior preterm labor.

the authors conducted a national survey of Canadian Royal College emergency medicine (EM) residents and program directors to determine the extent to which active outcome feedback and follow-up occurred. the authors received 210 completed surveys from 260 eligible residents (80.8%) and 21 of 24 program directors (87.5%) (overall 81.3%).
Mandatory active outcome feedback was not present in any EM training program for admitted or discharged patients (0/21).
Follow-up was performed electively by 89.4% of residents for patients admitted to the hospital, and by 44.2% of residents for patients discharged home.
A majority of residents (76.9%) believed that patient follow-up should be mandatory compared to 42.9% of program directors (p=0.002).

The perceived educational value of outcome feedback was 5.8/7 for residents and 5.1/7 for program directors (difference 0.7; p=0.002) based on a seven-point Likert scale (1=not important; 7=very important).
The retrieved evidence does not establish: opportunity to apply the theory of deliberate practice.
A total of 80,565 Papanicolaou (Pap) smears underwent RPS during a 25-month period.
The final cytologic interpretation was a glandular cell abnormality (≥AGC) in 107 samples (0.13%); 39 of these (36.4%) were flagged as R on RPS.

Twenty-four patients (33.8%) out of 71 who had histologic follow-up were found to harbor a high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion or carcinoma; 13 of those 24 Pap smears (54.2%) had been flagged as R on RPS.
Notably, 11 AGC cases were picked up by RPS only and not by FS and represented false-negative cases; 2 of these showed endometrial adenocarcinoma on histologic follow-up.

The efficacy of RPS has been previously studied but mostly with respect to squamous lesions; in fact, there has been no study so far specifically looking at the sensitivity of RPS for detecting glandular cell abnormalities.

A randomised controlled study of 395 elective cardiac surgery patients (intervention group 205, control group 190) found that nurse-led preoperative education reduced anxiety: patients in the intervention group received preoperative education from specially trained nurses, while the control group received standard information from ward personnel.

State anxiety on the day before surgery decreased only in the intervention group (34.0 (8.4) versus 36.9 (10.7); P=0.001), and the mean decrease in state score during the follow-up period was greater in the intervention group (P=0.001).
Multivariate linear regression showed that education and the score on the trait anxiety scale on admission were independent predictors of a reduction in state anxiety.

In the same trial, lower proportions of chest infection were reported in the intervention group (10 (5.3) versus 1 (0.5); P=0.004), whereas no significant difference was found in length of stay or readmission.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: reduction in postoperative complications overall or complications other than chest infection.

The cited evidence supports that financial incentives of up to £400 for smoking cessation in pregnancy were cost-effective in a UK NHS-perspective economic evaluation: the incremental cost per quitter at 34-38 weeks pregnant was £1127 ($1716), and the life-time Markov model gave an incremental cost of £17 (95% CI = -£93, £107) with a gain of 0.04 QALYs (95% CI = -0.058, 0.145), an ICER of £482/QALY ($734/QALY).

The cost-effectiveness analysis was based on a Phase II randomized controlled trial plus a cost-utility analysis using a life-time Markov model, conducted from the UK National Health Service perspective; the analysis compared usual support and incentive interventions in terms of cotinine-validated quitters, QALYs and direct costs to the NHS.

The trial randomized 612 pregnant women in Glasgow, Scotland, to receive usual cessation support plus or minus financial incentives of up to £400 in vouchers (US $609), contingent upon smoking cessation.

The incremental cost per quitter of £1127 ($1716) was reported as similar to the standard look-up value of £1390 per quitter derived from Stapleton & West's published ICER tables using the Cessation in Pregnancy Incentives Trial (CIPT) incremental cost of £157 and incremental 6-month quit outcome of 0.14.

Probabilistic sensitivity analysis indicated uncertainty in these results, particularly regarding relapse after birth, and the expected value of perfect information was £30 million at a willingness to pay of £30 000/QALY, so given the current uncertainty additional research is potentially worthwhile.

Because the life-time cost-utility estimate comes from a Markov model rather than observed long-term follow-up of the trial participants, the reported ICER of £482/QALY depends on modelled assumptions about outcomes such as post-birth relapse, which the probabilistic sensitivity analysis flagged as a source of uncertainty.

Yes — in a cadaveric study of 10 human hips, drilling and suture anchor insertion for arthroscopic acetabular labral repair placed pelvic structures at risk: free drill penetrations caused 14 injuries in 60 penetrations (23.3%), whereas no injuries occurred with stopped drill penetrations, and the risk of perforation into the pelvic cavity began at a 20 mm drill depth (mean insertion depth 31.7 mm, SD 2.6).

These findings come from ten human cadaveric hips (six male, four female) drilled at defined labral zones (12, 1 and 3 o'clock for right hips; 12, 11 and 9 o'clock for left hips, defined as anterior, anterior-superior and superior zones), so they describe ex vivo anatomy rather than injuries observed in living patients during surgery.
Yes, for the optical diagnosis strategy evaluated in PMID:26418441, a cut-and-discard approach would have resulted in a saving of $319.77 per patient.

For unsedated colonoscopy, PMID:19080759 states that access to potentially life-saving screening colonoscopy is limited by the high cost of sedation and that the authors explored the practicability of having supervised trainees perform unsedated colonoscopies, but no actual cost savings from unsedated colonoscopy are reported in the retrieved evidence.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: Actual cost savings from unsedated colonoscopy.

The cited evidence does not establish whether octogenarians benefit from cardiac reoperation: it reports only that 84 consecutive patients aged ≥80 years who underwent a cardiac reoperation at the Department for Cardiothoracic Surgery, Heart&Vessel Center Bad Bevensen, between January 2007 and 2013 were retrospectively identified, that these patients were prospectively followed with demographic and operative data analyzed, and that functional status and quality of life were assessed with the Barthel Index, New York Heart Association class and the short form-12 questionnaire, without reporting postoperative mortality, survival, functional status or quality-of-life results for this cohort.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: postoperative mortality, survival, functional status, or quality-of-life benefit after cardiac reoperation in octogenarians.

In a hospital natural experiment, patients treated by doctors in the evidence-based practice (EBP) unit had a lower risk of death and a shorter length of stay than standard practice (SP) patients, while readmission rates were similar between the two groups.

The study was a natural experiment in which part of a hospital's internal medicine service was reorganized in 2003 to form an EBP unit while the rest of the service remained unchanged; the two units attended similar patients until 2012, and routinely collected statistics from 2004-11 were used to compare the two methods of practice.
Before the reorganization, using 2000-2003 statistics to check for pre-existing differences, no statistically significant differences in outcomes were detected between the EBP and SP doctors.

After the unit was established, the mortality of patients treated by EBP doctors fell from 7.4% to 6.3% (P < 0.02) and length of stay fell from 9.15 to 6.01 days (P = 0.002) relative to those doctors' own previous performance, whereas no statistically significant improvements were seen in SP physicians' performance.

Comparing the two services, EBP patients had a lower risk of death, 6.27% versus 7.75% (P < 0.001), and a shorter length of stay, 6.01 versus 8.46 days (P < 0.001), than SP patients, while readmission rates were similar at 14.4% (EBP) and 14.5% (SP).

Data across the periods were combined and tested with the Mann-Whitney test, and no differences were detected between the services in the proportion of patients admitted or in their complexity; EBP doctors attended twice as many patients per doctor as SP doctors.

Because the comparison rests on a non-randomized natural experiment using routinely collected hospital statistics at a single institution, the reported differences between EBP and SP patients represent an association with the reorganization rather than proof that adopting EBP itself causes better outcomes.

The cited evidence on whether mammographic density affects margin re-excision rate after breast-conserving surgery is mixed: denser breasts showed a trend toward more frequent re-excision in bivariable analysis, but this association was not seen in the multivariable analysis.

Among 655 patients in the study cohort, 398 (60.8%) underwent breast-conserving surgery and 226 (34.5%) underwent initial mastectomy; of those treated with breast-conserving surgery, 166 (41.7%) required a separate re-excision.

In the bivariable analysis, patients with denser breasts classified by BI-RADS category and by volumetric density showed a trend toward requiring more frequent re-excision, whereas this association was not observed in the multivariable analysis.

As a limitation entailed by the design, this was a retrospective review of operative and pathology reports in women diagnosed from 2003 to 2012, so the density-re-excision relationship reported here is an observational association rather than evidence that altering density changes re-excision rates.

The retrieved single study does not establish that sst2a immunohistochemistry has additional value over somatostatin receptor scintigraphy uptake in predicting gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumor response; it reported no statistically significant relationship between in vitro sst2a expression and in vivo best GEP-NET response 1 year after PRRT (p = 0.47).

A limitation entailed by the study design is that all 73 consecutive patients were selected for PRRT based on a positive somatostatin receptor scintigraphy (SRS) result, so the study did not compare the predictive performance of sst2a immunohistochemistry against SRS uptake head-to-head.

In the same study, radiological response was scored according to RECIST 1.0 criteria and sst2a status was detected on tumor samples by immunohistochemistry, with 93% of GEP-NET samples showing sst2a IHC positivity.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: sst2a immunohistochemistry has additional value compared with somatostatin receptor scintigraphy uptake in predicting GEP-NET response.

Type 1 diabetes mellitus did not measurably alter the Achilles tendon response to a 10 km run: baseline tendon structure was similar in the T1DM and control groups (ultrasound tissue characterisation echo-types I-IV and anterior-posterior thickness all p > 0.05), and no response to load was seen in either group over the 4 days post exercise.

In the study comparing Achilles tendon load-response between participants with T1DM and controls, tendon structure was quantified by ultrasound tissue characterisation at day-0, day-2 and day-4 after a 10 km run.

The comparison involved 7 individuals with T1DM and 10 controls, all of whom regularly ran distances greater than 5 km, with VISA-A scores indicating good tendon function (T1DM 94 ± 11, control 94 ± 10).

Because the study design was a small comparative load-response study without a longer follow-up beyond 4 days post exercise, these findings describe absence of a detectable short-term structural load response rather than any conclusion about longer-term clinical outcomes in T1DM.

Yes, the cited evidence supports that chemotherapy can be delivered safely to rural patients under a teleoncology model: in a quasi-experimental comparison, patients treated at Mount Isa Hospital with the same medical oncologists supervising via teleoncology showed no significant differences from patients treated at the tertiary Townsville Cancer Centre (TCC) in dose intensity, proportions of side effects or hospital admissions, and there were no toxicity-related deaths in either group.

Over 5 years, 89 patients received a total of 626 cycles of various chemotherapy regimens in Mount Isa, while during the same period 117 patients who received a total of 799 cycles of chemotherapy at TCC were eligible for inclusion in the comparison group.

Between the Mount Isa and TCC patients there were no significant differences in most demographic characteristics, mean numbers of treatment cycles, dose intensities, proportions of side effects, and hospital admissions, and no toxicity-related deaths occurred in either group.

The finding rests on a quasi-experimental design comparing two patient groups, which can show that outcomes under teleoncology-supervised care were not significantly different from those at the tertiary centre but does not by itself establish causal equivalence of the two models of care.

Yes, a role for viral infection in benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) is supported by a retrospective serologic study, in which all viral serology values except those for influenza and parainfluenza virus were higher in the BPPV group than in the control group.
That retrospective study comprised a study group of 483 patients with BPPV and a control group of 461 healthy subjects.
Serologic analysis of the viral agents HSV1, HSV2, Herpes zoster, EBV, CMV, adenovirus, influenza and parainfluenza virus was performed in both groups.

Seasonal variation was also observed: compared with controls, the BPPV group had elevated values for HSV1 and adenovirus in March and May, for Herpes zoster, adenovirus and influenza in April, for HSV1 in June, and for HSV1 and CMV in September, while in October the BPPV group showed increased values for all of the viruses studied.

As an interpretation of the stated design, the retrospective case-control serologic comparison can demonstrate higher antibody values in BPPV patients than in healthy controls but cannot by itself establish that viral infection causes BPPV.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: Paired PROM scores per administration mode (phone interview vs in-clinic self-survey) for the same patients.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: Agreement/equivalence analysis between phone-interview and in-clinic self-survey PROM measurements.

In a single pilot observational study, intravenous opioid patient-controlled therapy (PCT) reduced self-reported breathlessness in inpatients with advanced disease and refractory breathlessness, so the cited evidence supports breathlessness relief with this mode of application.

The numeric rating scale of current breathlessness decreased from a baseline median of 5 (range 1-10) to a median of 4 (range 0-8) on Day 1 (P < 0.01) and a median of 4 (range 0-5) on Day 2 (P < 0.01).
On Day 3, 12/12 patients confirmed that this mode of application provided relief of breathlessness.
The treated group comprised 18 of 815 patients with advanced cancer (median age = 57.5 years [range 36-81]; 77.8% female) who received breathlessness symptom control with opioid PCT.

Daily morphine equivalent dose in the opioid PCT group was a median of 20.3 mg (5.0-49.6 mg) at Day 1, 13.0 mg (1.0-78.5 mg) at Day 2, and 16.0 mg (8.3-47.0 mg) at Day 3, and physiological parameters were stable over time.

The retrieved report does not compare opioid PCT against the described oral, buccal, and parenteral provider-controlled routes, so the claim that opioid PCT is a new therapeutic concept relative to existing provider-controlled administration cannot be established from this evidence; the single-arm pilot observational design of 18 inpatients supports only feasibility and symptom-response findings, not superiority over provider-controlled routes.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: opioid PCT is novel compared with existing provider-controlled routes.

Yes — in a retrospective review of 241 patients with acetabular fractures treated through a posterior approach and followed radiographically for at least 6 months, surrogates of injury severity were significantly associated with the development of heterotopic ossification (HO) in a multivariate model: ICU length of stay (LOS) of 1-2 days had an odds ratio (OR) of 4.33 (95% CI 1.03-18.25), 3-6 days an OR of 4.1 (95% CI 1.27-13.27), and >6 days an OR of 11.7 (95% CI 3.24-42.22).

In the same multivariate model, non-ICU LOS >10 days versus 0-6 days was associated with HO development (OR = 7.6, 95% CI 2.6-22.25), while HO prophylaxis with external radiation beam therapy (XRT) was associated with lower odds of HO (OR = 0.29, 95% CI 0.10-0.85).

Other variables evaluated in the multivariate modeling that were not significantly associated with either the development or the severity of HO included age, gender, mechanism of injury, injury severity score, presence of neurologic injury, Letournel fracture type, occurrence of hip dislocation, interval from injury to surgery, operative time, and estimated blood loss.

In 19 patients with cervical cancer treated with image-guided brachytherapy after concurrent radiochemotherapy, mean prescribed doses at the PIBS -2, PIBS and PIBS +2 points were 2.23 ± 1.4, 6.39 ± 6.6 and 31.85 ± 36.06 Gy, respectively, with delivered doses evaluated on each plan as representative of one-third of the treatment.

Prescribed doses differed significantly between the 5 patients with vaginal involvement and the remaining 14 patients at PIBS +2 (+47.60 Gy) and at PIBS (+7.46 Gy), with p = 0.023 and p = 0.03, respectively.

The cited evidence is mixed on whether dose-point evaluation can be relied on: variations between delivered and prescribed doses at the PIBS points were not significant, yet at the International Commission on Radiation Units and Measurements rectovaginal point the delivered dose was decreased by 1.43 ± 2.49 Gy from the planned dose (p = 0.019).

Delivered doses at the four points were strongly correlated with prescribed doses, with R(2) ranging from 0.93 to 0.95, and the movements of the applicator with regard to the PIBS point, assessed with Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine coordinates, were insignificant.

These delivered-versus-prescribed dose comparisons come from a single series of 19 patients and address dosimetric agreement at the evaluated points rather than clinical outcomes, so they cannot by themselves establish that dose-point evaluation is reliable for patient outcomes.

Management of a synchronous contralateral hydrocele in neonatal testicular torsion is controversial, and in the reported single-institution practice the policy was not to address the contralateral hydrocele through an inguinal incision in order to minimize potential injury to the spermatic cord; consequently, all hydroceles were opened through a scrotal approach at the time of contralateral scrotal fixation, and no patient underwent inguinal exploration to examine for a patent processus vaginalis.

The cited evidence does not establish that less invasive management is superior: the report is a single-institution series of neonatal torsion (37 patients, 22 of whom had a contralateral hydrocele at presentation) in which none of the patients who presented with a hydrocele developed a clinical hydrocele or hernia after an average 7.5 years (range 4.3-11.2) follow-up, but no group managed with inguinal exploration was studied for comparison, so the scrotal-only approach cannot be shown to be superior to a more invasive approach.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: direct comparison of scrotal-only versus inguinal management to establish superiority of less invasive treatment.

Yes — based on a single-institution comparison of 203 young patients (≤50 years at diagnosis) with 203 matched older patients (>50 years), colorectal cancer in young patients was characterized as showing distinct epidemiological and clinicopathological features rather than merely typical CRC, and the study was designed specifically to evaluate whether it constitutes a unique entity.

The study population comprised 406 patients, 203 in each group: consecutive young patients diagnosed at ages ≤50 years during 1997–2007 and treated at the institution, plus a matching group diagnosed at >50 years, whose medical files were reviewed and compared for epidemiological, clinical and pathological features.

The features of the older group (>50 years) were typical for patients with CRC, whereas the younger group (≤50 years) showed female predominance, a different ethnic composition, a prevalence of family history of cancer and hereditary CRC syndromes, and a lower incidence of polyps.
The incidence of left-sided tumors and of advanced stages (III–IV) at diagnosis was higher in the younger patients than in the older group.
Mucinous/signet ring histology, grade, stage, and lymphatic and vascular invasion were all predictive of survival, whereas age was not.

Adjustment for reporting heterogeneity was necessary in this study of sleep disorders: the authors explicitly evaluated the need for adjusting for reporting heterogeneity in the management of sleep and energy related problems in Japan, and correcting for it changed which factors remained significantly associated with sleep-related problems.

The analysis used a dataset of 1002 respondents aged 18 years and over from the Japanese World Health Survey collected by face-to-face interview in 2002-2003, in which the prevalence of self-reported problems with sleep and energy was 53%, and applied both an ordered probit model and a Compound Hierarchical Ordered Probit (CHOPIT) model incorporating anchoring vignettes to estimate and compare associations of sleep and energy with socio-demographic and life-style factors before and after adjustment for differences in response category cut-points for each individual.
Without correction of cut-point shifts, age, sex, and the number of comorbidities were significantly associated with a greater severity of sleep-related problems.
After correction, age, the number of comorbidities, and regular exercise were significantly associated with a greater severity of sleep-related problems, while sex was no longer a significant factor.
Compared with the ordered probit model, the CHOPIT model produced two changes with only a subtle difference in the magnitude of regression coefficients after correction for reporting heterogeneity.

The cited evidence is mixed: the automated GAPS score was comparable to triage nurses' visual analogue scale (VAS) estimate of admission probability across the whole cohort, but in the majority of attendances where nurses were less than 95% certain, GAPS significantly outperformed the nurses, and a combined strategy was best.

In this single-centre prospective study of 1829 attendances, 745 (40.7%) were admitted, not significantly different from GAPS' prediction of 750 (41.0%, p=0.678), whereas the nurses' mean VAS predicted 865 admissions (47.3%), an overestimate of 6.6% (p<0.0001).

Over the whole cohort, GAPS discriminated between admission and discharge as well as the nurses, with an AUC of 0.876 versus 0.875 for VAS (p=0.93), and as a binary predictor its accuracy was 80.6%, comparable with VAS at 79.0% (p=0.18).
In the minority of attendances where nurses felt at least 95% certain of the outcome, VAS accuracy was excellent at 92.4%.

In the remaining majority of attendances, GAPS significantly outperformed VAS on calibration (+1.2% vs +9.2%, p<0.0001), discrimination (AUC 0.810 vs 0.759, p=0.001) and accuracy (75.1% vs 68.9%, p=0.0009).
Using GAPS but over-ruling it when clinical certainty was at least 95% significantly outperformed either method alone, with AUC 0.891 (0.877-0.907) and accuracy 82.5% (80.7%-84.2%).

Interpretation is limited by the design: the comparison comes from a single-centre prospective study in which nurses estimated admission probability using a 100 mm VAS while GAPS was generated automatically from triage data, so the head-to-head performance figures describe that one centre's cohort.

Yes — in a whole-population analysis of GP records for just over one million patients registered in Lambeth, Hackney, Tower Hamlets and Newham in 2013, both new depression diagnosis and antidepressant use varied with neighbourhood ethnic density, with neighbourhood effects assessed independently of GP practice using a cross-classified multilevel model.

For Indian, Pakistani, Bangladeshi and black African patients, an increase of 10% in own-ethnic density was associated with statistically significant (p<0.05) reduced odds of a new depression diagnosis: Pakistani OR 0.81 (95% CI 0.70-0.93), Indian OR 0.88 (95% CI 0.81-0.95), black African OR 0.88 (95% CI 0.78-0.99) and Bangladeshi OR 0.94 (95% CI 0.90-0.99).
Black Caribbean patients showed the opposite pattern, with higher own-ethnic density associated with increased odds of new depression diagnosis (OR 1.26, 95% CI 1.09-1.46).

Results for antidepressant use were very similar to those for new depression diagnosis, although the corresponding effect for black Caribbean patients was no longer statistically significant (p = 0.07).

Because the analysis relates neighbourhood ethnic density to recorded diagnoses and prescriptions within a single year of GP records, it reports associations between location and recorded depression care rather than demonstrating that changing neighbourhood characteristics would alter clinical outcomes.

The cited evidence is insufficient to show that the vascular-guided multilayer preauricular approach (VMPA) improves access to the temporomandibular joint relative to another surgical approach; the single retrospective series reports only that all patients (606 joints) had successful TMJ surgeries through the VMPA, with no comparison group or access measure reported against an alternative approach.
Because this was a single-arm retrospective evaluation of a consecutive series of patients operated from January through December 2013, it cannot establish comparative superiority in access.

The cited evidence is insufficient to show that the VMPA reduces complications relative to another surgical approach; in the reported series, all incisions healed favorably with an uneventful recovery and no patient developed permanent weakness of the facial nerve or other severe complications, with all patients followed for at least 6 months.
These are single-arm descriptive outcomes with no comparator arm, so the retrospective design cannot establish a comparative reduction in complications.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: comparative improvement in access versus another surgical approach.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: comparative reduction in complications versus another surgical approach.

Yes — duplex Doppler ultrasonography allowed non-invasive prediction of esophageal varices in patients with compensated hepatic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh class A), with the splenoportal index (SPI) at a cut-off of 5.0 offering the highest diagnostic accuracy (88%) when screening endoscopy was used as the reference standard.

Fifty-six enrolled patients with compensated hepatic cirrhosis underwent duplex Doppler ultrasonography followed by screening endoscopy, and mean portal vein velocity (PVV), splenic index (SI), splenoportal index (SPI), and hepatic and splenic arterial resistive and pulsatility indices (HARI, HAPI, SARI, SAPI) were recorded.

Univariate logistic regression analysis was followed by receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve construction for the significant indices; HARI, HAPI, SARI and SAPI were not helpful (p > 0.05), whereas mean PVV, SI and SPI were all predictive of the presence of esophageal varices (p < 0.05), and SPI was found to be the most accurate parameter.
Of the various SPI cut-off levels evaluated, a cut-off value of 5.0 offered the highest diagnostic accuracy (88%).

For the 28 patients with SPI < 5.0, absence of esophageal varices in 27 of them could be correctly diagnosed using SPI alone without invasive screening endoscopy, with a high negative predictive value (96%) and sensitivity (96%).

Of the remaining 28 patients with SPI ≥ 5.0, presence of esophageal varices could similarly be correctly diagnosed in 22 of them using SPI without screening endoscopy, with a high positive predictive value (79%) and specificity (82%).

Septoplasty did not significantly change the dimensions of the middle turbinate's compensatory hypertrophy: the bony and mucosal components of the middle turbinate on both the concave and convex sides of the septum showed no significant change after surgery.

This finding rests on radiological measurement of the middle turbinate's mucosal and bony structures and of the septal angle taken before septoplasty and at least one year after septoplasty in patients with nasal septal deviation.
All pre- and post-operative middle turbinate measurements were compared using the paired sample t-test and the Wilcoxon rank sum test.
A significant negative correlation was found after septoplasty between the angle of the septum and the middle turbinate total area on the deviated side (p = 0.033).

In high bleeding risk (HBR) patients undergoing PCI in the ZEUS trial, the zotarolimus-eluting Endeavor Sprint stent (E-ZES) was associated with fewer ischemic events than BMS, so BMS implantation was not favored on ischemic outcomes: 12-month major adverse cardiovascular events occurred in 22.6% of E-ZES versus 29% of BMS patients (hazard ratio 0.75; 95% CI 0.57 to 0.98; p = 0.033).
The MACE difference was driven by lower myocardial infarction (3.5% vs.
10.4%; p<0.001) and target vessel revascularization (5.9% vs.
11.4%; p = 0.005) rates in the E-ZES arm compared with BMS, and the composite of definite or probable stent thrombosis was also significantly reduced in E-ZES recipients.

These ischemic results come from the multinational, randomized, single-blinded ZEUS trial, which randomized 828 patients meeting pre-defined clinical or biochemical HBR criteria — including advanced age, indication to oral anticoagulants or other pro-hemorrhagic medications, history of bleeding and known anemia — to E-ZES or BMS followed by a protocol-mandated 30-day DAPT regimen.

On bleeding outcomes, BMS offered no advantage over the drug-eluting E-ZES in HBR patients: in the ZEUS trial, bleeding events did not differ between the stent groups, whereas the composite of definite or probable stent thrombosis was significantly reduced in E-ZES recipients.

DES implantation is described as the treatment of choice for coronary artery disease, leaving only marginal indications for BMS use; nevertheless, selected treatment populations with DES contraindications, such as patients who cannot sustain 6-12 months of dual antiplatelet therapy, remain candidates for BMS implantation.

The analysis was a retrospective cross-sectional study of 833 asthmatics recruited from the University Asthma Clinic of Liege compared with 194 healthy subjects, in which asthmatics were classified into inflammatory phenotypes.

The total non-squamous cell count per gram of sputum was greater in the mixed granulocytic and neutrophilic phenotypes than in eosinophilic and paucigranulocytic asthma and healthy subjects (p < 0.005).

Sputum eosinophils, both in absolute values and as percentages, were increased in all asthma phenotypes, including paucigranulocytic asthma, compared with healthy subjects (p < 0.005); eosinophilic asthma also showed higher absolute sputum neutrophil and lymphocyte counts than healthy subjects (p < 0.005), whereas neutrophilic asthmatics had a particularly low number of sputum macrophages and epithelial cells.

For systemic inflammation, all asthma phenotypes showed an increased blood leukocyte count compared with healthy subjects (p < 0.005), and neutrophilic asthma had raised CRP and fibrinogen while eosinophilic asthma showed only raised fibrinogen compared with healthy subjects (p < 0.005).

Paucigranulocytic asthmatics were not truly non-inflammatory: compared with healthy subjects, sputum eosinophils in absolute values and percentages were increased in all asthma phenotypes including paucigranulocytic asthma (p < 0.005), and paucigranulocytic asthmatics additionally had an increased absolute blood eosinophil count alongside the increased blood leukocyte count seen in all asthma phenotypes (p < 0.005).

In children admitted with acute respiratory infection, the number of detected respiratory viruses did not correlate with any markers of severity, indicating that viral co-infection did not influence the severity of acute respiratory infection in this cohort.

This finding came from a Spanish prospective multicenter study (GENDRES network) of children admitted with acute respiratory infection between 2011 and 2013, in which 204 children were recruited in the main cohort and 97 in the replication cohort.
All these findings were replicated in the independent UK cohort.
Among 561 patients in whom a misty mesentery appearance was depicted on abdominopelvic CT scans, 80 cases were found to have isolated incidental idiopathic misty mesentery, giving a prevalence of 7%.

The study included cases with no known cause of misty mesentery according to associated CT findings, clinical history, or biochemical manifestations, and excluded patients with diseases known to cause misty mesentery, lymph nodes greater than a short-axis diameter of 5 mm, discrete mesenteric masses, or bowel wall thickening.
In this cohort, 67.5% of all patients were classified as obese and 17.5% as overweight.

The reported design provides only the frequency of obesity and overweight status in patients with incidental idiopathic misty mesentery, with no control or comparison group and no causal analysis, so these proportions cannot establish that obesity is a triggering cause of the finding.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: obesity is a triggering cause.

LAA occlusion was associated with ECG changes in patients with atrial fibrillation: in a study of 73 patients treated with Watchman, LAmbre and Lefort devices, echocardiography and ECG results were collected before and after the operation, and after LAA occlusion a slight and measurable movement of the QRS electric axis was observed in most patients.
In the same cohort of patients with atrial fibrillation, significant differences were also observed in heart rate and the mean-mean QT interval between pre- and post-operation for all patients.

Echocardiography was also performed during follow-up visits at 1, 6 and 12 months after discharge, and there existed no significant difference in echocardiographic parameters between before and after device implantation.

However, a larger left atrial diameter was detected by echocardiography during the follow-up visit at 6 months when compared with pre-operation parameters, and aortic root diameter was also larger during follow-up at 12 months than the baseline dimension in pre-operation.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: anastomotic leakage/safety outcomes after rectal anastomosis without a diverting stoma.

In a prospective database of 125 patients with locally advanced or locally recurrent gastrointestinal stromal tumours treated with neoadjuvant imatinib between May 2008 and March 2015, patients who underwent surgery had significantly improved event-free survival compared with those who did not (p < 0.001), with the same trend for overall survival (p = 0.021).

Among the same neoadjuvant imatinib cohort, patients with stable disease as their response had a lower event-free survival (p = 0.076) and lower overall survival than patients achieving complete or partial response.

The duration of neoadjuvant imatinib used for locally advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumours is not based on the tumour biology reflected by KIT mutation analysis, and archived formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissues were used to test KIT exons 9, 11, 13 and 17 by PCR.

Of the 45 patients (36%) who had c-kit mutation testing, exon 11 was seen in 25 patients (55.5%), exon 9 in 3 (6.7%) and exon 13 in 2 (4.4%); 12 were wild type (26.6%) and 3 (6.7%) were declared uninterpretable.
The response rate for exon 11 mutants was higher than for the non-exon 11 mutant group (84 vs.
40%, p = 0.01), and the disease stabilization rate was also higher in the exon 11 subgroup than in the non-exon 11 group (92 vs.
75%); 84% of exon 11 and 75% of non-exon 11 mutants were surgical candidates.
No differences were observed between the various exon variants in terms of outcomes and responses.

Yes, infectious disease and clinical microbiology experts agreed substantially but not completely in judging the appropriateness of antimicrobial prescribing: specialists agreed with the modal-expert reference standard in 80% of cases (range 75%-86%).
Against that reference standard, built from the modal assessment of 16 specialists, the specialists' criterion validity corresponded to a sensitivity of 75% and a specificity of 84%.
Agreement with the reference standard did not differ by clinical specialty, hospital or years of experience, and the residents in the panel had similar results to the specialists.

Interrater agreement was also incomplete, with specialists agreeing with the index expert in 76% of cases, while the index expert agreed with his own previous assessments in 71% of cases (intrarater agreement).

These agreement estimates come from 24 doctors (16 specialists and 8 residents) in five hospitals who assessed antimicrobial appropriateness in 56 paper cases covering a broad spectrum of indications, so the findings describe expert assessment of written case vignettes rather than of prescriptions issued to real patients.

Yes — in a cadaveric study of ten fresh cadaveric knees, femoral tunnel lengths greater than 20 mm could be created with a flexible reamer system at 90° of knee flexion, where the mean intra-osseous length was 32.1 mm (range 22–45 mm); flexible guide pins were inserted with the knee at 70°, 90°, and 120° of flexion and the intra-osseous length was measured with the dedicated measuring device, showing a trend of progressively increasing mean intra-osseous length with increased knee flexion.
The mean intra-osseous length at 70° of flexion was 25.2 mm (20–32 mm), which was statistically significantly shorter than the 32.1 mm (22–45 mm) at 90° and 38.0 mm (34–45 mm) at 120° (p<0.05).

Yes — in the TrialNet autoantibody-positive population, electrochemiluminescence (ECL) assays improved prediction of time to type 1 diabetes: the multivariate Cox model including positivity for ECL-GADA and/or ECL-IAA was the best of the compared models, and adding ECL to the Diabetes Prevention Trial risk score (DPTRS) improved the receiver operating characteristic curves to an AUC of 0.83 (P<0.0001).

The analysis included 1,287 TrialNet subjects who were positive for one or more autoantibodies (microinsulin autoantibody, GAD65 autoantibody [GADA], IA-2A, and ZnT8A) and had ECL-insulin autoantibody (IAA) and ECL-GADA data available at their initial visit; after a median follow-up of 24 months, 177 of these 1,287 subjects developed diabetes.

Multivariate Cox proportional hazards models were compared, with the base model including age, sex, OGTT measurements, and number of positive autoantibodies by radioimmunoassays (RIAs); in the best model, the factors that remained significantly associated with time to diabetes were area under the curve (AUC) C-peptide, fasting C-peptide, AUC glucose, number of positive autoantibodies by RIAs, and ECL positivity.

Univariate analyses showed that autoantibodies by RIAs, ECL-IAA, ECL-GADA, age, sex, number of positive autoantibodies, presence of the HLA DR3/4-DQ8 genotype, HbA1c, and OGTT measurements were each significantly associated with progression to diabetes.
Subjects who were ECL positive had a risk of progression to diabetes within 6 years of 58%, compared with 5% for ECL-negative subjects (P<0.0001).

External validation in open ventral hernia repair indicates that existing risk calculators do not accurately predict surgical site occurrence: the areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) for SSO were low in both the retrospective multicenter Ventral Hernia Outcomes Collaborative database (0.56, 0.54, 0.52, and 0.60) and the single-center Prospective database (0.63, 0.54, 0.50, 0.57, and 0.69).

In this validation, patients in the retrospective multicenter (n = 795, SSO rate 23%, SSI rate 17%) and prospective single-center (n = 88, SSO 14%, SSI 8%) databases were each assigned a predicted risk using the Ventral Hernia Risk Score (VHRS), Ventral Hernia Working Group (VHWG), Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Wound Class, and Hernia Wound Risk Assessment Tool (HW-RAT), with the prospective patients also assigned an American College of Surgeons National Surgical Quality Improvement Program (ACS-NSQIP) risk; AUCs were compared to assess predictive accuracy for SSO and SSI, and Pearson's chi-square tested which models risk-stratified patients into groups with significantly differing rates of actual SSO and SSI.

For risk stratification of actual SSO, the VHRS (P = 0.01) and HW-RAT (P < 0.01) significantly separated patients into tiers in the retrospective multicenter database, where the VHWG (P < 0.05) and HW-RAT (P < 0.05) stratified for SSI; in the prospective database ACS-NSQIP (P < 0.01) stratified for SSO, whereas the VHRS (P < 0.01) and ACS-NSQIP (P < 0.05) stratified for SSI.

Calibration was also imperfect in both databases: VHRS, VHWG, and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Wound Class overestimated the risk of SSO and SSI, whereas HW-RAT and ACS-NSQIP underestimated risk for all groups.

In chronic posttraumatic anterior shoulder instability with bone defects in both the glenoid and humerus, no significant correlation was found between humeral and glenoid bone defects by observer 1 (r = 0.23, p = 0.22) or by observer 2 (r = 0.05, p = 0.78).

In that study the correlations between the humeral and glenoid measurements were determined using Spearman correlation coefficients (r), Bland and Altman diagrams, and intra-class correlation coefficients (ICC).

The evidence comes from a retrospective study performed between 2000 and 2011 that included patients who underwent primary surgical shoulder stabilization for chronic posttraumatic anterior shoulder instability, with bone defects in both the glenoid and humerus and a healthy contralateral shoulder.
Thirty patients were included in this analysis, 25 men and 5 women, with a mean age of 29.8 ± 11.2 years.

Yes — in a randomized controlled trial of 38 patients with cervicogenic somatic tinnitus (severe subjective tinnitus on the Tinnitus Functional Index, 25-90 points, plus neck complaints with Neck Bournemouth Questionnaire > 14 points), multimodal cervical physical therapy given for 6 weeks (12 sessions) was associated with significantly reduced tinnitus and neck-complaint scores: TFI and NBQ scores decreased significantly after treatment (p = 0.04 and p < 0.001, respectively).

Immediately after treatment, 53% of the 38 patients experienced substantial improvement of tinnitus, and this effect was maintained in 24% of patients at six-week follow-up; NBQ scores also remained significantly lower after follow-up (p = 0.001).

Because every participant received cervical physical therapy, with randomization only to an immediate-start (n = 19) versus a 6-week delayed-start (n = 19) group, the reported improvements are within-group findings rather than a comparison against an untreated or placebo control.

The cited evidence is mixed: in a Swedish longitudinal study (n=744), young adults whose families were abstainers in 2000 drank substantially less across quintiles in 2010 than offspring of non-abstaining families, but that difference was not statistically significant between quintiles of the conditional distribution.

The same study assessed the relationship between familial drinking in 2000 and offspring drinking in 2010 using simultaneous quantile regression, with data on familial drinking from the Swedish level-of-living surveys (LNU) and partner LNU in 2000 and data on offspring drinking in young adulthood from LNU 2010.
Drinking among offspring, parents and potential stepparents was measured through identical quantity-frequency indices referring to the past 12 months in 2010 and 2000 respectively.
Actual drinking levels in drinking families were not at all or weakly associated with drinking in offspring, and supplementary analyses confirmed these patterns.

As an interpretation of the reported analysis, the non-significant difference between quintiles of the conditional distribution means the study does not establish statistically significant transmission of actual drinking levels among drinking families into young adulthood.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: statistically significant transmission of actual drinking levels among drinking families into young adulthood.

In a qualitative study nested in a larger six-country mixed-method project examining two English-language MPH programs (a distance program offered from South Africa and a residential program in the Netherlands) that train students from a diversity of countries, in-depth interviews with 10 graduates per program working in low- and middle-income health systems, together with their peers and supervisors, found that impact on the workplace was reported as considerable, including changes in management and leadership: many participants reported promotion to a leadership position as well as expanded or revitalized management roles.
The development of leadership capacity was highly valued among many graduates, and this capacity was cited by a number of supervisors and peers.

Because the findings rest on self-reported accounts from a small purposive qualitative sample, the authors note that self-selection of graduates and their role in selecting peers and supervisors may have resulted in some bias, some graduates could not be traced, and social acceptability bias may have influenced findings, so the reported leadership and management impact cannot be read as an unbiased measured effect.

Wider impact in the workplace took the form of introducing workplace innovations such as setting up an AIDS and addiction research center and research involvement, while teaching and training, advocacy, and community engagement were other ways in which graduates' influence reached a wider target grouping.

Beyond the workplace, graduates were reported to use an intersectoral approach and to achieve national reach through policy advisory roles to Ministries of Health, policy development, and capacity building.
Work conditions and context influenced how conducive the setting was for innovation and the extent to which graduates were able to have an effect.

In a longitudinal analysis of MD/AUD status at ages 15-18 years, all three adolescent disorder groups (MD-only, AUD-only, and comorbid MD/AUD) had rates of adult major depression during ages 18-35 years that were significantly higher (p<.05) than the rate in the group with neither disorder.

Within that same analysis, adolescents in the comorbid MD/AUD group had significantly higher rates of adult MD than those in the AUD-only group (p<.05), and marginally higher rates of adult MD than those in the MD-only group (p<.10).

After adjustment for confounding by factors measured in childhood, the difference in adult MD rates between the MD-only group and the comorbid MD/AUD group was no longer statistically significant; the factors that explained the associations were gender, childhood behavior problems, and exposure to physical and sexual abuse.

In August 2015, the Catholic bishops in Kenya called for a boycott of a polio vaccination campaign citing safety concerns with the polio vaccine; a cross-sectional survey conducted in all 32 counties that participated in the campaign found national vaccination coverage of 93% compared with 94% in the November 2014 campaign, indicating that overall coverage was not substantially reduced.

In that survey, 31% of parents/guardians belonged to the Catholic Church, compared with 7% of the children who were missed, and the proportion of children not vaccinated because of parental refusal increased significantly from 6% in the November 2014 campaign to 12% in August 2015.

Reasons reported for missed vaccination in the August 2015 campaign were the house not being visited (44%), children not being at home at the time of the visit (38%), refusal by parents (12%), children being asleep (1%) and various other reasons (5%), based on a sample of 90,157 children and 37,732 parents/guardians.

Because the evidence comes from a cross-sectional survey, it can describe coverage and reasons for missed vaccination in the campaign period but cannot by itself establish that the boycott call caused any change in coverage.

Treating amblyopia did not normalise subfoveal choroidal thickness in anisometropic hyperopic children with unilateral amblyopia: after a six-month treatment period, the mean choroidal thickness remained significantly higher in the amblyopic eyes than in the fellow eyes (p = 0.006), and there were no significant differences between the pre- and post-treatment mean choroidal thickness in either the amblyopic eyes (p = 0.428) or the fellow eyes (p = 0.343).

In this prospective study of 32 anisometropic hyperopic children with unilateral amblyopia, the mean initial choroidal thickness was already significantly higher in the amblyopic eyes than in the fellow eyes (p = 0.019), and this between-eye difference persisted after treatment (p = 0.006).

Yes — in a retrospective series of 22 patients treated with TEVAR for traumatic aortic injury between 2009 and 2014, aortic arch anatomy was associated with aortic trauma severity: a multivariate analysis confirmed that the aortic arch angle was significantly associated with the occurrence of type III damage (OR 1.5; 95% CI 1.03-2.2).

In that study, aortic injury was assessed according to the recommendations of the Society of Vascular Surgery, and the aortic arch angle and aortic arch index were measured from the initial angio-CT scan in each analyzed case.

The mean aortic arch index and mean aortic arch angle were 6.8 cm and 58.3° in the type I injury group, 4.4 cm and 45.9° in the type III group, and 3.3 cm and 37° in the type IV group, with substantial differences in both the aortic arch index and the aortic arch angle between the type III and type IV groups.

Because the evidence comes from a retrospective observational series of 22 cases, the reported association between aortic arch angle and type III injury reflects an observed relationship in that cohort rather than an established causal effect of arch anatomy on trauma severity.
This study included 438 VPS procedures, 49 in which an endoscope was used (11.2%) and 389 in which an endoscope was not used (88.8%).

The overall infection rate was 18.5%, including 22.4% in the groups in which an endoscope was used and 18% in those in which an endoscope was not used (P = 0.449), indicating that simultaneous use of an endoscope did not significantly influence the incidence of ventriculoperitoneal shunt infection.

Subsequently, 4 new groups were created, composed of patients with a shunt inserted for the first time (groups 1A and 1B) and patients with a shunt reviewed or inserted for a second time (groups 2A and 2B).
Groups 1A and 2A comprised patients in whom an endoscope was used simultaneously with VPS surgery, and groups 1B and 2B comprised patients in whom an endoscope was not used.
Groups 1A and 1B and groups 2A and 2B were matched for possible intervening risk factors.
The infection rate was 28.6% in group 1A and 16.2% in group 1B (P = 0.27), and 20% in group 2A and 19.8% in group 2B (P = 0.977).

A retrospective evaluation of patients who underwent surgical reduction of a condylar fracture from January 2012 to December 2014 at the Clinic of Dentistry and Maxillofacial Surgery of the University Hospital of Verona (Verona, Italy) was performed; the sample was composed of 25 patients.

In that series, preinjury occlusion and temporomandibular joint health were restored in most patients, esthetic outcomes were deemed satisfactory by clinicians and patients, and neither permanent neurologic impairments nor major postoperative complications were observed.
These outcomes support the reliability of the retromandibular transparotid approach for surgical treatment of condylar fractures in this series.

Because the findings come from a retrospective evaluation of 25 patients, they support an observational association but do not establish the effect of choosing the retromandibular transparotid approach over another approach.

The cited evidence is mixed on whether non-HDL-cholesterol is a better predictor of long-term outcome after acute myocardial infarction than LDL-cholesterol: in a retrospective Thai cohort of 868 patients after AMI with mean follow-up of 2.6 ± 1.6 years, non-HDL-C showed the expected risk gradient whereas LDL-C showed an inverse association with MACE.

In that cohort, the mean non-HDL-C and LDL-C during long-term follow-up were used to predict MACE at each time point, and target attainment was classified as non-HDL-C <100 mg/dl and/or LDL-C <70 mg/dl; 34.4% achieved the non-HDL-C target, 23.7% achieved the LDL-C target, and 21.2% experienced MACEs.
LDL-C and non-HDL-C were directly compared in a Cox regression model.
Compared with non-HDL-C <100 mg/dl, patients with non-HDL-C >130 mg/dl had a higher incidence of MACEs (HR 3.15, 95% CI 1.46-6.80, P = 0.003).
In the same direct pairwise comparison, LDL-C >100 mg/dl was associated with a reduced risk of MACE compared with LDL-C <70 mg/dl (HR 0.42, 95% CI 0.18-0.98, p = 0.046).

Because the data were obtained retrospectively from patients admitted with AMI during 2006-2013, these associations cannot establish that modifying non-HDL-C or LDL-C levels changes long-term outcomes.

Yes — the first urinary albumin/creatinine ratio (ACR) was a prognostic factor for adverse maternal and neonatal composite outcomes in women with suspected preeclampsia, with adjusted odds ratios above 1 for both outcomes in a retrospective cohort of 717 pregnant women.

The cohort comprised 717 pregnant women with singleton pregnancies beyond 20 weeks' gestation who were referred for evaluation of suspected preeclampsia and had their first ACR performed, drawn from two obstetric day assessment units in Southeast Scotland (retrospective cohort, December 2009 to February 2012).
Among these 717 women, 204 (28.5%) had a composite adverse maternal outcome and 146 (20.4%) had a composite adverse neonatal outcome.

In multivariable analysis of log-transformed ACR, a 1-unit increase in log ACR was associated with higher odds of the adverse maternal composite outcome (odds ratio 1.60, 95% CI 1.45-1.80) and the adverse neonatal composite outcome (odds ratio 1.15, 95% CI 1.02-1.29), and with reduced gestational age at delivery (coefficient -0.46, 95% CI -0.54 to -0.38).

As an interpretation of the study design: these are associations from a retrospective cohort, so they indicate prognostic value of the first ACR rather than establishing that altering ACR would change maternal or neonatal outcomes.

Exposure to antiretroviral therapy (ART) leads to serious medication-related adverse effects mainly explained by mitochondrial toxicities, and although the introduction and widespread use of ART have drastically changed the natural history of HIV/AIDS, the situation is expected to get worse in the near future; specifically, ART is associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular disease, lipodystrophy, prediabetes and overt diabetes, insulin resistance, and hyperlactatemia/lactic acidosis.

The WHO "test and treat" policy rests on studies showing that early ART initiation significantly reduces HIV transmission, and its implementation is expected to increase the incidence of ART-related adverse effects, especially in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), where the prevalence of these disorders is already high and the situation will be exacerbated by the new WHO recommendations.

Most SSA countries are characterized by (extreme) poverty, very weak health systems, inadequate and low quality of health services, inaccessibility to existing health facilities, lack of (qualified) health personnel, lack of adequate equipment, inaccessibility and unaffordability of medicines, and heavy workload in a context of a double burden of disease; in addition, there is a dearth of data on the incidence and predictive factors of ART-related adverse effects in SSA, which are required to anticipate prevention strategies, estimate the upcoming burden and prepare an adequate response plan.
