The cited article is framed as a commentary that asks whether the region is yet ready to cope with the challenge, rather than reporting primary incidence data; it therefore raises the readiness question without quantifying the expected increase in ART-related adverse effects in SSA.

The retrieved evidence does not establish that healthier lifestyles lead to less utilization of healthcare resources; in a 2005 survey of 2911 people older than 15 years in Kaohsiung, Taiwan, four health behaviors (exercise habits, dietary habits, regular blood pressure measurement and drinking habits) were significantly correlated with healthcare utilization (P<0.05), but no direction, magnitude, or comparison of utilization between healthier and less healthy lifestyle groups was reported.

Because the source is a cross-sectional on-site questionnaire survey, the reported correlation between health behaviors and healthcare utilization cannot establish that adopting healthier lifestyles reduces healthcare resource use.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: healthier lifestyles lead to less utilization of healthcare resources.

Yes — in a study of repeated abdominal CT in men, visceral adipose tissue (VAT) area measured at a single slice showed its strongest correlation with both VAT volume and body weight change at a slice 3 cm above the lower margin of L3, with r values of 0.853 and 0.902 respectively, indicating that a single-level VAT area can reflect VAT volume.

The study's aim was to determine the CT slice location at which VAT area best reflects changes in VAT volume and body weight; 60 plain abdominal CT images from 30 males (mean age 51 years, range 41-68; mean body weight 71.1 kg, range 101.9-50.9 kg) who underwent workplace screenings twice within a 1-year interval were evaluated, with automatically calculated and manually corrected VAT areas at various scan levels recorded using a "freeform curve" region of interest on CT and compared with body weight changes.

Because the reported evidence consists of correlations between single-slice VAT area and VAT volume or body weight change, it demonstrates association rather than agreement, so a strong correlation does not by itself establish that a single-level area measurement can substitute for direct VAT volume measurement in an individual.

The evidence is mixed on the usefulness of performance measurement systems: a strategic use of performance measurement systems (PMS) in health care organizations directly and significantly (p < 0.001) enhanced performance in terms of improved processes in a PLS analysis of a survey of 97 Italian managers working for health care organizations in the Lombardy region (response rate 77.6%), while the retrieved evidence does not establish cost-effective resource use or the superiority of objective measures over self-report measures.
A strategic use of PMS has been found to enhance quality compared to non-strategic use, although a clear understanding of this linkage is still to be achieved.

Perceived managerial discretion was positively and significantly (p < 0.001) affected by the strategic use of PMS, whereas the mediation effect through perceived managerial discretion was non-significant.

It has been suggested that performance measures of functional status have several advantages over self-report measures for both clinical and research purposes, including greater patient acceptability, interpretability, reproducibility, sensitivity to change, and the focus on actual ability rather than presumed capability.

This article challenges this assumed superiority of "objective," "behavioral" measures by directly comparing self-assessments and blindly rated performance assessments on a specific item by task basis, using an identical rating format.

While the limitations of self-report measures are clearly acknowledged, less apparent is attention to the potential limitations of their 'objective' counterparts leading to the assumption that objectivity results in more robust and scientifically valid measurement tools.
This article aims to: (1) test this assumption; (2) consider the implications of advocating for a measure on the basis of its objectivity; (3) propose an alternative approach to measure selection.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: cost-effective resource use.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: superiority of objective/performance measures over self-report measures.

The cited evidence indicates that cardiopulmonary bypass temperature did not affect the postoperative changes in thyroid hormone levels measured: in a prospective study comparing cold (26 +/- 5 degrees C) and warm (35 +/- 1 degree C) CPB in 12 patients undergoing cardiac operations (hypothermic n = 6, normothermic n = 6), the two groups were comparable with regard to age, body weight, duration of CPB, cross-clamp time, use of inotropes, total heparin dose, and length of hospital stay.

In both the cold and warm CPB groups, TT4 and TT3 were reduced below baseline from the start of CPB and remained reduced for up to 5 days after CPB (p<0.05), free T3 was reduced for up to 3 days after CPB (p<0.05), mean serum rT3 was elevated on postoperative day 1 and day 3 (p<0.05), and TSH remained unchanged, so the same thyroid hormone pattern was observed regardless of bypass temperature.
Because the comparison rests on only 6 patients in each temperature group, the absence of a temperature-related difference in thyroid hormone changes is based on a very small sample.

In a retrospective evaluation of treatment outcome in 37 patients treated for necrotizing fasciitis between 1984 and 1993, 25 patients received hyperbaric oxygenation (HBO) as part of their treatment protocol and the remaining 12 were treated by surgical excision and antibiotics alone; the two groups were similar in age, gender, incidence of individual risk factors for ominous prognosis, and Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation (APACHE) II score for disease severity on presentation.

The mortality rate among the HBO-treated patients was 36%, as opposed to 25% in the non-HBO group; the mean number of surgical débridements required per patient was significantly higher in the HBO group (3.3 compared with 1.5 in the non-HBO-treated patients); and although the average length of hospitalization for survivors was shorter for the HBO group, the difference between the groups did not reach statistical significance.

The report states that HBO has been recommended as adjuvant therapy for necrotizing fasciitis, improving patient mortality and outcome, but that the beneficial effect of HBO for necrotizing fasciitis remains controversial.

Because the evidence comes from a retrospective evaluation of treatment outcome rather than a controlled prospective trial, it cannot establish that adding HBO to surgery and antibiotics improves clinical outcomes in necrotizing fasciitis; on the basis of these comparative outcomes, the source does not establish necrotizing fasciitis as an indication for HBO as adjuvant therapy.

Continuous intravenous infusion of low-concentration epinephrine did not impair uterine blood flow in near-term pregnant ewes: in 10 gravid ewes with maternal and fetal vascular catheters and a maternal electromagnetic uterine artery flow probe, infusion of saline, 0.125% bupivacaine, 0.125% bupivacaine with 1:200,000 epinephrine, 0.125% bupivacaine with 1:400,000 epinephrine, and 0.125% bupivacaine with 1:800,000 epinephrine into the maternal superior vena cava had no effect on any measured hemodynamic variable.

The infusions were given at 10 mL/h for 30 minutes and then at 20 mL/h for an additional 30 minutes, and throughout all infusions the investigators measured maternal heart rate, systemic and pulmonary blood pressures, uterine blood flow, cardiac output, and acid-base balance, as well as fetal heart rate, blood pressure, and acid-base balance.

In contrast to the infusions, a bolus intravenous dose of epinephrine 15 micrograms in the same animals decreased uterine blood flow to 68 +/- 14% of baseline (mean +/- SD), indicating that the reduction in uterine blood flow followed bolus epinephrine rather than continuous low-concentration infusion.

Yes — among cancer patients on Medicaid, greater travel burden was associated with later stage at diagnosis and longer time-to-treatment, based on regression models of stage at diagnosis and days between diagnosis and surgery (PMID:22236315).

Driving distances and driving times from patient residence to primary care provider were calculated with MapQuest.com for 3,917 breast, colorectal (CRC) and lung cancer Medicaid patients in Washington State from 1997 to 2003.
Later stage at diagnosis for breast cancer Medicaid patients was associated with travel burden, with an odds ratio of 1.488 per 100 driving miles (P =.037) and 1.270 per driving hour (P =.016).
Time-to-treatment after diagnosis of colorectal cancer was also associated with travel burden, at 14.57 days per 100 driving miles (P =.002) and 5.86 days per driving hour (P =.018).

Because the reported figures come from fitted regression models of an observational Medicaid cohort, they describe associations between travel burden and stage at diagnosis or time-to-treatment and do not establish that reducing travel distance would itself change these outcomes.

Among cervical cancer patients evaluated for a relationship between outcomes and distance from the Comprehensive Cancer Center (CCC), 390 patients living a median distance of 58.1 miles (range 1.2–571 miles) from the CCC were identified, and patients were divided into quartiles as well as two strata of <100 and ≥100 miles for comparison.
Progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) favored patients living closer to the center, with a lower median OS for patients living ≥100 miles (65.4 vs.

Cox proportional hazard modeling noted that advanced stage was predictive of inferior PFS and OS, while other clinical covariates including age, BMI, race, smoking status and histology had a variable impact on outcomes, and distance >100 miles was associated with a higher risk of death (hazard ratio [HR] = 1.68, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.11–2.54).

The evidence supports that 30-day data are largely enough for measuring hospital mortality rates: in a comparison of 30-day and 180-day postadmission hospital mortality, the 30-day data discriminated the top and bottom fifths of the 180-day data extremely well, especially for acute myocardial infarction (AMI) outcomes.

The analysis used hospital-level public use files of actual and predicted mortality at 30 and 180 days to construct residual mortality measures for each hospital, then ranked hospitals and used receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves to compare 0-30, 31-180, and 0-180-day postadmission mortality.

Ranking hospitals using the 30-day data produced a broad range of hospital performance, with some hospitals having much lower than predicted 30-day mortality rates and others much higher than predicted mortality rates.

Mortality data from the 31-180 day postadmission period corroborated the 0-30 day postadmission data, and hospital performance on one condition was related to performance on the other conditions, though that correlation was much weaker in the 31-180-day interval than in the 0-30-day period.

The comparison covered all Medicare patients and three categories of cardiac care (coronary artery bypass graft surgery, acute myocardial infarction, and congestive heart failure), using Health Care Financing Administration (HCFA) hospital mortality data for FY 1989.

In a single reported series of penile squamous cell carcinoma, ultrasound as part of the staging procedure identified all tumors as hypoechoic lesions and clearly demonstrated absence or presence of invasion into the tunica albuginea of the corpus cavernosum, but it could not differentiate invasion of subepithelial tissue from invasion into the corpus spongiosum in the glans and measured maximum tumor thickness accurately in only 7 of 16 examinations, so the cited evidence supports a partial rather than a complete addition to clinical staging.

From 1988 until 1992, all patients referred for primary treatment underwent ultrasound assessment with a 7.5 MHz linear array small parts transducer as part of the clinical workup, and the images were reviewed by one radiologist without knowledge of the clinical outcome and compared with histopathologic examination results.
The ultrasound examination covered 16 patients with a primary tumor and 1 patient with recurrent cancer after primary therapy.

Because this evidence comes from a descriptive single-centre series of 17 examinations in which images were compared with histopathology rather than from a comparative study, it does not establish that adding ultrasound to clinical staging changes staging accuracy, treatment decisions or patient outcomes.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: Effect of earlier discharge from Winnipeg hospitals on quality-of-care outcomes.

In a cross-sectional study of 103 non-insulin-dependent diabetic (NIDDM) and 533 nondiabetic white subjects in which ACE genotype was related to components of the insulin-resistance syndrome, the insertion (II) genotype was associated with lower insulin sensitivity among NIDDM subjects, whereas no such association was present in nondiabetic subjects, so support for the insertion allele as a candidate for insulin resistance is limited to the diabetic group and is mixed overall.

NIDDM subjects with the DD genotype had significantly lower levels of specific insulin (DD 38.6, ID 57.1, and II 87.4 pmol.L-1 by ANOVA, P =.011), indicating higher circulating insulin in the II group.

Among non-insulin-treated subjects, those with the DD genotype had increased insulin sensitivity by HOMA % (DD 56.4%, II 29.4%, P =.027) and lower levels of des 31,32 proinsulin (DD 3.3, II 7.6 pmol.L-1, P =.012) compared with II subjects.
In nondiabetic subjects there were no differences in insulin sensitivity, levels of insulin-like molecules, blood pressure, PAI-1, serum lipids, or CHD prevalence between the three ACE genotypes.

Because the genotype groups were compared observationally at a single assessment rather than through an intervention, these associations between the insertion allele and insulin-resistance measures cannot establish that the allele causes insulin resistance or that altering it would change clinical outcomes.
The study aimed to explore expressed needs, both formal and informal, of family caregivers of frail elderly.
The study aimed to evaluate roles of physicians.

Volunteer caregivers who were caring for a family member or friend 60 years or older, who had greatest responsibility for providing physical or emotional support to an elderly person, who saw themselves as caregivers, and who could speak English or French were studied.
Of 118 volunteers, 32 were excluded because they withdrew for personal reasons or because they did not meet study criteria.
An average of 75.4% respondents did not use formal support services.
Just under half of caregivers were dissatisfied with the attention they received from the health care system, and more than one third expressed feelings of stress, depression, guilt, and isolation.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: physician-specific evidence of meeting family caregivers' needs.

The cited evidence indicates that serovar-specific immunity to Neisseria gonorrhoeae does not appear to exist: no significant difference was seen in the prevalence of serovars isolated following a repeat infection compared with those without repeat infections.

The study was designed to determine whether the host immune response to gonorrhoea provides limited serovar-specific protection from reinfection, and it analysed patients with recurrent gonococcal infection with respect to the initial and subsequent serovars isolated.
The analysis was based on 508 episodes of gonorrhoea diagnosed at a city centre genitourinary medicine clinic, including 22 patients with multiple infections, over a 4 year period.
The site of the initial infection did not appear to influence the subsequent serovar isolated.

As an interpretation of the reported design, the conclusion rests on an observed absence of a significant difference in serovar prevalence in a retrospective series that included only 22 patients with multiple infections, so it is an observational finding about reinfection patterns rather than a direct measurement of protective immunity.

Among 794 children with a family history of atopy studied with a historic cohort approach, breastfeeding was related to lower levels of childhood illness both in the first year and in the first three years of life, but the cited evidence does not establish that breastfeeding is 'best' for these children.

In that cohort, breastfed children had fewer episodes of gastroenteritis, lower respiratory tract infections, and digestive tract disorders in the first year of life, and fewer respiratory tract infections and skin infections over the next three years.

In a separate cohort followed from childhood to 18 years, children who were breastfed had a lower risk for lifetime asthma at 7 years; the same study found that a family history of atopy was significantly positively associated with lifetime asthma at 18 years in logistic regression analyses.
The retrieved evidence does not establish the effect of breastfeeding on lifetime asthma specifically among children with a family history of atopy.

In the entire sample, FEF(50) was higher by 130 ml in children breastfed for 4 to 6 months and by 164 ml in those breastfed longer than 6 months, compared with children not breastfed (P = 0.048 and 0.041), with larger effects if the mother had asthma.

FVC and FEV(1) were associated with breastfeeding only in children of mothers with asthma (P for interaction, 0.018 and 0.008): FVC was increased by 123 ml and 164 ml for those breastfed 4 to 6 months or longer than 6 months, respectively (P = 0.177 and 0.040), and FEV(1) was increased by 148 ml and 167 ml, respectively (P = 0.050 and 0.016).
These lung-function results were unchanged after adjustment for respiratory infections in infancy and for asthma and atopy in the child.

The 794-child study used a historic cohort design to compare illness rates between children with a family history of atopy who were and were not breastfed, so the reported associations cannot by themselves establish that breastfeeding is causally superior to alternatives for these children.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: effect of breastfeeding on lifetime asthma specifically among children with a family history of atopy.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: causal proof that breastfeeding is superior to alternatives for children with a family history of atopy.

A slightly elevated risk of diabetes mellitus was found among Swedish art glassworks employees (Mantel-Haenszel odds ratio 1.2, 95% CI 0.82-1.8), and especially in combination with cardiovascular disease (MH-OR 1.4, 95% CI 0.81-2.3), in a case-referent analysis of death records of 5498 individuals in the art glass-producing part of southeastern Sweden, of whom 888 were glass workers.

In that study, cases were persons with a diagnosis of diabetes mellitus recorded as either an underlying or a contributing cause of death, and referents were decedents without any indication of cancer, cardiovascular disease, or diabetes.

According to occupational title, glassblowers, foundry workers and unspecified workers were regarded as potentially exposed to arsenic; for these workers probably exposed to arsenic the M-H odds ratio was 1.4 (95% CI 0.92-2.2), while unspecified glass workers, who probably included persons with high exposure, carried the higher risk (MH-OR 1.8, 95% CI 1.1-2.8).

Because the evidence comes from a case-referent analysis of death records rather than a study with exposure and outcome follow-up, these odds ratios for occupationally defined arsenic exposure cannot establish that arsenic exposure causes diabetes mellitus.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: a causal effect of arsenic exposure on diabetes mellitus.

In a single study of 76 patients with solitary small HCCs up to 3 cm in diameter who underwent hepatectomy and were observed for at least 2 years, patients were divided into 10 with well differentiated (w-d) HCC (Edmondson and Steiner's grade I) and 66 with less differentiated (l-d) HCC (grades I-II, II-III and III).

Disease-free survival did not differ significantly between the well differentiated and less differentiated groups, and an analysis of tumor volume doubling time in recurrent foci suggested that minute cancerous foci had already been present at the time of operation.

Histological analysis showed that w-d HCCs had a lower incidence of fibrous capsule formation than l-d HCCs (P<0.01), while there were no significant differences in the incidence of intrahepatic metastasis or portal vein invasion.

In a resected specimen of w-d HCC, barium sulfate and gelatin were injected into the portal vein and a transparent specimen was made; the transparent specimen showed the portal vein in the tumor to appear intact, but microscopically cancer cell infiltration into the fibrous frame of the portal tract was present.

Because portal-tract infiltration was demonstrable microscopically in a w-d HCC whose portal vein appeared intact, and because disease-free survival did not differ from less differentiated tumors with recurrent foci already seeded at operation, the reported findings do not support treating well differentiated small HCC as clinically early cancer; this is an interpretation of the study's results rather than a directly reported conclusion.

In a prospective evaluation of 55 potential brain-dead heart donors (mean age 38 +/- 11 years) by transesophageal echocardiography before harvesting, fractional area change (FAC) was used to assess left ventricular function; 20 of the 55 donors had an FAC below 50%, and in 18 hearts studied by TEE both in donors and afterwards in recipients, FAC increased significantly from 51 +/- 15% to 57 +/- 11%.

Marginally acceptable donor hearts were suitable for transplantation in this series: transplanted hearts were assessed on the fifth postoperative day, with success defined as the recipient being alive, not retransplanted, free of an assistance device or an epinephrine infusion above 1 mg/h, and having an ejection fraction above 40%; 40 hearts were harvested and 36 were transplanted successfully.
Among the recipients, 9 had a donor FAC below 50% (group H2) and 27 had a donor FAC above 50% (group H1).
Four patients died: 2 from hemorrhage (donor FAC >50%), and 1 each from right and left ventricular dysfunction (donor FAC <50%).
Overall actuarial survival was 86.2% versus 64.6% at 1 and 2 years in groups H1 and H2, respectively (p = NS).

Yes — socioeconomic differences in mortality persisted after retirement in the first Whitehall study of 18,133 male civil servants aged 40-69 screened between 1967 and 1970, though the ability of employment grade to predict mortality declined after retirement (rate ratio 1.86, 95% confidence interval 1.6 to 2.2).

Grade of employment was a strong predictor of mortality before retirement; among men dying at ages 40-64, the lowest employment grade had 3.12 times the mortality of the highest grade (95% confidence interval 2.4 to 4.1).

Car ownership, a non-work-based measure of socioeconomic status, predicted mortality less well than employment grade before retirement, but its ability to predict mortality declined less after retirement.

Using a relative index of inequality sensitive to the distribution among socioeconomic groups, employment grade and car ownership showed independent associations with mortality that were of equal magnitude after retirement.
The absolute difference in death rates between the lowest and highest employment grades increased with age, from 12.9 per 1000 person years at ages 40-64 to 38.3 per 1000 person years at ages 70-89.

No: in the Queensland-based simulation study, extreme types of misclassification of gestational age were required to remove the divergence in median birthweights between Australian Aborigines and whites, indicating that gestational age misclassification does not readily explain the birthweight difference.

The pattern under investigation was that after 34 weeks gestation, summary measures of location for birthweight (such as means and centiles) increase more slowly for Australian Aborigines than for whites, a pattern also observed for blacks in the US.

The study tested whether this reported pattern was due to differential misclassification of gestational age by simulating the potential effect of differential misclassification, using reported gestational age data from the Queensland Perinatal Data Collection and deriving estimates of the true gestational age distributions by applying various plausible types of misclassification to the reported distributions.

Robustness varied by gestational age and centile: at full term the parameters of the birthweight distributions were robust to gestational age misclassification, and at preterm the 10th centiles were robust, whereas the 90th centiles were sensitive to even minor misclassification.

Among the cytologic features tested, nonproliferative breast disease (NPBD) and proliferative breast disease without atypia (PBD) were distinguished by only one feature: a swirling pattern of epithelial cells was the sole cytologic feature found to be significantly different between PBD and NPBD.

That assessment was based on 51 air-dried, Diff-Quik-stained fine-needle aspirates of palpable breast lesions with biopsy-proven diagnoses of NPBD (34 cases) or PBD (17 cases), with smears evaluated for cellularity, size, and architectural arrangement of the epithelial groups, the presence of single epithelial cells and myoepithelial cells, and nuclear characteristics.

A swirling pattern was noted in 13 of 17 PBD cases (76%) and 12 of 34 NPBD cases (35%) (P = 0.008), so the feature was significantly more frequent in PBD but was also present in over a third of NPBD cases, limiting clean cytologic separation of the two groups.

Yes — pediatric housestaff experience did influence test ordering in the neonatal ICU: in a prospective cohort study of 785 infants admitted to one academic Level III neonatal ICU over one academic year (July 1993–June 1994), interns ordered significantly more arterial blood gases per infant than residents after controlling for infant severity of illness, call-night workload and supervision (p =.02), a difference of 0.33 blood gases per infant per call night (3.22 vs.
2.89 arterial blood gases per infant per night).
That 0.33 blood gas per infant increase corresponded to interns ordering 169 more arterial blood gases per call night at that institution.
The same study found no difference between interns and residents in ordering radiographs or electrolytes.

In a pediatric series of 255 esophageal biopsies performed between January 1, 1992, and August 31, 1994, an endoscopic abnormality was observed in children with histological esophagitis and was termed "vertical lines in esophageal mucosa" (VLEM), supporting VLEM as an endoscopic manifestation of esophagitis in children.

The esophageal mucosa appeared normal on 160 endoscopic studies (Group 1) while VLEM were the only mucosal abnormalities in 41 endoscopies (Group 2); histology was normal in 92 of 160 biopsies (57.5%) in Group 1 versus 1 of 41 biopsies (2.4%) in Group 2.

Most Group 2 patients had eosinophilic esophagitis (34 of 41, 83%; specificity 0.85, sensitivity 0.5, p>0.001), and in 31 of those 34 (91.2%) it was of moderate to severe intensity (specificity 0.88, sensitivity 0.73, p<0.001).

The evidence comes from a review of procedure reports, available endoscopic photographs and histology reports rather than a prospective design, so the reported association between VLEM and histological esophagitis cannot by itself establish that VLEM causes esophagitis.

Yes — in a study of 17 astrocytoma surgical specimens (seven from children and 10 from adults) and four normal autopsy brains stained for glial fibrillary acidic protein and von Willebrand factor and examined by confocal microscopy under a modified WHO classification, the endothelial/vascular pattern differed across tumor grades, with higher-grade tumors showing greater vessel density.
Control brain tissues showed a few, widely separated vessels.
Pilocytic astrocytomas (four cases) showed lacy clusters of small-to-medium sized vessels with intact vessel wall integrity.

Diffuse low grade astrocytoma (three cases) showed a staining pattern similar to control tissue, whereas intermediate grade (one case), anaplastic astrocytoma (three cases) and glioblastoma multiforme (six cases) showed increased vessel density with multiple small vessels forming glomeruloid clusters, some with prominent intimal hyperplasia, loss of vessel wall integrity, and numerous vWF-positive single cells/microvessels within the tumor substance.

Because this is a descriptive morphologic evaluation of surgical specimens with small case numbers in several grade categories (for example, one intermediate grade case), it supports an association between vascular pattern and grade rather than establishing the diagnostic accuracy of endothelial patterns for grading.

Retrospective evidence on occupational nuclear power plant radiation and conception is mixed: in a pair-matched analysis of 270 infertile couples and a fertile control population, no difference was noted in the frequency of nuclear power plant exposure between the sterile and fertile groups, yet the male partners who were nuclear power plant workers showed a higher rate of anomalous spermiograms.

In that study, the frequency of men and women exposed to ionizing radiation through work in a nuclear power plant in Greifswald, Germany was compared retrospectively between the 270 infertile couples and the pair-matched fertile controls, and the total cumulative equivalent radiation dose was determined.

The spermiograms of the male partners in both the infertile and fertile groups were compared and correlated with the degree of exposure; the anomalous spermiograms in nuclear power plant workers were temporary, and no correlation was found between the cumulative equivalent radiation dose and abnormal spermiograms.

Because the comparison was a retrospective pair-matched analysis of exposure frequency rather than a prospective or randomized design, it cannot establish that occupational radiation exposure causes the observed differences in conception or semen findings.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: Effect of occupational nuclear power plant radiation on pregnancy outcomes.

Paracervical anaesthesia does not appear to add a clear advantage to second-trimester abortion induction with gemeprost: in a prospective randomised study of 20 women at 16-23 weeks given 1 mg gemeprost vaginally every 6 hours, the median induction-to-abortion interval was 20 hours (range 8-44) in the 10 women receiving only intravenous Pethidin and rectal Butylscopolamine versus 13 hours (range 8-36) in the 10 women who additionally received paracervical anaesthesia, a difference that was not statistically significant.

A median of 3 gemeprost applications were given in both groups, and the intervals from the last prostaglandin application to abortion and from 3 cm cervical dilatation to abortion were slightly, but not significantly, shorter in the paracervical anaesthesia group.

The requirement for Butylscopolamine was higher in the paracervical anaesthesia group (p<0.05), whereas the requirement for Pethidin and the intensity of pain measured by the Huskisson pain scale, especially in the late first stage of labour, did not differ statistically significantly between the two groups; no side effects of paracervical anaesthesia occurred.
The paracervical anaesthesia consisted of 2 x 10 ml 0.5% Bupivacain solution administered at a cervical dilatation of 2-3 cm in the 10 women randomised to that additional treatment.

Because the reported interval and pain outcomes were not statistically significant in this small randomised study of 10 women per group, the data do not establish that paracervical anaesthesia improves the clinical course of gemeprost-induced second-trimester abortion, although the design does not exclude a benefit.

In a case series of eight infants aged 2 to 15 months admitted over a 6-year period, all suffered similar maladies in the bath: on immersion they became pale, hypotonic, still and unreactive, and recovery took a few seconds after withdrawal from the bath and stimulation.

In the same series, an equivalent of aquagenic urticaria was considered as a hypothesis; each infant's family contained members suffering from dermographism, maladies or eruption after exposure to water or sun, all six infants had dermographism, and blood histamine levels increased after a trial bath in the two infants tested; after a 2-7 year follow-up, three out of seven infants continued to suffer from troubles associated with sun or water.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: confirmed diagnosis of water-induced urticaria.
Occult post-traumatic osteochondral injuries of the knee are defined as trauma-related bone and/or cartilage damage that is missed at plain radiography.

The study population comprised 70 retrospectively selected patients (men:women = 7:3; age range 35 +/- 7 years) with a history of acute musculoskeletal trauma, negative conventional radiographs, pain and limited joint movements.

MRI identified three types of occult post-traumatic injuries by morpho-topographic and signal intensity patterns: bone bruises (n = 25), subchondral injuries (n = 33) and osteochondral injuries (n = 35).

A bone bruise was defined as a typical subcortical area of signal loss of various shapes on T1-weighted images and of increased signal intensity on T2-weighted and FIR images, with cortical bone and articular cartilage normal in all such cases.
Osteochondral injuries exhibited associated bone and cartilage damage with the same abnormal MR signal intensity seen in the other occult injury types.
At arthroscopy, 45 osteochondral and 19 chondral injuries were depicted in this cohort of occult post-traumatic knee injuries.
All 70 patients were submitted to conventional radiography, arthroscopy and MRI, the MRI performed with 0.5 T units using T1-weighted SE, T2-weighted GE and FIR sequences with fat suppression.
In the same cohort MRI identified 25 bone bruises, 33 subchondral injuries and 35 osteochondral injuries, whereas arthroscopy depicted 45 osteochondral and 19 chondral injuries.

Although the study set out to investigate the actual role of MRI versus arthroscopy in detecting and characterizing occult bone and/or cartilage injuries after knee trauma, the retrieved report provides no direct comparative diagnostic accuracy or concordance measure, and no stated conclusion that MRI can substitute for diagnostic arthroscopy.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: direct comparative diagnostic accuracy, concordance, or a stated conclusion that MRI can substitute for diagnostic arthroscopy.

No: in a prospective study of 19 adults with biopsy-confirmed malignant brain tumors assessed with a neuropsychological test battery prior to aggressive chemotherapy, the SCL 90-R Obsessive-Compulsive subscale was not related to objective measures of attention, verbal memory, or age.

The same SCL 90-R Obsessive-Compulsive subscale was related significantly to symptoms of depression (r =.81, P<.005), anxiety (r =.66, P<.005), and subjective complaints of memory problems (r =.75, P<.005), indicating it tracked self-reported distress and subjective memory complaints rather than objective cognitive performance in this sample.

Multivariate analyses indicated that reported symptoms of depression contributed 66% of the variance in predicting SCL 90-R Obsessive-Compulsive scores, whereas symptoms of anxiety contributed an additional 6% (P<.0001).

Yes — in an observational study comparing two general hospitals serving the population of Finnmark county in north Norway, based on 35,435 admissions from five years of routine recordings, the total rate of admission to general hospitals was 26% lower for men and 28% lower for women in peripheral municipalities with a GP hospital than in central municipalities without this kind of institution.

In the same comparison, the corresponding differences for occupied bed days in general hospitals were 38% lower for men and 52% lower for women in peripheral municipalities with a GP hospital relative to central municipalities without one.

The differences were most pronounced for patients with respiratory diseases, cardiac failure and cancer, who are primarily or intermediately treated or cared for in GP hospitals, and for patients with stroke and fractures, who are regularly transferred from general hospitals to GP hospitals for longer-term follow-up care.

Because this was an observational comparison of populations with and without access to GP hospitals rather than a randomised or otherwise controlled intervention, it documents lower general hospital admission and occupied-bed-day rates in areas with GP hospitals but cannot by itself establish that the GP hospitals caused that reduction.
The three midwife obstetric units (MOUs) in a health district of Mpumalanga were included; two MOUs enrolled in the Perinatal Education Programme (PEP) and the third did not.

A 'before-and-after' study design was used to assess any changes in practice, and to monitor whether any changes occurred in the district during the time of the study; data were also collected at the third MOU.
Eight of the 13 midwives at the two MOUs completed the PEP and all demonstrated an improvement in knowledge.
Case notes of 303 patients from the various clinics were studied.
There was no change in the referral patterns of any of the clinics during the study period.
The obstetric history was well documented, but in no group was there a satisfactory response to a detected problem; appropriate action was taken in between 0% and 12% of cases.
Syphilis testing was performed in 56-82% of cases, with no difference between the groups.
The haemoglobin level was measured in only 4-15% of patients, with no difference before or after completion of the PEP.
Where a problem in uterine growth was detected, an appropriate response occurred in 0-8% of patients and no difference before or after completion of the PEP was ascertained.

In all groups, estimation of fetal weight and pelvimetry were seldom performed, the urine and fetal heart rate documentation were moderately well done and the blood pressure monitoring, assessment of head above pelvis, monitoring of contractions and plotting of cervical dilatation were usually performed.
No differences before or after the PEP were detected.
Where problems were detected, appropriate actions taken during labour improved, but not significantly.

Overall, the evidence indicates that successful completion of the PEP did not result in improved obstetric practice: despite improved knowledge among midwives who completed the PEP, no differences before or after the PEP were detected in the assessed practices.

Because the study used a 'before-and-after' design, with two MOUs enrolled in the PEP and the third not enrolled, the observed associations do not establish that completion of the PEP itself caused any change in obstetric practice.

Among 149,177 elderly Medicare beneficiaries with acute myocardial infarction in 1994 or 1995 in the Cooperative Cardiovascular Project, admission to a hospital ranked at the top in cardiology by "America's Best Hospitals" was associated with lower adjusted 30-day mortality than admission to the other hospitals (odds ratio, 0.87; 95 percent confidence interval, 0.76 to 1.00; P=0.05), a difference that was of borderline statistical significance because the confidence interval reached 1.00, and the comparison is an observational association rather than evidence that admission to a ranked hospital causes better survival.
The survival difference reflected differences in use of recommended therapies: among patients without contraindications, top-ranked hospitals had higher rates of aspirin use (96.2 percent vs.
88.6 percent for similarly equipped hospitals and 83.4 percent for non-similarly equipped hospitals; P<0.01) and beta-blocker use (75.0 percent vs.
61.8 percent and 58.7 percent; P<0.01), but lower rates of reperfusion therapy (61.0 percent vs.

70.7 percent and 65.6 percent; P=0.03); after adjustment for factors including aspirin and beta-blocker use, the survival advantage of top-ranked hospitals was less strong and no longer significant (odds ratio, 0.94; 95 percent confidence interval, 0.82 to 1.08; P=0.38).

Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)-infected patients have generally been excluded from transplantation, and the source states that recent advances in the management and prognosis of these patients suggest that this policy should be reevaluated.

To explore the current views of U.S. transplant centers toward transplanting asymptomatic HIV-infected patients with end-stage renal disease, a written survey was mailed to the directors of transplantation at all 248 renal transplant centers in the United States.

The vast majority of responding centers would not transplant a kidney from a cadaveric donor (88%) or a living donor (91%) into an asymptomatic HIV-infected patient who is otherwise a good candidate for transplantation.
Among the few centers that would consider transplanting an HIV-infected patient, not a single center had performed such a transplant in the year prior to the survey.
Most centers fear that transplantation in the face of HIV infection would be harmful to the individual, and some believe that it would be a waste of precious organs.

The cited source is a survey of transplant-center directors' views and reported practices concerning asymptomatic HIV-infected patients with end-stage renal disease; because it reports attitudes and center policies rather than clinical outcomes, it does not establish whether transplantation versus exclusion changes patient or graft outcomes.
The retrieved evidence does not establish: Comparative clinical outcomes of transplantation versus exclusion.
A new modification of percutaneous needle suspension that fixes the suture at the pubic bone with a bone anchor system was evaluated in female stress urinary incontinence.

From March 1996, 37 patients with stress urinary incontinence of more than 2 years' duration were treated with the bone anchor system; on each side the suture was attached to the pubocervical fascia and the vaginal wall via a broad 'Z'-stitch.

Preoperative urodynamic investigation in all patients confirmed stress incontinence and excluded detrusor instability, and outcome was assessed by clinical follow-up investigation or a standardized questionnaire over a mean follow-up of 11 months (range 6-18).
In the 37 patients, the procedure was successful in 25 (68%), with 16 (43%) completely dry and nine (24%) significantly improved.

Complications included removal of the bone anchor and suture in two patients (unilateral bacterial infection in one, bilateral soft tissue granuloma in the other), dislocation of one bone anchor in a third patient, new urodynamically documented detrusor instability in two treatment failures, and minor complications of prolonged wound pain in 10 (26%) and transient urinary retention or residual urine in 12 (32%).
The retrieved evidence does not establish: comparative improvement in outcome versus percutaneous bladder neck suspension without bone anchor fixation.
